O Lord, I have no people to carry it; please command them to carry it), is the 20th Thiruppathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattaragam. This Thiruppathigam was sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, praying for people to carry this paddy to Thiruvarur so that Paravaiyar would not suffer. In the first verse, he says, "Aal Ilai Emperumaan Avai Attiththara Paniye" (O Lord, I have no people to carry it; please command them to carry it). In the sixth verse, he says, "Paravai Pasi Varuttham Athu Neeyum Arithiyanre" (Is not Paravai's hunger and suffering known to you?). In the eighth verse, he says, "Paravai Val Vaaduginraal" (Paravai is suffering). In the tenth verse, he says, "Nellida Aatkal Vendi" (Praying for people to carry the paddy). Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has composed this Thiruppathigam. Now, the twenty-first verse: "Pagal Pozhuthu Kazhinthu Adhanpin Paravai Manaiyalavu Andri Mika Perugum Nel Ulakil Vilangiya Aaroor Niraiya Pugappeythu Tharuvana Nam Boothangal Ena Visumbil Nigappu Ariyathu Oru Vaakku Nigazhnthathu Ninmalan Arulaal." As soon as Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang this Thiruppathigam, by the grace of Lord Shiva, an ethereal voice arose in the sky. After the day had passed, the voice said that not only would the paddy, which was greatly abundant, fill Paravaiyar's house, but it would also fill Thiruvarur, which is renowned in the world, and our Bhoothaganas (celestial attendants) would bring and add it. An ethereal voice, incomparable, arose in the sky. The actions of the Shivaganas (attendants of Shiva) are invisible to human eyes. Therefore, the situation was that the entire paddy mountain would be transferred from Kundaiyur to Thiruvarur within ten Nazhigai (a unit of time). The divine voice appeared, saying that the Shivabhootha Ganas would do it after the day had passed. The ethereal voice proclaimed that this entire paddy mountain could not be stored in Paravaiyar's mansion alone; it would be stored throughout Thiruvarur. The voice said, "Our Shivaganas are the Bhoothas with a deep voice." We have contemplated the glories of the Shivabhootha Ganas at the beginning of the Periya Puranam. We have seen in the sixteenth verse, "Needu Devar Nilaigalum Vendidi Naadum Aim Perum Boothamum Naattuva" (If the positions of the long-lived gods are desired, the five great elements will also be created). Now, the twenty-second verse: "Thampiraan Arul Potri Tharainmisai Vizhunthu Ezunthe Omparaal Unarvu Ariya Thiruppaatham Thozhuthu Eththi Sempon Ner Sadaiyaarai Pirappathiyum Thozhuthu Poy Nambar Aaroor Anaiththaar Naavalanar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the grace of Lord Shiva, falls to the ground, rises, and worships the sacred feet that are incomprehensible even to the gods. He praises and worships the Lord of Thirukozhili. He then visits other holy places like Thiruvalivalam, Thirunellikka, Thirukkarayil, and Thiru Ema Perur, and then returns to Thiruvarur. The twenty-third verse: "Poongoyil Magizhndharulum Puraathanarai Pokku Irai Neengaatha Perumagizhchiyudan Eththi Puramponthu Paangaanaar Pudaisoozhndhu Potrisaikka Paravaiyaar Oongu Thiru Maaligaiyin Ul Anainthaar Aaroorar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who resides in the Poongoyil (flower temple) in Thiruvarur, where the ancient Lord who took refuge in an anthill resides, praises the Lord with unending great joy. Nambi Aaroorar, who returned to Thiruvarur after going to Kundaiyur and singing the Thirukozhili Thiruppathigam, does not go directly to his mansion. He first enters the Poongoyil and worships, and only then goes to his mansion. All Saivites should note this tradition well. The nature of a Jeevanmuktha (liberated soul) who does nothing without His grace is like this. Every time Sundaramoorthy Swamigal comes to Thiruvarur, he demonstrates this to us. Thus, after praising the Lord in the Poongoyil, he comes out, surrounded by his attendants and others who praise him, and then Nambi Aaroorar enters Paravai Nachiyar's glorious mansion. Now, the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth verses are as follows: "Kovai Vaai Paravaiyaar Thaam Magizhumbadi Kuri Meviyavar Thammōdu Mika Inpurru Irunthatharpin Sevin Mel Umaiyōdum Varuvaartham Thiru Arulin Evalinaal Avviravu Boothangal Mikku Ezunthu Kundaiyur Nelmalaiyai Kural Padai Kavarndhu Vandulaang Kuzhal Paravai Maaligaiyai Niraiviththu Andarpiraan Thiruvarur Adanga Nel Malaiyaakki Kandavar Arputham Eythum Kaatchi Pera Amaiththanaal." These two verses are arranged in sequence. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal narrates the events of that day to Paravaiyar, who has lips like the Kovai fruit, making her happy. After that, he enjoys great happiness with her. By the command of Lord Shiva, who comes on the bull with Uma Devi, the Shivabhoothas (celestial attendants) rise that night. The Bhoothaganas take the paddy mountain from Kundaiyur and fill Paravaiyar's mansion, which has hair where bees hum. Then, they turn the entire Thiruvarur, the city of the Lord of the celestials, into a paddy mountain. This scene was arranged so that all who saw it were filled with wonder. The Shivabhootha Ganas first brought the paddy to Paravaiyar's mansion. Only after filling Paravaiyar's mansion to its capacity did they fill the entire Thiruvarur. Therefore, paddy was piled up like mountains in all the streets of Thiruvarur. All who saw that paddy mountain were filled with a sense of wonder. The reason for their wonder was that the paddy was piled up like mountains, and they were filled with a sense of pride that arose from not knowing how this paddy came here, and other such inexplicable wonders. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam.

Sekkizhar Peruman, by divine grace, continues to compose the verses 844, 26, 27, and 28 of Periya Puranam, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. "That night, as dawn broke, the people living in Thiruvarur saw the mountains of paddy and wondered, 'From what world have these paddy mountains come?' They said, 'Nambi has given these to Paravaiyar, whose eyes are like a doe's, for this world to live.' Seeing the insurmountable mountains of paddy, and realizing it was difficult to pass through them, they returned to their homes. They praised Paravaiyar, who is the embodiment of good fortune, saying, 'It is difficult to find a place to move this paddy.'" "Today, all the paddy mountains within the boundary of your houses, take them into your golden mansions," he announced with the drum of victory. We saw that the Shiva Bhuta Ganas (divine attendants of Shiva) filled the whole of Thiruvarur with paddy mountains overnight. As that night ended and dawn broke, the people of Thiruvarur were astonished to see the mountains of paddy piled up there. They wondered, "From what world have these paddy mountains come?" The people said that these paddy mountains were given to Paravaiyar by Nambiyarurar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. When they came out of their houses, they saw paddy mountains piled up all over the streets, leaving no room to go out. So, they went back into their houses and praised Paravaiyar, who is the embodiment of Shiva's good deeds, saying that it was difficult to find a place to move this paddy.

Paravai Nachiyar, who possessed great fame, was very happy to see the paddy given to her by Vanthondar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. In addition, she made an announcement by beating a drum. She made an announcement to the people of Thiruvarur that all the paddy within the boundaries of their houses could be taken into their respective mansions. This highlights the greatness of Paravaiyar, who announced this with a drum to the people of Thiruvarur. This also clarifies that the mistaken notion held by some ignorant people, that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang and received gold and other things for Paravai Nachiyar, is completely wrong. It is because Paravai Nachiyar spoke these sweet words, saying that everyone could take the paddy that was within the boundaries of their respective houses, that Sekkizhar Peruman praises her as "Kovai Vaay Paravaiyar" (Paravaiyar with coral-like lips) and "Kovvai Vaay Paravaiyar" (Paravaiyar with beautiful lips), due to the nature of her words flowing with grace. We must consider that the act performed by Paravaiyar during a time of drought, when people suffered without paddy, was a great act of kindness done at the right time. The 29th verse: "By the announcement made with the drum in the streets, people filled their houses with paddy, built granaries everywhere without any delay, and the city rejoiced. Paravaiyar bowed to Vanthondar, who wore a garland of gems on his chest." We saw that the streets were filled with paddy mountains, making it impossible for people to walk. To remove that situation, a path was made through the paddy mountain for people to walk, and this was announced by beating a drum. Therefore, according to that, people took the paddy that was in front of their houses, filled their houses with it, and also built granaries to store the paddy. The people of the city were happy. They praised Paravaiyar and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, believing them to be the cause of this happiness. Now, the 30th verse: "Nambiyarurar, in Thiruvarur, on the days he desired to speak, praised the abundant honey that resided in the anthill, the flourishing deity, with great devotion, drinking it with his consciousness, to the astonishment of both earthly and heavenly beings." In Thiruvarur, the Lord Shiva, who is the God of gods, is known as Vanmeekanathar, the honey that resides in the anthill. He is the one who has taken the anthill as his abode.

This verse praises the Lord who resides in the anthill, Vanmeekanathar, as abundant honey. The Lord is called honey because honey is not only sweet but also beneficial to the body. Similarly, the Lord is the one who brings joy to the soul, sweetening it with bliss. Therefore, He is abundant honey. The Thiruvachagam praises the Lord as "the honey that resides in the pot in Idaimaruthu." In many other places, the Thirumurai praises the Lord as honey. Just as one should drink honey, one should experience the Lord, who is honey, with one's consciousness. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with great devotion, bowed and drank with his consciousness the abundant honey that resided as the Lord of the anthill, worshipping Him daily. The Devas (celestial beings) have gathered in Thiruvarur, sitting in the Devasiriya Mandapam, to worship Thyagesar and receive blessings. The people of this world are also gathered there. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with devotion, bows and praises Thyagesa Peruman, who is worshipped by both earthly and heavenly beings. At this time, Kotpuli Nayanar arrives in Thiruvarur to have a darshan (vision) of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 31st verse: "Kotpuliyar, of great fame, requested that the renowned Arurar come to his city. He bowed at his feet, and the steadfast Vanthondar agreed. Then, he, of praised character, returned to his city." Kotpuli Nayanar is one of the 63 Nayanmars. We will see the Puranam of Kotpuli Nayanar in a later section of Periya Puranam.

Such a Kotpuli Nayanar was of great fame. He came to Thiruvarur, worshipped Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and requested Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to visit his city, Thirunattiyathankudi. He fell at the feet of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, explained all his shortcomings, and expressed his wish. He considered it a shortcoming that Nambiyarurar had not yet visited his city, and he expressed that wish, remaining prostrate at the feet of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Kotpuli Nayanar, who possessed good character, returned to his sacred city, Thirunattiyathankudi. Now, Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing the history of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's visit to Thirunattiyathankudi. The 32nd and 33rd verses are as follows: "The Lord of Thiruvarur, who rules alone, guarded by the Devas and crowded by the devotees, bowed at his feet. Nambiyarurar, having received his grace, desired to worship and sing of the Lord with the Goddess as half, in other sacred places. He went to many places that are difficult for Brahma and Vishnu to comprehend, and worshipped them. Kotpuliyar, of great fame, adorned his Natthiyathankudi in a fitting manner. He also came forward, worshipped him sweetly, and brought him into his beautiful gem-studded mansion with great affection." The Thiruvarur temple is a temple where Devas wait. The Devas wait outside the temple, awaiting the command of Thirunandhidevar to enter the temple. But the devotees, having received divine grace, are allowed to enter without any hindrance, pushing aside these Devas. Although this applies to all sacred places, it is a special characteristic of Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the Lord of Thirunavalur, bowed at the feet of the Lord who resides in the anthill, who guards and rules alone in such a Thiruvarur. He received permission from the Lord of the anthill and went to Thirunattiyathankudi, the city of Kotpuli Nayanar, worshipping many other sacred places of Lord Shiva. On the way from Thiruvarur to Thirunattiyathankudi, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visited and had darshan of places like Thiruvalamar, Thiruyemaperur, Mavoor, and others that were in between and nearby, and then reached Thirunattiyathankudi. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reached Thirunattiyathankudi, Kotpuli Nayanar had decorated the entire city in a grand manner. He welcomed Sundaramoorthy Swamigal with great joy, bowed and worshipped him, and brought Nambi into his beautiful gem-studded mansion. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also entered the sacred home of Kotpuli Nayanar. Now, the three verses, 34, 35, and 36, are arranged in sequence. In these verses, Sekkizhar Peruman sings how Kotpuli Nayanar welcomed, served, and worshipped Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Those verses are as follows: "He seated him on a golden throne, washed his lotus-like feet with pure water, and sprinkled that pure water, which had touched his feet, all over his radiant mansion, filling his heart with joy. He performed all the prescribed worships naturally. He offered a unique blend of fragrant sandalwood paste made with cool flower dew, fragrant agarwood paste, musk paste, fragrant civet oil, pure green camphor, and betel nut, all presented in countless gem-studded vessels. He brought various types of beautiful garlands and many unparalleled gem-studded ornaments. He arranged countless types of garments in order, bowed before him, and offered boundless worship to the devotee of the Lord who wears the Ganga." These verses are composed. Kotpuli Nayanar, having brought Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to his sacred home, first seated Nambi on a golden throne inlaid with pure gems. He then washed Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's feet, which were like red lotus flowers, with pure water. He sprinkled that holy water, which had touched Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's feet, over himself and then over the entire mansion, making it radiant. Kotpuli Nayanar naturally performed all the prescribed worships with great devotion. He offered a unique blend of fragrant sandalwood paste made with beautiful, cool flower dew, fragrant agarwood paste, musk paste, fragrant civet oil, and camphor. He brought all these items, including betel nut, in countless beautiful plates and vessels, each in its own separate container. He brought various types of garlands for decoration.

He also brought many unparalleled gem-studded ornaments. He systematically arranged countless types of garments. Having arranged all these, he stood before him, bowed, and made the devotee of Lord Shiva, who wears the Ganga, accept the boundless worship. In this verse, "Poonthan Panineer" refers to cool dew collected from flowers. "Maan Madham" refers to musk. "Pugai" refers to fragrant items that produce smoke. "Naavi" refers to civet. "Adaikkai Amudhu" refers to betel nut. In ancient inscriptions, betel nut was referred to as "Adaikkai Amudhu." He brought all these in various plates and vessels, separately, and arranged them before the Lord. "Maarillatha Mani Thiru Aabharana Varkkam" refers to ornaments made of gold and gems, which are of various types. These were offered as ornaments to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. "Parivattam" here refers to garments like upper garments. It is our tradition to refer to garments offered to the Lord and devotees as "Parivattam." He arranged all these systematically and performed the puja to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, making him accept the puja. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman, by divine grace, continues to sing the Periya Puranam, Part 845, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Kotpuli Nayanar worships Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having brought him to his sacred mansion. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about this. The 37th verse: "Kotpuliyar, the commander, who was entitled to the grace of the righteous king, with friendship, made our Lord, the king of Thirunavalur, partake of sacred food in his house, worshipped him, and then, like a surging ocean, showed great love and praised him." Kotpuli Nayanar belonged to a lineage that served as commanders for the Chola kings. The "righteous king" refers to the Chola king. Kotpuli Nayanar was entitled to the grace of such a Chola king, having inherited the right to be a commander through generations. It was customary in those days for the king to choose commanders from his family. Such a Kotpuli Nayanar, with friendly affection, made our Paramacharyar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the king of Thirunavalur, partake of sacred food in his palace and stood worshipping him. Our Lord, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, is our Paramacharyar of the Saiva religion. He is also the king of the city of Thirunavalur. Kotpuliyar is a commander. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman, with divine poetic grace, composes this verse, stating that Kotpuli Nayanar, the commander, worshipped Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who is our Lord and the king of Thirunavalur.

Having offered the sacred food, he praised Sundaramoorthy Swamigal with immense love, like an ocean. The next verse, the 38th verse: "With that great desire, he brought his two daughters, Singadiyar, whom he had lovingly begotten first, who wore garlands of honeyed flowers, and Vanappakaiyar, who had deer-like eyes, and made them bow at the lotus-like feet of Vanthondar, and he too bowed and spoke." Kotpuli Nayanar had two daughters. The first daughter was named Singadiyar, and the second was named Vanappakaiyar. He brought these two ladies, his daughters, Singadiyar, whom he had lovingly begotten first, and Vanappakaiyar, who had appeared after her, and made them bow at the lotus-like feet of Vanthondar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and he too bowed and spoke. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Singadiyar as "Thenaar Kothai Singadiyar" (Singadiyar who wears garlands of honeyed flowers) and Vanappakaiyar as "Maanar Nokkin Vanappakaiyar" (Vanappakaiyar with deer-like eyes). "Singadiyar who wears garlands adorned with honey" and "Vanappakaiyar with deer-like, startled eyes, like a goddess of wealth" are the meanings. Sekkizhar Peruman describes them in terms of their physical beauty and their inner grace. Both these meanings can be applied to both of them. Since they were women, they would naturally be shy and would remain inside, not coming before Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Therefore, Kotpuli Nayanar brought these two daughters himself and made them bow at the feet of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and he too bowed. Now, the 39th verse: "He said, 'These are my children, your servants. Please accept them as your own, and grant them the grace to worship your fragrant lotus feet and be saved.' Paravaiyar's husband accepted them as his own pure children, as if they were his own daughters." Kotpuli Nayanar bowed and made a request to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. "These two are my children. Please accept them as your servants, and grant them the grace to worship your fragrant lotus feet and be saved." This means that he requested Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to marry them and accept them as his own. Kotpuli Nayanar made this request to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's feet because he wanted his two daughters to always worship Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's feet. Kotpuli Nayanar made this request for two reasons: that his daughters should be accepted as servants and that they should worship Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's feet. Hearing this, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal blessed them. Sekkizhar Peruman states in the verse, "He accepted them as his own pure children, as if they were his own daughters." As soon as Kotpuli Nayanar made the request, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal accepted them, saying, "These two are my pure children." He accepted them as if they were his own daughters. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as "Thodisér Thalirkaai Ivar" (these with tender hands adorned with bangles). "Thodi" refers to an ornament worn on the hand, a type of bangle. "Thalir" refers to a tender shoot, like a deer's tender shoot. The verse describes them as pure children with hands like tender shoots adorned with bangles. This description indicates that these two women possessed both natural beauty and cultivated grace. Furthermore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal accepts them as "pure children." "Pure" here means "children of good character," as stated in the Thirukkural, "If one begets children who are free from evil in seven births and whose character is blameless." He accepted both these women as if they were his own children. Although Kotpuli Nayanar intended to give them in marriage, the gift is complete only if the recipient accepts it. However, the recipient here accepts them not as wives but as daughters. The Lord states that he accepted them exactly as Kotpuli Nayanar had intended when he made the request. The verse says, "He accepted them as his own pure children, as if they were his own daughters." Kotpuli Nayanar requested him to marry them, but the verse says that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal accepted them as daughters, exactly as Kotpuli Nayanar wished. This is because the two reasons Kotpuli Nayanar had in mind for marriage were that his daughters should serve Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and that they should always worship his holy feet. These two reasons are fulfilled even if they are accepted as daughters. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who accepted them in this manner, was the husband of Paravaiyar. He had already become the husband of Paravaiyar. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman has composed this verse in such a way as to imply that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was not in a position to accept this request according to Kotpuli Nayanar's intention. Now, the 40th verse: "He kept the women with braided hair on his lap, and with overflowing love for his daughters, he embraced them, kissed their foreheads with tears falling, gave them whatever they desired, and then Nambi, Thambiran Thozhar, went to the Lord's temple." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal kept the women with braided hair on his lap. He accepted them as daughters and placed them on his lap. With great love for his daughters, he embraced them, kissed their foreheads with tears falling, and blessed them. His heart melted, and tears of love flowed, falling on their foreheads as he kissed them. He also gave them whatever they desired and blessed them. Then, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal went to the temple of Lord Shiva in Thirunattiyathankudi. The 41st and 42nd verses are as follows: "He bowed at the sacred gopuram (temple tower) of the Lord, who raises the victorious white bull, and with a focused mind and folded hands, he entered, bowed, and sang a Thiruppathigam (hymn), praising Kotpuliyar, who was worthy of the Lord's grace. In that Thirukkadaikkappu (concluding verse), he mentioned Singadiyar, and thinking of himself as her father, he named himself Singadiyappan, and sang with great joy, receiving abundant grace." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bowed at the sacred gopuram of Lord Shiva, the pure one, who raises the victorious white bull on his flag. He entered the temple with a focused mind and folded hands, bowed, and sang a Thiruppathigam. This Thiruppathigam begins with "Poonan." It is a Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thirunattiyathankudi. Thirunattiyathankudi is near Thiruvarur. The Lord is Manikka Vannar, Rathnapurishwarar, Karinalleshwarar, Natthiyathu Nambi. The Goddess is Mangalambigai. The sacred waters are Surya Theertham and Kari Theertham.

In the temple history, it is said that when brothers had to divide their inheritance, they could not agree on the valuation and division of the gems. They appealed to the Lord, and the Lord came as a gem merchant and divided them. Hence, He is known as Rathnapurishwarar. The temple history describes the divine event of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's visit here. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was staying at Kotpuli Nayanar's house, he went to worship at the Thirunattiyathankudi temple. He was surprised not to find the Lord and Goddess there. He asked Ganesha, who, without speaking, pointed towards the northeast. When Sundarar went in that direction, he saw the Lord and Goddess in the field, working as a farmer and his wife, planting paddy. Seeing this, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang, "Enough of planting today, we can plant the rest tomorrow. The mud is still there. Enough of planting, come out, Nambi of Natthiyathankudi." Hearing this, the Lord and Goddess disappeared from there and entered the temple. When Sundarar followed them into the temple, a snake blocked the entrance. Then, he sang the Thiruppathigam starting with "Poonan Aavadhor" and had darshan. This is how the temple history describes Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's singing of the Thiruppathigam. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is the 15th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It begins with "Poonan Aavadhor Aravu" and is set to the tune of Thakkaragam. "I am not afraid of seeing a snake that is an ornament, nor do I despise seeing the dance in the cremation ground. Even if I am not born, I will realize your greatness. Even if I do not see you, I will see you in my mind. Even if you do not think of me, I will think of you. I will not stop singing your feet, Nambi of Natthiyathankudi." He begins with this first verse and sings ten verses. In this Thiruppathigam, in the tenth verse, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal concludes by singing, "The Lord of Natthiyathankudi, whose ancient fame is known throughout the land, who defeated the hostile kings in battle, the Lord of Thiruvarur, who is always remembered, sung by Vanthondar, the son of Sadaiyan, the father of Vanappakai, the Lord of Thirunavalur, who is like a fragrant garden." In this Thiruppathigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has highly praised Kotpuli Nayanar. The reason Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang about Kotpuli Nayanar's greatness in the Lord's Thiruppathigam, due to divine grace, is that he was worthy of the Lord's grace. We have seen how Aludaiya Pillaiyar praised Thirunilanakka Nayanar in the Thiruchathamangai Thiruppathigam and Siruthondar Nayanar in the Thiruchenkattankudi Thiruppathigam. We have also seen how Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal praised Appoothiyadigal Nayanar in the Thiruppazhanam Thiruppathigam. Similarly, here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises Kotpuli Nayanar in the Thirunattiyathankudi Thiruppathigam. In addition, in the Thirukkadaikkappu (concluding verse), he inscribes his name as "Singadiyappan," remembering Singadiyar as his own father. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings this, considering Singadi Nachiyar and Vanappagai Nachiyar as his own daughters, even though he is not their biological father. He sings as if he were their biological father. Just as there are ways for children to be related to their father through adoption, fostering, or acceptance, here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, referring to himself as "Singadiyappan," having boldly accepted them as if he were their biological father. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who sang this Thiruppathigam in this temple, which is the 118th temple on the south bank of the Cauvery in the Chola country, continues to visit other temples. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about this. The 43rd verse is as follows: "From there, with a joyful heart, he went to Thiruvalivalam, where the Lord with the red third eye resides, worshipped him, and composed a Tamil garland of verses, each ending with 'I saw him in Valivalam,' and adorned it with music." From Thirunattiyathankudi, having received permission from the Lord, with boundless love and a joyful heart, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal went to Thiruvalivalam, where Lord Shiva, who has a red third eye, resides. There, he worshipped the Lord, who has Uma as half of his body, and composed a Tamil garland of verses, each ending with "I saw him in Valivalam," and adorned it with music. Thiruvalivalam is a temple located on the way from Thirunattiyathankudi to Thiruvarur. We have contemplated the special features of Thiruvalivalam in the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvalivalam is the 67th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It is set to the tune of Thakkési. In the fifth verse of this Thiruppathigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions this in the 44th verse: "Having danced in between, he went to Thiruvarur, the great city, and bowed at the sacred feet of the Lord of the temple." In this, Sekkizhar Peruman states that in the fifth verse of the Thiruppathigam for Thiruvalivalam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with joy, praises and worships the Lord, saying, "You were pleased to hear the sacred verses of Thirugnanasambandha and Thirunavukkarasu, who bring forth goodness." Accordingly, the fifth verse of this Thiruppathigam is as follows: "My servant's heart melted, and you showed me your sacred feet, cutting off my sufferings. You stood, worshipped by the mighty celestials. I saw you in Valivalam, who sang the good songs of Gnanasambandhan and Navinukkarasar." "Nallisai" refers to the Thiruppathigam. The meaning is that the Lord is very pleased and rejoices in the sacred verses of the great saints, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar and Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. We have contemplated these truths very well in their Puranams. It is a great honor that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal highlights and praises them here. We realize that this honor also applies to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's own sacred verses. Having sung thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to Thiruvarur, where the Lord resides. He refers to it as "Mandrur." In reality, the Lord of the dance, Ambazhakoothar, resides in Chidambaram. But here, Thyagesa Peruman resides in Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has sung about him as "the one who dances in the Mandram." Therefore, it is understood here that Thyagaraja and Nataraja are one and the same. In the Thaduthathkondar Puranam, we also remember that when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had a darshan in Thillai, the Lord said, "Come to us in Thiruvarur." Similarly, when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal came to Thiruvarur, the Lord of Thiruvarur gave him the first line for the Thiruthondar Thogai Thiruppathigam, "Adiyen to the devotees of Thillai," thus starting with Thillai. Furthermore, historically, there is a record that Thillai Nataraja Peruman once resided in Thiruvarur. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having visited Thirunattiyathankudi and the temples in between, arrives in Thiruvarur. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman, by divine grace, continues to sing the Periya Puranam, Part 846, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having visited the temples from Thirunattiyathankudi, has a darshan of the Lord who resides in the anthill in Thiruvarur. He worships the Lord, and then resides in Paravai Nachiyar's mansion with great pleasure. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was taken as a servant by the Lord and had attained the path of penance. Therefore, he did not have a specific village or place for himself; he considered the Lord's places as his own. Thus, in Thiruvarur, he considered Paravaiyar's mansion and the temple as his own abode. We see this throughout Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's sacred life.

During those days when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was residing in Thiruvarur, he visited temples like Thiruvalamar, Thirumalumanagai, Thiruchathamangai, Thiruppalliyin Mukkoodal, and others near Thiruvarur. He also had darshan of the Lord of Thiruvarur and resided there. Even though he visited nearby temples every day, he would return to Thiruvarur on the same day and worship Thyagesa Peruman and the Lord who resides in the anthill without fail. During these days, the Thiruppanguni Uthiram festival arrives in Thiruvarur. It was customary for Paravai Nachiyar to provide whatever was needed for the devotees who came to Thiruvarur for this festival, and to give them gold, clothes, and other necessary items every year. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal thought of needing gold to provide these items to the devotees. So, he went to Thiruppugalur to worship the Lord, and the Lord granted him gold there. Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing this sacred history. The 46th verse: "As the Thiruppanguni Uthiram festival in Thiruvarur approached, Nambi thought of obtaining abundant gold for Paravaiyar's charity and for the festival's needs. He went to Thiruppugalur to worship the feet of the Lord there and arrived." This is the 46th verse. As Nambi worshipped the Lord who resides in the anthill and was enjoying himself there, the Thiruppanguni Uthiram festival approached very closely. The Thiruppanguni Uthiram festival in Thiruvarur is very special. It is celebrated for 48 days. During this festival, there are separate celebrations for Ganesha, Subramaniyar, Chandrasekarar, and even Chandesar. On the Panguni Uthiram day, Sri Thyagesa Peruman, as Veethividangar, gives darshan of Rudrapatham and goes on a procession in the great chariot, which is a very special event. During this festival, it was customary for Paravaiyar to give jewels, clothes, and other necessities to the people who came to the festival, and to serve food and other things to the devotees without any shortage. It was also customary for Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to ask the Lord for gold for such expenses. We will see this in the later history of Thirumuthukundram and Thiruppachilachiramam, where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal received gold by asking. Here, the Panguni Uthiram festival is approaching. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asks the Lord for gold to provide for the devotees and pilgrims who come to the festival. Those who do not deeply understand all this speak carelessly, saying that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asked the Lord for gold for Paravaiyar, and the Lord gave it. They speak thus out of ignorance. There are also poets who have sung, "Sundaran will sing for gold," and so on. Therefore, setting aside these words, this world should realize the truth and be saved from offending great people. Charity means giving gold and other things. This is done for everyone who comes to the festival. "Kurai Varuththal" means serving food to devotees, arranging mansions for them to stay, and many other types of hospitality. All these regulations for performing during festivals are great Shiva Punya (meritorious deeds) as stated in the Shivagamas (Saiva scriptures). We have contemplated these in the Puranams of Amarneethi Nayanar and others. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sets out to Thiruppugalur, which is near Thiruvarur, to worship the Lord's feet and ask for gold for Paravai Nachiyar to perform these Shiva Punya. If the question arises as to why Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had to go to Thiruppugalur when he could have asked for gold from his Lord in Thiruvarur itself, the answer is no. What is stated in the Shivagamas? What is stated in the Shiva Puja rules?

It is stated in the Shivagamas that one should not ask for any material desires like gold from one's Atmarttha Nayaka (the Lord worshipped for one's soul's liberation). The Shivagamas prescribe that all puja benefits, karmic benefits, and so on, should be offered to the Lord in His sacred seat. Therefore, Nambiyarurar, who was Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Atmarttha Nayaka, the Lord who resides in the anthill in Thiruvarur, did not ask for gold or other things from Him. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's sacred history states that he asked for and received gold only in Thiruppugalur, Thiruppachilachiramam, and Thirumuthukundram, and used it to provide for the devotees during the Thiruvarur festival. We should also remember here that Paravaiyar spent all the items given by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for the devotees of Shiva in Thiruvarur, just as she had previously announced that everyone could take the paddy from Kundaiyur within the boundaries of their respective houses in Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to Thiruppugalur. The 47th verse is as follows: "He went to Thiruppugalur, worshipped at the beautiful temple courtyard of the Lord of gods, circumambulated, prostrated before the Lord, and then, with love born of ancient tradition, he praised Him, stood up, and sang a Thiruppathigam, expressing his intention." This verse is composed. He went to Thiruppugalur, worshipped at the beautiful temple courtyard of the Lord of gods, circumambulated, prostrated before the Lord, and then, with love born of ancient tradition, he praised Him, stood up, and sang a Thiruppathigam, expressing his intention. We have previously contemplated the special features of Thiruppugalur in the Puranams of Muruga Nayanar and Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman sings all these details in this single verse. Sekkizhar Peruman sings the news of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal leaving Thiruvarur, worshipping in Thiruppugalur, and singing a Thiruppathigam, all in a single verse, to show how quickly he did it. Unfortunately, due to our lack of merit, the Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal at this time is not available to us. Now, the 48th verse: "He worshipped for a short while, leaving his mind there, and then came out and did not go to any nearby monastery. The steadfast Vanthondar, with his discerning love, sat on one side of the beautiful courtyard. Was it the grace of the Lord with the deer in his hand, or was it sleep that came to his lotus-like eyes?" This verse is composed. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stood worshipping before the Lord for a short while. Then, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's mind remained there before the Lord, realizing that he had not received the gold he had intended to ask for. So, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal came out of the temple. He did not go to any nearby monastery; he sat on one side of the temple courtyard. Generally, it was not customary or permissible for great people to stay or sleep in the temple or its courtyard at times other than worship hours, because doing so could lead to physical discomfort and many other improprieties. Therefore, great people would not stay there. So, it is a rule that one should not stay or sleep in the temple courtyard. But here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is staying in the temple courtyard, contrary to the rule. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is well-versed in worship methods and rules, and he excels in conduct. Even so, due to the Lord's grace, sleep came to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's lotus-like eyes. The 49th verse: "As sleep came, Thambiran Thozhar brought many fired clay planks for the temple work, piled them up, and spread his white silk upper garment over them, and lay down to sleep." This verse is composed. As sleep came to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's eyes, Nambiyarurar, Thambiran Thozhar, brought many fired clay planks, which were used for the temple work, piled them up, arranged them like a pillow, spread his white silk upper garment over them, and lay down to sleep. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal as "Thambiran Thozhar" (the Lord's friend). This implies that he was entitled to do such an act. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the bricks, which were kept for temple work, as "Sudumman Palagai" (fired clay planks) in the verse. It is a historical fact that most of the temples in the Chola country in those days were built with bricks. We can still see in old temples that the bricks were very well made, like ingots of pure gold. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as "Palagai Sudumman Palagai" (fired clay planks). Just as wooden planks are planed and smoothed, here, the bricks were also fired and were so beautiful and strong. It is a rule of physical comfort that one should rest one's head on a high pillow. Therefore, since Sekkizhar Peruman mentions "Sudumman Palagai Pal" (many fired clay planks), we can assume that he took about two, three, or four bricks and arranged them like a pillow. He then spread his white silk upper garment, which he wore, over the bricks, which were like a pillow. The bricks were hard, so to make them soft enough to rest his head on, he spread his white silk upper garment over them. The upper garment was made of white silk. We have seen that the Lord of Thiruvarur had previously told Nambi that he should always be in wedding attire. Accordingly, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was always in wedding attire, wearing white silk. In addition, he would arrange his beautiful hair into a topknot and adorn it with a garland of flowers where bees would hum. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal lay down to sleep, making the bricks a pillow for his sacred head, which was adorned with such a garland of flowers where bees would hum, and spreading his white silk upper garment over them. Now, the 50th and 51st verses are as follows: "As the surrounding devotees also slept, the husband of Paravaiyar, whose lotus-like eyes were free from sleep, awoke. By the grace of the Lord with the victorious bull, the fired clay bricks became solid gold, shining brightly. He praised the grace of the Lord of Pugazhur, rejoiced, and rose. With his lotus-bud hands folded over his head, he entered the temple, worshipped the Lord with boundless love and overflowing devotion, and sang a sweet Tamil garland of verses, beginning with 'Praising himself,' set to ancient music."

As the surrounding devotees also slept, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the husband of Paravaiyar, whose two sacred eyes were free from sleep, awoke. He rose, worshipping the Lord. At that time, by the grace of Lord Shiva, the fired clay bricks, which were placed as a pillow, became solid gold, shining brightly. Seeing this, he praised the Lord. He glorified the Lord's grace. The bricks that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had placed as a pillow had turned into solid gold ingots. Among metals, gold is dense and heavy. In those days, it was customary to cast and store gold ingots in the shape of bricks. The bricks had turned into such gold ingots. The devotees who were sleeping with him also awoke. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal rose with joy, folded his two hands like lotus buds over his head, entered the temple, worshipped the Lord with boundless love and overflowing devotion that could not be contained by his intellect, and sang a sweet Tamil garland of verses, beginning with "Praising himself," set to ancient music. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is the 34th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai, for Thiruppugalur. It is set to the tune of Kolli. The first and last verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "O poets, do not sing of the deceitful ones who praise themselves and speak as they please. Sing of my father, the Lord of Pugazhur. In this world, He will give you food and clothing, and your troubles will cease. There is no doubt that you will attain Shiva Loka in the next world." "The Lord of Pugazhur, who resides in the flourishing lotus-filled south, the Lord of Thirunavalur, the son of Sadaiyan, the father of Vanappakai, Vanthondar, who sang these ten verses, those who are skilled in them will enter the supreme world without any doubt." Thiruchitrambalam. This Thiruppathigam was sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to guide the people of this world, praising the Lord for having turned the bricks into gold for him, saying, "O poets, do not sing of the deceitful ones in this world. Sing of my father, the Lord of Pugazhur. In this world, He will give you food and clothing, and your troubles will cease. There is no doubt that you will attain Shiva Loka in the next world." Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 52nd verse: "Having sung the Thiruppathigam, adorned the Thirukkadaikkappu (concluding verse), and praised Him, he came out. Having received the grace of the Lord who gives incomparable joy in this very life, he rose, took the heaps of wealth, and entered Thiruppanaiyur, where the Lord with the moon and the river in his matted hair resides, the Lord with the sacred thread on his chest." This verse is composed. Having sung the Thiruppathigam, adorned the Thirukkadaikkappu, and praised Him, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal came out. Having received the grace of the Lord of Thiruppugalur, who gives incomparable joy in this very life, he rose, took the heaps of gold ingots he had received in Thiruppugalur, and went to Thiruppanaiyur. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman, by divine grace, continues to sing the Periya Puranam, Part 847, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to Thiruppanaiyur and worships. Thiruppanaiyur is a temple located on the way from Thiruppugalur to Thiruvarur. As Sundaramoorthy Swamigal approaches Thiruppanaiyur, just outside the village, at the boundary of Thiruppanaiyur, Lord Shiva grants him a divine vision of His sacred dance. The 53rd verse: "The Lord with the red matted hair granted a vision of His sacred dance at the outskirts of Thiruppanaiyur. With overflowing desire, he prostrated himself there and sang a Thiruppathigam, saying, 'The Lord who is skilled in dancing is indeed beautiful,' for the world to be saved, and then departed with grace." Lord Shiva, who has red matted hair, granted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal a vision of His sacred dance at the boundary of Thiruppanaiyur. At the very spot where the vision was granted, he went forward, prostrated himself on the ground with overflowing desire, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang a Thiruppathigam with the meaning, "The Lord who is skilled in dancing on the stage is indeed beautiful," for the world to attain salvation and live. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruppanaiyur is the 87th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It is set to the tune of Seegamarappann. The first and last verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "The Lord who is skilled in dancing is indeed beautiful, in Thiruppanaiyur, where mansions, towers, and mandapams (halls) flourish, and where humming bees sing in the groves, and where a ear-stud and a dangling ear-ring are worn in one ear, and devotees dance with joy." "The Lord who is skilled in dancing is indeed beautiful, the one whose half is the slender-waisted Goddess, the great ascetic, in Thiruppanaiyur, where groves flourish and where women with cotton-soft feet reside. The Lord of Thirunavalur, Vanappakai's father, Vanthondar, whose sweet words please Him, is indeed beautiful." Thiruchitrambalam. Thiruppanaiyur is the 73rd temple on the south bank of the Cauvery in the Chola country. This temple can be reached by going past Thiruvarur Sannanallur and taking a branch road to Panaiyur. The Lord is Soundareswarar, Azhagiyanathar, Thalavaneswarar. The Goddess is Piriruhanayagi, Periyanayagi. The sacred waters are Parachara Theertham, Amirtha Pushkarani, Thirumagal Theertham. The Sanskrit name for this village is Thalavanam, which is called Panaiyur in Tamil. Upon entering the temple, one sees Thunaithirundha Vinayagar (Ganesha who helped). This Ganesha helped King Karikala Chola. Karikalan was born after losing his father. His relatives intended to kill the child and seize the kingdom. Irumbidar Thalaiyar, a Sangam poet and Karikalan's maternal uncle, who tried to protect him, secretly sent the child Karikalan and his mother to this Panaiyur. The queen came to this village with her son, took refuge in this temple, appealed to this Vinayagar, and was protected for eight years with his help. Therefore, this Vinayagar was named Thunaithirundha Vinayagar (Ganesha who helped) because he helped King Karikala Chola. The pond there is named Santhitha Theertham, commemorating the place where the Lord granted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal a vision of His sacred dance at the boundary. It is a small village with many palm trees and sandy soil. It is an ancient temple. There are two palm trees as sacred trees. These trees have been there for a long time. When these mature trees reach their old age, they do not sprout from seeds like banana trees; instead, other palm saplings spontaneously appear and grow at the base of these two palm trees. In inscriptions, the Lord is referred to as Panaiyadiyappan, the Lord of Panangattu. There are seven Shiva Lingams worshipped by the Saptharishis (seven sages). The Shiva Lingam worshipped by Parachara Muni is Thalavaneswarar, the Moolavar (presiding deity), facing west, with a square Aavudaiyar (pedestal). The Somaskandar idol in this temple has a unique posture, holding a fruit in its left hand. These are the details about Thiruppanaiyur. Now, the 54th and 55th verses: "He went to Thiruppanaiyur, which is rich in glory, worshipped by its inhabitants. The servants carried the countless gold ingots to Paravaiyar's mansion in Thiruvarur, which is adorned with jasmine-like smiles. He also worshipped his Lord, who was enshrined in his heart, and then went to Paravaiyar's mansion. The Lord of Munaippadi, the protector, stayed there happily, worshipping the Lord of Thiruvarur first." These two verses are composed. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to Thiruppanaiyur, which is rich in glory and worshipped by its inhabitants, and then proceeds to Thiruvarur. At that time, the servants carried all the gold ingots, which were like bricks, to Paravaiyar's mansion. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also worshipped his Lord, who was enshrined in his heart, and then went to Paravaiyar's mansion with joy. During the days he stayed happily with Paravai Pirattiyar, he visited many temples near the beautiful, cool Thiruvarur, worshipped them, and with great joy and desire, he first worshipped Thyagesa Peruman, the Lord of gods, who resides in Thiruvarur, and stayed there. He is the leader of the people of Thirumunaippadi country. Now, the 56th verse: "After staying there for many days, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, he went from there to Thirunannilam, where the Lord, the hero with the great Meru mountain as his bow, resides. He entered the temple, worshipped with joy, and sang a Tamil garland of verses beginning with 'Thanniyal Vemaiyanan,' which is characteristic of that place." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stayed in Thiruvarur for many days with pleasure. During that time, by the grace of the Lord, he went from there to Thirunannilam Perungoyil, where the Lord, the hero who has the great Meru mountain as his bow, resides. He went to the temple there, worshipped with joy, and sang a Tamil garland of verses, the Thiruppathigam, beginning with "Thanniyal Vemaiyanan," which is characteristic of that place. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is the 98th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It is set to the tune of Panchamam. The first and last verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

"The Lord, who is cool and hot, begs for alms at every threshold, taking it from women with sweet words. He is the Lord of the cremation ground. The pure Brahmins praise His feet according to tradition. He is the beloved Lord of Thirunannilam Perungoyil." "Those who are skilled in these ten verses sung by Sadaiyan's son, Thiruvaruran, the father of Singi, who loves the Lord of Thirunannilam Perungoyil, built by Ko-Chenganan, who has high white bulls, will enter the supreme world." Thiruchitrambalam. The Thiruppathigam states that Lord Shiva is the beloved Lord of Thirunannilam Perungoyil, built by Ko-Chenganan. This Thirunannilam Perungoyil is the 71st temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is one of the Madakkoils (temples built on a raised platform). It is called Madhuvanam. Nannilam is located on the way from Mayiladuthurai to Thiruvarur. The Lord is Madhuvaneeswarar, Pirakasanathar, Devaranyeswarar. The Goddess is Madhuvaneeswari, Devagantharanayagi. The sacred waters are Brahma Theertham, Soola Theertham. Nannilam is the name of the village, and Perungoyil is the name of the temple. This is the place where the Devas, unable to bear the suffering caused by Vrithrasura, transformed into bees and worshipped. Hence, it is called Madhuvanam. As proof of this, a beehive in the form of a lamp flame still exists inside the temple and is worshipped. This is one of the Madakkoils built by Ko-Chenganan Chola Nayanar. This temple has many names like Madhuvanam, Devaranyam, Sundaravanam, Piruhathpuram. Inside the temple, there are also the Mahadevalingam worshipped by Brahma and the Agastheeswarar Lingam worshipped by Agastya. These are the details about this temple. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having worshipped in Thirunannilam, then proceeds to Thiruvezhimizhalai. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing this history. The 57th verse: "After staying there and singing, the Supreme Lord went to Thiruvezhimizhalai, where the Brahmins, who were exalted by the ancient Vedas, gathered in abundance. The country rejoiced as they laid out a path with a pavadai (carpet), and adorned it with plantain trees, areca nut trees, and beautiful gem-studded toranams (arches)." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes from Thirunannilam to Thiruvezhimizhalai. In Thiruvezhimizhalai, the Brahmins, who were exalted by the ancient Vedic traditions, gathered in abundance. The country rejoiced as they laid out a path with a pavadai, and adorned it with plantain trees, areca nut trees, and beautiful gem-studded toranams, arranged in rows, and welcomed Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The 58th verse: "They came and welcomed Nambi, and he too, with a joyful mind, went to Thiruvezhimizhalai, worshipped the Lord, and bowed before the temple, which had risen with abundant light from the ancient sky. He then praised and worshipped the feet of his Lord, who cuts off worldly bonds." This verse is composed. As they came to welcome Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, he entered the temple. Nambi, with a joyful mind, went to Thiruvezhimizhalai, worshipped the Lord, and bowed before the temple, which had risen with abundant light from the ancient sky. After bowing, he praised and worshipped the feet of his Lord, who cuts off worldly bonds.

The 59th and 60th verses are as follows: "He praised the Lord, who is worshipped by Vishnu, who sleeps on the coiled serpent, and by Brahma, who is on the lotus, the Lord who is beyond all, with overflowing joy. He sang a Tamil garland of verses with profound words, saying, 'You have taken the form of a beggar in Vizhi. Please bless me too.' On those days, he received the divine grace from the Lord of Vizhi, who was able to give coins according to the exchange rate. He then worshipped the feet of the Lord of Thiruvanjiyam, who cuts off the bonds of souls and takes them as His own, and sang the flawless Thiruppathigam beginning with 'Poruvanar,' and then went to Arisilkarai Puthur." These verses are composed. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai. He praises Lord Shiva, the Lord of gods, who is beyond all, worshipped by Vishnu, who sleeps on the coiled serpent, and by Brahma, who is on the lotus, with overflowing joy. He sings a Tamil garland of verses with profound words, saying, "You have taken the form of a beggar in Vizhi. Please bless me too." He resides there. The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvezhimizhalai is the 88th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It is set to the tune of Seegamarappann. The first and last verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "The Lord who grants grace to those who believe, the Brahmin who is the abode of the four Vedas, in Thirumizhalai, where beautiful women adorn themselves, the Lord whom the celestials worship, who resides with the great mountain goddess, you have taken the form of a beggar. Please bless me too." "The Vedic Brahmins, who follow the Vedic law, in Vizhi, where the wide waters flow, you have taken the form of a beggar. Please bless me too. The Lord of Thirunavalur, Vanthondar, who sings sweet Tamil verses, those who are skilled in them will join the Supreme Lord." Thiruchitrambalam. We have contemplated the special features of Thiruvezhimizhalai in the Puranams of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal receives the divine grace from the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai, who was able to give coins according to the exchange rate. This refers to the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman receiving coins with interest and Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal receiving coins without interest. The Thiruppathigam also states, "You gave coins daily, desiring to hear Tamil with music." Having received the divine grace from the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships the feet of the Lord of Thiruvanjiyam, who cuts off the bonds of souls and takes them as His own, and sings the flawless Thiruppathigam beginning with "Poruvanar." The Thiruppathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvanjiyam is the 76th Thiruppathigam of the 7th Thirumurai. It is set to the tune of Piyanthai Kantharam. The first and last verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "The Lord who is like a thread, wearing the sacred thread, with Uma, whose breasts are like tender shoots, does not come to those who are hostile. Our Lord, who is worshipped by the celestials, resides in Thiruvanjiyam. He does not allow karma to afflict His devotees." "In Thiruvanjiyam, where paddy fields shine, the Lord with the lightning-like matted hair, whose feet are worshipped, the Lord of Thirunavalur, who sings sweet Tamil verses, please grant us the joy of singing." Thiruchitrambalam. We have contemplated the temple history of Thiruvanjiyam in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having worshipped in Thiruvanjiyam, then proceeds to Arisilkarai Puthur. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 848, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Before Sundaramoorthy Swamigal arrived at Thiruarisilkari Puthur, he went to Thirunaraiyur Siddheechcharam on the way and praised the Lord there, singing a Thirupathigam (hymn). The 61st verse, "Sezhuneer Naraiyur Nilavu Thiruchittheechcharamum Panindhu Ethi Vizhuneermaiyinil Perum Thondar Virippinodum Ethirkolla Mazhuvodu Ilamaan Karathalaththil Udaiyar Thirupputhur Vanangi Thozhu Neermaiyinil Thuthiththu Ethi Thondar Suzh Uraiyum Naal," is followed by the 62nd verse, which states: "Punithanaar Mun Pugazh Thunaiyaarkku Arulum Thiramum Pottraisaitthu Munivar Potra Ezhuntharuli Moori Vellakkangaiyinil Pani Venthingal Ani Sadaiyaar Pathigal Palavum Panindhu Ponthu Iniya Ninaivil Eythinaar Iraivar Thiruvaavaduthuraiyil." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bows and praises Thiruchittheechcharam, which is situated in Naraiyur, a place of abundant water. Naraiyur is the name of the town, and Siddheechcharam is the name of the temple. The Lord of Thirunaraiyur Siddheechcharam is Siddhanathar, and the Goddess is Azhagammai. We have already discussed the special features of this holy place in the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. This Thirupathigam is the 7th Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thirunaraiyur Siddheechcharam. The Thirupathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Neerum Malarum Nilavum Sadai Mel Oorum Aravum Udaiyaan Idam Am Vaarum Aruvi Mani Pon Kozhiththu Seram Naraiyur Siddheechcharame Poraar Puramai Punithan Amarum Seeraar Naraiyur Siddhi Imai Or Ulaga Eythuvare." Thiruchitrambalam. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bowing and worshipping Thirunaraiyur Siddheechcharam, as stated in Sivagnana Siddhiyar that it is rare to attain the Saiva faith with a humble disposition, proceeds to Thirupputhur, where Lord Shiva, holding a battle-axe and a young deer in His hand, is worshipped. The devotees, with great eagerness, come forward to receive him. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after worshipping Thiruarisilkari Puthur, sings a Thirupathigam in praise of the Lord, who, in the past, bestowed gold coins upon Pugazhthunai Nayanar at this very place. We will learn about Pugazhthunai Nayanar's Puranam in a later section of Periya Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, when he visited this place, included the nature of the Lord who bestowed grace there in his Thirupathigam. This Thirupathigam is the 9th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Indalam. The first and last verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Malaikku Magal Anja Madakariyai Uriththeer Eriththeer Varumuppurangal Silaikkum Kolai Sevuganthu Etroliyeer Silpalikku Ilgal Thorum Selavoliyeer Kalai Kombum Kari Maruppum Idari Kalavam Mayil Peeliym Kaar Agilum Alaikkum Punal Ser Arisil Thenkarai Azhagaar Thirupputhur Azhaga Neere. Kaarur Mazhai Peythu Pozhi Aruvik Kalaiyoda Agil Undittu Iru Karaiyum Porur Punal Ser Arisil Thenkarai Pozhilaar Thirupputhur Punithar Thammai Aarooran Arum Thamizh Ainthinodu Ainthu Azhagaal Uraippaargalum Ketpavargalum Seerur Tharu Devar Ganangalodum Inangi Sivalogam Eythuvare." Thiruchitrambalam. In the 6th verse of this Thirupathigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the grace of the Lord who bestowed gold coins upon Pugazhthunai Nayanar. That verse is as follows: "Agathadimai Seyyum Anthana Than Arisil Punal Kondu Vanthu Aattugindraan Miga Thalarvu Eythi Kudaththaiyum Num Mudimel Vizhththittu Nadunguthalum Vaguththu Avanukku Nitthal Padiyum Varum Endru Oru Kaasinai." We have already discussed the Sthala Puranam (history of the temple) of Thiruarisilkari Puthur in the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bowing and worshipping Arisilkari Puthur, received the Lord's permission and proceeded to visit various holy places such as Thirunageswaram, Thiruvaidaimarudur, Thenkurangaduthurai, and finally arrived at Thiruvaavaduthurai. The 63rd verse states: "Vilangum Thiruvaavaduthuraiyil Meyaar Koyil Pudai Valam Kondu Ulam Kondu Urugum Anbinudan Ulpukku Irainghi Ethuvar Valam Kol Pathigam Maraiyavan Endru Eduththu Valavan Sengannan Thalam Kol Pirappum Sirappiththu Thamizh Solmalai Saaththinaar." Thiruvaavaduthurai is a glorious holy place that causes the world to shine. This glory is attributed to Thirumooladevar Nayanar, who revealed the meaning of Sivagama (Saiva scriptures) in Tamil as Thirumandhiram for the benefit of cows, and also to many other special features of Thiruvaavaduthurai. In such a glorious Thiruvaavaduthurai, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with his heart captivated and melting with love, enters the temple, bows, and praises the Lord. At that time, he offers a garland of Tamil words, a rich Thirupathigam beginning with "Maraiyavan." In this Thirupathigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal describes the story of Kochchengan Chozha Nayanar, who was born as a king in the same place where he had previously served as a spider. Sekkizhar Peruman, in this verse, mentions the beginning of this Thirupathigam as "Maraiyavan Endru Eduththu Sirappiththu Saaththinaar" (began with "Maraiyavan" and praised it). After this, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal will visit Thiruvaavaduthurai again and sing many more Thirupathigams. Those are parts of later stories. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang the Thirupathigam beginning with "Maraiyavan" at this time. The Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvaavaduthurai is the 66th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. Only 5 verses of this Thirupathigam are available to us. The first two verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Maraiyavan Oru Maani Vanthu Adaiya Vaaramay Avan Aaruyir Niruththa Karaikkol Veludai Kaalanai Kaalaal Kadandha Kaaranam Kandu Kandu Adiyen Iraivan Emperumaan Endru Eppothum Ethi Ethi Nindru Anjali Seythu Un Araikkol Sevadiyarku Anbodum Adaindhen Aavaduthurai Aathi Emmane. Therundavaiyidai Noolkondu Silanthi Siththirappanthar Sikkana Iyathra Surunda Senchadaiyaayathu Thannai Chozhan Aakkiya Thodarchi Kandu Adiyen Purandu Vizhnthu Nin Pon Malar Paatham Potri Potri Endru Anbodum Pulambi Arundu En Mel Vinaikku Anji Vanthu Adaindhen Aavaduthurai Aathi Emmane." Thiruchitrambalam. "O Lord of Thiruvaavaduthurai, having seen many of Your acts of grace with my own eyes, I have come to You, fearing my strong karma. Please protect me." This is the gist of this Thirupathigam. We have already discussed the special features of Thiruvaavaduthurai in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Now, the 64th verse states: "Saaththi Angu Vaigu Naal Thayangum Anbarudan Kooda Perthum Irainghi Arul Petru Pennor Paagi Thenkarai Mel Thigazhum Pathigal Pala Paninthu Adainthaar Munaippadi Thalaivar." After offering the garland of Tamil words and staying there for some days, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, accompanied by the shining devotees, again bowed, received the Lord's grace, and proceeded to visit many holy places on the south bank of the Cauvery, where the Lord, with Uma as one half of His body, is pleased to reside. From Thiruvaavaduthurai, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visits various holy places on the south bank of the Cauvery, such as Thirukozhambam, Thiruchathanur, Thenkurangaduthurai, and also the holy places on the south bank of the tributary rivers that branch off from the Cauvery. He then proceeds to Thiruvaidaimarudur to worship the Lord, who is known as Mahalingam and Idai Marudhu Eesar. The verse states: "Mannu Maruthin Amarnthavarai Vanangi Madhurachchon Malargal Panni Punainthu Paninthu Ethi Paravi Ponthu Thondarudan Annathiyil Irunthu Agazhvaar Aranaar Thirunagechcharaththai Munni Pukku Valam Kondu Muthalvar Thiruththaal Vananginaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bows and praises Idai Marudhu Eesar, Mahalingam Peruman, the Lord who resides in the stable Marutha tree, and offers a garland of sweet Tamil words. The Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvaidaimarudur is the 60th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. The first and last verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Kazhuthai Kungumam Thaan Sumanthu Eyththaar Kaippar Paazh Puga Matrathu Pola Pazhuthu Naan Uzhandru Ulthadumaari Padusuzhiththalai Pattanan Enthaay Azhuthu Nee Irunthu En Seythi Manane Angana Arane Enamaattaa Iluthaaiyenukku Or Oyvagai Arulaay Idai Maruthu Urai Enthai Pirane. Araikkum Santhanaththodu Agil Undi Aivanam Sumanthu Aarnthu Iru Paalum Iraikkum Kaveri Thenkarai Thanmel Idai Maruthu Urai Enthai Piranaai Uraikkum Ooran Ozhiththigal Maalai Ullaththaal Ugandhu Eththa Vallaargal Naraippu Mooppodu Nadalaiyum Indri Naathan Sevadi Nannuvar Thaame." Thiruchitrambalam. "O Lord, my Father, who resides in Idai Marudhu, please grant me a way to escape, for I am a fool." This is the crown jewel of the Thirupathigam. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bowing and worshipping Thiruvaidaimarudur, proceeds to Thirunageswaram, enters the temple, circumambulates it, and bows at the feet of the Lord. The 66th verse states: "Perugum Pathigam Pirai Ani Vaazh Nuthalaal Paadi Peyarnthu Nirai Thiruvin Maliyum Sivapuraththu Devar Perumaan Kazhal Vanangi Urugum Sinthaiyudan Ponthai Umaiyor Paagar Thaam Magizhndhu Maruvum Pathigal Pira Paninthu Kalaiyanallur Marungu Adainthaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bowing and worshipping Thirunageswaram, sings a Thirupathigam beginning with "Pirai Ani Vaazh Nuthalaal." The Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thirunageswaram is the 99th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Panchamam. The first and last verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Pirai Ani Vaazh Nuthalaal Umaiyaal Aval Pezhganikka Nirai Ani Nenju Anunga Neelamaal Vidam Undathu Enna Kurai Ani Kullai Mullai Azhaiththu Kulir Maathavi Mel Sirai Ani Vandugal Ser Thirunageschcharaththane. Kongu Anai Vandu Arathra Kuyilum Mayilum Payilum Thenkamizh Poombazhil Suzh Thirunageschcharaththanaai Vangam Mali Kadal Suzh Vayal Naaval Ooran Sonna Pangam Il Paadal Vallaar Avardham Vinai Pattarume." Thiruchitrambalam. "O Lord of Thirunageswaram, who swallowed the poison, I inquire about Your acts of grace, such as when Uma, with a crescent moon on her forehead, was frightened." This Thirupathigam praises the Lord by asking about His acts of grace. Thus, after singing the Thirupathigam and receiving the Lord's permission, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal proceeds to Thiruchivapuram, a holy place filled with complete Shiva wealth, bows at the feet of Lord Shiva, the chief of the Devas, and with a melting heart, proceeds further to visit many holy places where the Lord, with Uma as one half of His body, is pleased to reside. He then arrives at Thirukalaiyanallur. The 67th verse states: "Semmai Maraiyur Thirukalaiyanallur Iraivar Sevadi Keezh Pommai Vanakkam Pera Irainghi Munbu Paravi Thozhuthu Ezhuvaar Kommai Maruvu Kurumbai Mulai Umaiyaal Enum Thirupathigam Meymai Pura Palavum Miga Sirappiththu Isaiyin Vilambinaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, bowing at the feet of the Lord of Thirukalaiyanallur, where righteous Brahmins reside, offers a complete obeisance with his three instruments (mind, speech, and body), praises the Lord, and then sings a Thirupathigam beginning with "Kurumbai Mulai Malarkuzhali." In this Thirupathigam, he beautifully describes many true Puranic stories with musical melody. In this Thirupathigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal includes the stories mentioned in the Maha Puranas, which are called "Meymai Puranam" (true Puranas) by Sekkizhar Peruman. Therefore, all the stories mentioned in the Maha Puranas are true, and they convey a unique truth. Sekkizhar Peruman shows us that they are "Meymai Puranam," meaning they are about the true Lord, Sat. The Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thirukalaiyanallur is the 16th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragam. The first and last verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Kurumbai Malarkuzhali Konda Thavam Kandu Kurippinodum Sendru Aval Than Gunaththinai Nangu Arinthu Virumbum Varam Koduththu Avalai Vettu Aruli Seytha Vinnvar Kon Kan Meviya Oor Vinavil Arumbu Aruge Surumbu Aruva Arupatham Panpaada Ani Mayilgal Nadamaadum Ani Pozhil Suzh Ayalin Karumbu Aruge Karunguvalai Kanvalarum Kazhanik Kamalangal Muga Malarum Kalaiyanallur Kaane. Thanpulun Mathiyum Thaangiya Senchadaiyan Thaamaraiyon Thalai Kalanaa Kaamara Munpaadi Un Bali Kondu Uzhal Paraman Uraiyum Oor Niraineer Ozhugu Punal Arisilin Then Kalaiyanallur Athanaai Nanbudaiya Nan Sadaiyan Isaignani Siruvan Naavalarkon Aarooran Naavin Nayanthu Uraisai Panpayilum Paththum Ivai Paththi Seythu Paadavallavargal Allalodu Paavam Ilargal Thaame." Thiruchitrambalam. Thirukalaiyanallur is the 68th holy place on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is currently known as Sakkottai and is located near Kumbakonam. The word "Kalaiyam" refers to a pot, and "Kumbam" refers to a pot that contained living beings. This place was where living beings took refuge during the great flood (Jalapralayam) at the time of the deluge. Hence, it is called Kalaiyanallur. It is a holy place situated on the south bank of the Arisil River, which has abundant water. The Lord is Amirthakala Natha, Amirthakalasa Natha, Amirthakaleswarar, and the Goddess is Amirthavalli. The Theertham (holy water) is Amirthatheertham. People refer to this temple as Kottaichivan Koyil. The Dakshinamurthy idol here is a new idol with a wonderful structure. This idol has a Rudraksha mala in its upper right hand, fire in its upper left hand, Chinmudra in its right hand, and a book in its left hand. The hair is like a solar halo. It is adorned with a boar, and Brahma and Vishnu are seen bowing on either side. The Ardhanari (half-male, half-female) and Thapasviyammai (ascetic mother) forms here are also special. These are the special features of Thirukalaiyanallur. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bowing and worshipping Thirukalaiyanallur, proceeds to Thirukudamookku, also known as Kumbakonam. We will continue our discussion. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 849, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. From Thirukalaiyanallur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal proceeds to Thirukudamookku. The 68th verse states: "Angu Nindru Thirukudamookku Adainthu Paninthu Paadi Poy Mangai Paagar Valanjoliyai Maruvi Perugum Anbu Uruga Thangu Kaathaludan Vanangi Thamizhaal Parasi Arasinukku Thingal Mudiyaarum Adiyaliiththa Thirunallurai Sendru Adainthaar." From Thirukalaiyanallur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal arrives at Thirukudamookku, bows, and sings a Thirupathigam. He then proceeds to Thiruvalanjoli, the abode of the Lord who has Uma as one half of His body. With overflowing love, his heart melting, and abundant devotion, he bows and praises the Lord with a Tamil Thirupathigam. Afterwards, he proceeds to Thirunallur, the holy place where the Lord bestowed His feet upon Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. The Thirupathigams sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thirukudamookku (Kumbakonam), Thiruvalanjoli, and Thirunallur are not available to us due to our lack of merit. The 69th and 70th verses continue as follows: "Nallur Iraivar Kazhal Potri Navindru Naduvar Nambar Pathiyellaam Irainghi Ethi Ponthu Isaiyaal Paravum Thammudaiya Aninthavar Tham Sottruththuraiyin Marungu Eythi Allur Kandar Koyilin Ulladainthu Valam Kondu Adipanivaar Azhalneer Ozhugi Anaiya Enum Ansol Pathigam Eduththaruli Kazhal Neediya Anbinil Potrum Kaathal Kura Paraviya Pin Sezhuneermaiyinil Arul Petru Ponthu Paravaiyaark Kezhvar Muzhuneeru Anivaar Amarntha Pathi Palavum Paninthu Munnuvaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the feet of the Lord of Thirunallur, and then proceeds to visit and praise many holy places of the Lord in between. From Thirunallur, he departs and visits various holy places in between, such as Thiruppalaithurai and Thiruchakkarappalli, and then arrives at Thiruchottruthurai. He enters the temple of Lord Shiva, who has poison in His throat, circumambulates it, and bows at His feet. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then praises the Lord of Thiruchottruthurai and sings a beautiful Thirupathigam beginning with "Azhalneer Ozhugiyanaiya." The Thirupathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruchottruthurai is the 94th Thirupathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kausikam. The first and last verses of this Thirupathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Azhalneer Ozhugiyanaiya Sadaiyum Uzhaieer Uriyum Udaiyaan Idam Am Kalaineer Muththum Kanaga Kuvaiyum Suzhalneer Ponni Chottruththurai Thaaru Neer Chottruththuraiyul Mutraa Mathiser Muthalvan Paathaththu Attraar Adiyaar Adinaayooran Solthaan Ivai Kattraar Thunbu Ilare." Thiruchitrambalam. After singing this Thirupathigam and bowing, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal proceeds further, visiting many holy places where the Lord is pleased to reside. He visits holy places such as Thandankurai and Thiruvethikudi. The 71st and 72nd verses are as follows: "Devar Perumaan Kandiyur Paninthu Thiruvaiaaru Athanaai Mevivanangi Poonthuruththi Vimalar Paatham Thozhuthu Irainghi Sevil Varuvaar Thiru Aalampozhilil Serndhu Thaazhnthu Iravu Paavusayanaththu Amarntharuli Palli Kolla Kanavin Kan Mazhapaadiyinil Varuvatharkku Ninaikka Maranthaayo Endru Kuzhagu Aagiya Tham Kolam Ethirkaatti Arulak Kuriththu Unarnthu Nizhalaar Solaikkarai Ponni Vada Paal Eri Nedumaadum Azhagaar Veethi Mazhapaadi Adainthaar Nambi Aaroorar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after singing and worshipping at Thiruchottruthurai, departs from there and visits holy places such as Thandankurai and Thiruvethikudi. He then desires to visit more holy places where the Lord resides. He bows and worships Thirukkandiyur, the abode of Lord Shiva, the God of gods, and then proceeds to Thiruvaiyaru, where he worships Aiyarrappar. Afterwards, he bows and worships the feet of the Lord of Thiruppoonthuruththi and then arrives at Thiruvalampozhil. He bows to the Lord there and spends the night sleeping there. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as "Paavusayanam." "Paavuthal" means to lie down on the ground, spreading the entire body. In medicine, it is considered unnatural to sleep with limbs bent. While he was sleeping, the Lord appeared in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's dream and asked, "Have you forgotten to come to Thirumazhapadi?" and showed him His beautiful, youthful form. The phrase "Have you forgotten to come to Thirumazhapadi?" would be sufficient here, but Sekkizhar Peruman states that Lord Shiva, in the dream, reminded Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, "Have you forgotten even to think of coming to Thirumazhapadi?" This is because Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was always in a state of Shiva Yoga, never forgetting the Lord's feet. He was not one who forgot the Lord. Forgetting is the absence of remembrance. Therefore, it would not be appropriate to say "forgotten." Here, for Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the thought of coming to Thirumazhapadi is a special remembrance. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman states that Lord Shiva, in the dream, reminded Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, "Have you forgotten even to think of coming to Thirumazhapadi?" He showed him His beautiful, unique, and joyful form. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praised this form as "Ponnaar Meniyane" in the Thirupathigam he sang for Thirumazhapadi. Thus, after the Lord showed him His form, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal woke up, understood the meaning, and proceeded to Thirumazhapadi, a holy place with beautiful streets and tall mansions, situated on the north bank of the Cauvery, which has shady groves along its banks. Nambi Aaroorar Peruman arrives there. The 73rd and 74th verses are as follows: "Adainthu Thirukopuram Irainghi Anbar Suzhudan Pugunthu Panam Kol Aravum Aninthaar Mun Paninthu Vizhnthu Param Karunai Gunam Kol Arulin Thiram Potri Konda Pulagaththudan Urugi Punarntha Isaiyaal Thirupathigam Ponnaar Meniyane Endru Eduththu Anne Unnai Allaai Yaar Yaarai Ninaikkene Ena Ethi Thanneer Illaa Pathigamalai Saaththi Thozhuthu Purambu Adainthu Mannum Pathiyil Sila Naatkal Vaigi Thondarudan Magizhndhu Ponni Karaiyin Irumarangum Paninthu Melpaal Pothuvaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having arrived at Thirumazhapadi, approaches the temple, bows at the Gopuram (temple tower), and with devotees surrounding him, enters the temple. He bows down before the Lord, who is adorned with a serpent with a hood, and praises His boundless compassion and grace. With his body covered in goosebumps and his heart melting, he sings a musical Thirupathigam beginning with "Ponnaar Meniyane" and ending with "Anne Unnai Allaai Ini Yaarai Ninaikkene," offering a unique garland of hymns. "Anne Unnai Allaai Ini Yaarai Ninaikkene" is the crown jewel and the essence of the Thirupathigam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang this Thirupathigam with this crown jewel, "Whom else can I think of but You?" in response to the Lord's question, "Have you forgotten to think of coming?" We can see the unique quality of this Thirupathigam in the fact that people still eagerly recite it today. We also see that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praised and expressed his deep devotion in this Thirupathigam.
