Sangili Ammaiyar, in Thirukailai, had performed the service of picking flowers from the Nandavanam (flower garden) and offering them to Uma Ammaiyar, out of devotion. Accordingly, even now, when she incarnated as Sangili Ammaiyar, she continued the same flower service and attained the greatness of serving the Lord alone in this earthly world. Therefore, if the Lord is going to go into Sangili Ammaiyar's dream and tell her the message that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal prayed for, Sekkizhar Peruman implies that the reason for this is the greatness of Sangili Ammaiyar's hereditary devotion, and leaves the answer to that question to be inferred. The hereditary devotion of Sangili Ammaiyar is the nature of her service that she had been performing from Thirukailai. In addition, the fact that Sangili Ammaiyar was born in the Vellalar community, which has the excellence of serving Shiva hereditarily, is also implied here. The 251st and 252nd verses say: "Then, the Lord, having blessed Sangiliyar as before, said, 'O maiden, Nambi Aruran will make a vow to you with love, as you desired. But do not agree to him making that vow before us in the temple. Let him make it under the Magizha tree with fragrant flowers.' And she, with folded hands, said, 'O Lord, whom Vishnu and Brahma cannot comprehend, I have been accepted as your servant by your grace to me.' And tears flowed from her eyes, and she fell at the feet of the Lord with the victorious young bull and rose." Lord Shiva, who had granted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's request, now appears in Sangili Ammaiyar's dream again. The Lord appears in Sangili Ammaiyar's dream as before and blesses her, saying, "O maiden, Sangili, Nambi Aruran will make a vow to you with love, as you desired. But do not agree to him making that vow before us in the temple. Tell him to make it under the Magizha tree and accept it." The Lord blesses Sangili Ammaiyar. Hearing that, Sangili Ammaiyar, with folded hands, worships him, saying, "O Lord, whom Vishnu and Brahma cannot comprehend, I have truly been accepted as your servant by your grace to me." Tears flow in great streams from her eyes, and she falls at the feet of the Lord and rises. The Lord, by performing this act of grace, has accepted me as one of his devotees. I understand that you have accepted me too. "I have been accepted as the Lord's servant," she says. When Sangili Ammaiyar witnessed this act of grace, being accepted as a servant by the Lord, her heart was filled with overflowing love and tears, as she contemplated the Lord's boundless great compassion and her own boundless insignificance. This is the overflowing tears of love that flow when one contemplates the Lord's great compassion and one's own boundless insignificance, upon witnessing the act of grace of being accepted as a servant by the Lord. With these tears flowing, Sangili Ammaiyar falls at the feet of the Lord and rises. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 877, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Lord Shiva appears to Sangili Ammaiyar in her dream for the second time and blesses her, telling her to receive the vow under the Magizha tree. The 253rd and 254th verses are: "When the Lord with matted hair, having blessed the maiden, departed, Sangiliyar, amazed, awoke from her sleep and, remembering the grace of the Lord with red matted hair, could not sleep. She woke up the maidens sleeping nearby and told them, who were still sleepy, all that the Lord, who is known by the letters, had graciously told her in her dream. Hearing her words, the maidens, with fear, wonder, and joy, bowed to Sangiliyar." The Lord with matted hair, having blessed Sangiliyar, the maiden, as mentioned before, departed. Due to the wonder that arose from this event, Sangiliyar wakes up from her sleep and sits up. She comes from the state of sleep to the state of wakefulness. These states are called "svapnam" (dream) and "jagrata" (waking). In that night, the Lord appeared twice in her dream and blessed her. Thinking of this abundant grace, Sangiliyar wakes up from her sleep and sits up. After that, she cannot sleep at all. She sits awake. If one has a good dream, it is customary to stay awake that night, apply sacred ash, and meditate on Lord Shiva. Here too, after the events of the dream, Sangiliyar wakes up from her sleep and, remembering the divine grace of Lord Shiva, stays awake without sleeping. With a doubt as to whether the events she saw in her dream were real, she wakes up her female friends who are sleeping nearby. A dream can occur due to many reasons, such as illness, distorted perception, or past memories. It can be a false vision, or it can be a divine event that makes one wonder if it is real. The great divine dream is such that one wonders if it will yield results as it happened, if it is truly real. There is a great difference between the body in a dream and the body in a waking state. Therefore, doubt usually arises as to what happened in such a way. Here, Sangili Ammaiyar sits amazed, thinking that Lord Shiva appeared twice in her dream in the middle of the night and blessed her. She wakes up all the female friends who are sleeping nearby. Female friends are maidens appointed for service and protection. In Tamil Akapporul (love poetry) tradition, they are called "thozhi" (female friend) or "uyirpangi" (soul-mate). One would not tell others, but one would tell a thozhi, which is a tradition in Tamil literature. It is very important to recall the events seen in a dream in the waking state as they were. Therefore, with a doubt that she might forget all that happened in the dream, she wakes up all the sleeping female friends and tells them all that happened. Sangili Ammaiyar does not wait for the female friends to wake up on their own. She immediately wakes them up and informs them of all that she saw in her dream. In addition, it is now dawn. It is the time to gather flowers for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi (waking up the Lord). Therefore, she also wakes up the female friends for that purpose. Moreover, the Lord has blessed Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to fulfill the vow that very night. Therefore, before Nambigal comes to the Thiruvottiyur temple, Sangili Ammaiyar wakes up the sleeping female friends for these and many other reasons, tells them all these stories, and asks them to go there. She tells the female friends who have woken up from sleep, "The Lord of Thiruvottiyur, who is known as 'Ezhuthariyum Peruman' (the Lord who knows the letters) because he wrote the letter 'Ezhuthu', appeared twice in my dream and blessed me." Sangili Ammaiyar tells all that happened to her female friends in detail. Hearing that, all those female friends, with fear, wonder, and joy, bow down to Sangili Ammaiyar. We have already contemplated in detail the story of how the Lord of Thiruvottiyur got the name "Ezhuthariyum Peruman." Such a great Lord blessed her, and when she told her female friends, these are all events about the Lord's acts of grace. Therefore, there was fear from hearing them with awe, and it was a great blessing that was rare to obtain, the power of the Lord's grace. The female friends witnessed it directly, so they were also amazed. In addition, since their mistress was about to get married, they were also joyful because they were going to serve their mistress in that special marriage. The 255th verse says: "When it was the pure time for the maiden to gather flowers for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi, and she went to perform her duty, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having understood that it was the time to make the vow, came to the front of the temple, looking for her arrival." This is the verse. The female friends go to the temple to gather flowers for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi. In Shiva temples, flowers prescribed for the respective puja (worship) for the respective time should be selected and gathered. This is the time for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi, so flowers suitable for that should be selected and gathered. Therefore, those female friends go to the temple to perform their duty. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is present in front of the temple, waiting for Sangili Ammaiyar to arrive. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, realizing that it is time to fulfill his vow, comes there to make the vow as the Lord had blessed him. The Lord had told Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to do it that very night. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who had agreed to it, comes there, thinking that it is the right time to meet Sangiliyar and make the vow before the night passes. If it is night, Sangili Ammaiyar will be in the maiden's chamber, and he cannot go there. If the night passes, the time given by the Lord will pass. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal comes to the front of the Lord's temple at that time, which is just before the time of Thiruppalli Ezhuchi, which is between night and dawn. He waits there for Sangili Ammaiyar. Nambigal comes and waits there even before Sangili Ammaiyar arrives. The 256th verse says: "He stood there, and when the maiden with beautiful ornaments came, he went to her side and spoke of the grace of his Lord. The maiden with a slender waist, out of shyness, did not speak her consent directly. She moved aside with her companions and entered the temple." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is waiting there. At that time, Sangili Ammaiyar comes there with her female friends. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to Sangiliyar's side and tells her all about the grace of the Lord to him. Sangili Ammaiyar, out of great shyness, could not directly express her consent to her husband-to-be. She moved aside with her companions and entered the temple. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes as far as necessary to speak to Sangiliyar, who came before him, so that she can hear him. The Lord had said, "Go to her now, this very night, and make the vow." Therefore, the Lord had informed both of them. So, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal tells Sangiliyar that message. Sangili Ammaiyar should express her consent to that. But Sangili Ammaiyar, out of great shyness, could not express it openly to Nambigal, who was to be her husband. She moved aside with her female friends and hid inside the temple. These are all the expressions that occur in a heroine when she sees her hero: inability to speak, inability to express the words that come, great shyness, covering her eyes, covering her face, and standing with a sense of inadequacy. These are all the expressions that occur in a heroine in the presence of her hero in Akapporul (love poetry) traditions. The 257th, 258th, and 259th verses are continuous verses. The 257th verse says: "There, Aruran (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal) followed her and said, 'O maiden with beautiful ornaments, I am here to make a vow that I will not leave you. Come before the Lord with the moon-crowned hair.' And the maidens, who had heard Sangiliyar's dream, replied." This is how the verse is structured. Sangili Ammaiyar goes inside the temple with her female friends. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also follows her and says to Sangili Ammaiyar, "O Sangili, adorned with beautiful ornaments, I am here to make a vow that I will not leave you. Therefore, come before the Lord." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says this to Sangili Ammaiyar. But the female friends, who knew the message that the Lord had told Sangili Ammaiyar in her dream, tell Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. In reality, Sangili Ammaiyar should have replied, but due to shyness, she remains there, and on her behalf, the female friends reply to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. That is the 258th verse. "The maidens said to Vanthondar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), 'Our Lord (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal) has come for this. Is it proper to make a vow before the Lord of the celestials? O creeper-like maiden, where else can I do it?'" This is how the verse is structured. The female friends of Sangili Ammaiyar say to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, "Our Lord has come for this. Is it proper to make this vow before the Lord of the celestials, the Lord of the gods? It is not fitting for this small act." They call Sundaramoorthy Swamigal "Our Lord" because they know that he is the husband-to-be of their mistress. Therefore, they say, "Our Lord," and convey this idea to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. "This vow or promise is a very small matter. Is it proper to do this small matter in a very high and sacred place, before the Lord? It is not fitting for that," they say. This is because the Lord had told Sangili Ammaiyar in her dream, "Do not accept this vow before the sanctum sanctorum. Accept it under the Magizha tree." Sangili Ammaiyar had also told this to her female friends. Therefore, this was a strategy adopted by the female friends to make Sundaramoorthy Swamigal make the vow under the Magizha tree. The female friends say that it is not necessary to do this small matter before the Lord, who is in a high and sacred place. To that, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asks, "Then where else can I make the vow?" To that, the female friends reply in the verse: "If the beautiful women refuse, then it is better to agree and decide to go under the Magizha tree." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who asked where he should make the vow, is told by the women that it is enough to make the vow under the Magizha tree. Hearing that, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is confused. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is mentally disturbed. He decides that if he refuses to do as they say, it will become a blame, so he must do as they say, and agreeing to it is appropriate. Why was Sundaramoorthy Swamigal disturbed when he heard this? It was because he had prayed to the Lord, "When I make a vow before your sanctum sanctorum, you should be present under the Magizha tree." He realized that this had become a problem for him due to the Lord's grace to them. He would be blamed for trying to deceive the women. But the Lord is present under the Magizha tree as promised. If he makes a vow before him that he will not leave Sangiliyar, it will hinder his duty of visiting temples and worshipping the Lord. He also thinks this. However, he can somehow obtain the grace of the Lord and the permission to undertake pilgrimages. He can obtain consent from the Lord by praying to him. But now, if he refuses to make this vow, he cannot avoid the blame that will come. Therefore, after considering all this, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal agrees to this. Therefore, he says, "I will make the vow under the Magizha tree. You go to the Magizha tree." Sangili Ammaiyar and her female friends go to the Magizha tree, and he also goes there. Now, the 260th verse says: "Before Sangiliyar, who had performed unfailing great penance, the Lord of Munaippadi, the protector of the three worlds, circumambulated the ancient Magizha tree three times and stood there, declaring, 'I will not leave this place.'" This is the verse. Before Sangiliyar, who had performed unfailing great penance, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal makes a vow under the sacred Magizha tree. That sacred Magizha tree is an eternal tree, an imperishable, ancient tree that is always there, even though it is old, it does not perish. He circumambulates it three times, worshipping it. Making a vow is a ritual that is part of the vow. After circumambulating three times, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stands before the Magizha tree and raises his hand, declaring with his mouth, "I will not leave this place." He makes this vow, saying, "I will not go away from here." After he finishes, the hesitation in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal causes external hesitation, which leads to hesitation in his actions, preventing him from performing the physical act quickly. Thus, he gives his vow, his promise, to Sangili Ammaiyar. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 878, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal makes a vow under the Magizha tree. The 261st verse: "மேவியசீர் ஆரூரர் மெய்ச்சபதம் வினை முடிப்ப காவியினேர் கண்ணாரும் கண்டு மிக மனம் கலங்கி பாவியேன் இது கண்டேன் தம்பிரான் பணியால் என்று ஆவிசோர்ந்து அழிவார் அங்கு ஒரு மருங்கு மறைந்து அயர்ந்தார்"

As Nambi Arurar thus fulfilled the vow, Sangiliyar, seeing it, was greatly distressed in her heart. Thinking, "Wretched me, I witnessed this by the command of Thampiran (Lord Shiva)," she became faint-hearted and hid herself in a corner, deeply saddened. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's vow was a true vow, a vow made with his physical body. The truth of the vow lay in his feet walking around, his hands raised, and his mouth uttering the oath. While the external organs of his body thus functioned at their own level, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's mind was confused and bewildered. It then somewhat recovered and became resolute, yet restless, thus fulfilling the vow. Moreover, the vow made by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was a true vow. As Sundaramoorthy Swamigal wished, the Lord appeared and was seated under the Magizha tree. Therefore, it was a true vow made in the presence of the Lord. Making a vow in the presence of the Lord is an unusual act, done under duress. Sangiliyar lamented, "My Lord, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, did this for my sake. How terrible that I became the cause of it!"

Therefore, she went to a corner, distressed, and hid herself. We only mentioned that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was very happy to be residing in Thiruvarur. We did not say that he sought any remedy for it. But the Lord Himself came and said, "He will make a vow not to leave you." And without agreeing to do it in front of our sacred shrine, the Lord Himself came to Sangiliyamman and said, "You shall receive that vow under the Magizha tree." If the Lord had not commanded thus, Sangiliyar's loving heart would not have insisted and requested this so much. This is the truth. Therefore, the Lord commanded Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to perform this act, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal made that vow, and Sangiliyar witnessed it. This is said to be due to the Lord's supreme grace. The truth is that the Lord, out of His immense grace for both of them, commanded and blessed them thus. Just as a physician gives medicine with insistence and treats a disease with force according to its nature, the Lord has shown His grace here. We must understand this. Even though such actions in this great Puranam may appear ordinary to other worldly people, we must keep in mind that these actions are all acts of grace commanded by the Lord.

The 262nd verse: "திரு நாவலூராளி தம்முடைய செயல் முற்றி பொறுநாக புனைந்தார் கோயிலின் உள் புகுந்து இறைஞ்சி அருள் நாளும் தரையிருந்தீர் செய்தவாறு அழகு இது என பெருநாமம் எடுத்து ஏத்தி பெருமகிழ்ச்சியுடன் போந்தார்"

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the leader of Thirunavalur, having completed his vow, entered the Lord's temple, worshipped the Lord, and said to Him, "O Lord, who always bestows grace upon me, what you did was beautiful and good." He then praised the Lord by uttering His great name (the sacred five-letter mantra, Thiruvaindheluthu) and departed with great joy. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, realizing by inference that the handmaidens' request to make the vow under the Magizha tree was due to the Lord's prompting, spoke to the Lord thus. He praised the Lord's great name, Sri Panchaksharam, and also expressed a hint of reproach to the Lord as he left. What happened now was grace. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was joyful, concluding that grace would continue to protect him in the events that would follow. He was also joyful because, with the fulfillment of the vow, the marriage would now be completed. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then departed from the temple.

The 263rd verse: "வார்புனையும் வனமுலையார் வன்தொண்டர் போனதற்பின் தார்ப்புனையும் மண்டபத்து தம்முடைய பணி செய்து கார்ப்புனையும் மணிகண்டர் செயல் கருத்தில் கொண்டு இறைஞ்சி ஏற்புனையும் கன்னிமாடம் புகுந்தார் இருள் புலர"

After Vantondar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal) left, Sangiliyamman went to the flower-garland-making hall, completed her service, and then, keeping the deeds of the blue-throated Lord in her mind, worshipped Him and entered the maiden's chamber as dawn broke. Here, according to Sangiliyamman's request, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal fulfilled the vow. Even after these events were completed, Sangiliyamman went into the flower-garland-making hall, completed her regular service of making flower garlands, and then proceeded to the maiden's chamber. Her regular service was the flower-garland service. Ordinary worldly people often neglect their Shiva service and devotee service when they experience worldly joys and sorrows. But Sangiliyar's life was disciplined in Shiva devotion. Therefore, whether joy or sorrow came, whatever happened, she continued her regular flower service. If worldly people were to observe and follow Sangiliyar's disciplined Shiva life, it would bring them immense good. Having completed her service, as darkness faded and morning arrived, she entered the maiden's chamber. The darkness here implicitly refers to this worldly life, which came about due to the events in Thirukailayam. The inner meaning is that she entered the maiden's chamber after the karmic effects of that day were completed.

The 264th and 265th verses: "அன்று இரவே ஆதிபுரி ஒற்றிக் கொண்டார் ஆட்கொண்ட பொன் திகழ் வன் தொண்டர் முடித்தருள நின்ற புகழ் திருவொற்றியூர் நிலவு தொண்டற்கு மன்றல் வினை செய்வதற்கு மனங்கொள்ள உணர்த்துவார் நம்பி ஆரூரனுக்கு நங்கை சங்கிலிதன்னை இம்பர் ஞாலத்திடை நம் ஏவலின மனவினை செய்து உம்பர் வாழும் உலகறிய அழிப்பீர் என்று உணர்த்துதலும் தம்பிரான் திருத்தொண்டர் அருள் தலைமேல் கொண்டு எழுவார் என்பவை"

That very night, the Lord of Thiruvottriyur, the primordial city, in order to fulfill the marriage desired by Vantondar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), whom He had taken as His own, instructed the devotees residing in the glorious Thiruvottriyur. He conveyed to them, "Perform the marriage of Nambi Aruran and Nankai Sangili in this world according to Our command, so that the inhabitants of the celestial world may also know of it." Upon this instruction, the Lord's devotees accepted His grace with reverence and proceeded to act. The Lord thus conveyed His intention to the Shiva devotees residing in Thiruvottriyur. He also made it clear that this was His command. He instructed them to perform the rituals according to the rules of chastity and the scriptures. He also instructed them to do it so that the inhabitants of the celestial world would know of it.

The 266th verse: "மண்ணிறைந்த பெருஞ்செல்வத் திரு ஒற்றியூர் மண்ணும் எண்ணிறைந்த திருத்தொண்டர் எழில் பதியோருடன் ஈண்டி உள் நிறைந்த மகிழ்ச்சியுடன் உம்பர் பூமழை பொழிய கண்ணிறைந்த பெரும் சிறப்பில் கலியாணம் செய்து அழித்தார்"

In Thiruvottriyur, filled with immense earthly wealth, countless devotees residing there, along with other beautiful people, gathered with hearts full of joy. As the celestials showered flowers like rain, they performed the marriage of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Sangiliyamman with great splendor, filling the eyes with delight.

The 267th verse: "பண்டு நிகழ் பான்மையில் பசுபதி தன் அருளாலே வண்டமர் பூங்குழலாரை மழம்புணர்ந்த வன்தொண்டர் புண்டரிக தவள் வனப்பை புறம் கொண்ட தூ நலத்தை கண்டு கேட்டு உண்டு உயிர்த்து உற்று அமர்ந்திருந்தார் காதலினால்"

According to the events that transpired before, by the grace of Pasupathi (Lord Shiva), Vantondar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), who was united with the lady whose hair was adorned with bees, beheld the pure beauty that surpassed the whiteness of a lotus. He saw, heard, enjoyed, breathed, and was deeply immersed in love. The marriage that took place now was a result of the karmic destiny that arose from the events in Thirukailayam. This marriage was successfully completed by the grace of Pasupathi, Lord Shiva, the leader of all beings. This marriage, which occurred through the grace of the Lord, who sent Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, Anindhithai, and Kamalini, protected them from accumulating further karma, and took them as His own, was thus fulfilled. Vantondar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who married Sangiliyamman, who surpassed the beauty of Lakshmi, lived a marital life with great affection. How was Sundaramoorthy Swamigal before, when he married Paravai Nachiyar, as described in the story of Thaduththaatkonda Puranam? It is said, "For many days, he desired the yoga of the supreme." We should apply the same idea here.

The 268th verse: "யாழின் மொழி எழில் முறுவல் இரு குழை மேல் கடைபிரழலும் மாழை விழிவன முளையார் மணி அல்குள் துறை படிந்து வீழும் அவர்க்கு இடை தோன்றி மிகும் புலவி புணர்ச்சிக்கண் ஊழியாம் ஒரு கணம்தான் அவ்வூழி ஒரு கணமாம்"

The days when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal lived united with Sangiliyamman, whose speech was as sweet as a lyre, whose smile was beautiful, whose sidelong glances played over the makara earrings in her ears, and whose eyes resembled mango blossoms, were such that a single moment felt like an eon. And an eon felt like a single moment. The marital life of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Sangiliyamman here was not consumed by lust, nor did it lead to the accumulation of further karma. Instead, it was contained within the supreme bliss of the Lord's Shivayoga, and only the physical aspect of karma was expended. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this in the next verse.

The 269th verse: "இந்நிலையில் பேரின்பம் இனிது அமர்வார் இறைவுரையும் மண்ணு புகழ் ஒற்றியோர் அதனில் மகிழ் சிறப்பினால் சென்னி மதிப்புனைவார்த்தம் திருப்பாதம் தொழுது இருந்தார் முன்னிய காலங்கள் பல முறைமையினால் வந்து அகல என்பது"

Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, residing in Thiruvottriyur, remained in supreme bliss. With the joy and glory of that sacred place, Thiruvottriyur, where the Lord resides with enduring fame, he worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord, who wears the crescent moon on His head. Many past periods came and went in due course. The experience of the state described in the Thirundhiyar Sastram, "The joy received is supreme bliss, and there is no illusion," is what we see in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's experience here. Thirukazhittruppadiyar further explains this: "A yogi with a body, when all small pleasures are absorbed into his supreme bliss, nothing begins, nothing ends, nothing is done by him." And the Thiruviruttham of Sivagnana Siddhiyar states: "Even when lying amidst women with fragrant hair, in the midst of fire-like eyes, those who attain divine knowledge, even in their homes, will worship with folded hands." Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal remained, worshipping the Lord of Thiruvottriyur. Many seasons came and went. It is inferred that these must have been at least three seasons. Considering the events that follow, it is reasonable to assume three seasons. It is known from the subsequent events that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal married Sangiliyamman during the rainy season, and he departed from Thiruvottriyur for Thiruvarur during the spring season. This is because Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, while still in Thiruvottriyur, yearned to see the Vasantha festival in Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then departed from Thiruvottriyur. Therefore, the period from the rainy season to the spring season is known to be the time Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stayed there. We will continue to reflect on this.

Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 879, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal lives in Thiruvottiyur with Sangiliyamman. The 270th verse:

"Poṅku tamiḻ potiyamalai piṟantu pūñcantana ttiṉ Koṅku aṇaintu kuḷircāral iṭaivaḷarnta koḻum teṉṟal Aṅku aṇaiya tiruvārūr aṇi vīti aḻakar avar Maṅkaḷa nāḷ vacantam etirkoṇṭu aruḷum vakai niṉaitār"

Tamil language is "pongu Tamil" (flourishing Tamil). It is a language that is always in common use among people, without stagnation in its growth, and without hindrances such as not adhering to grammatical rules. It is a Tamil that grows richer and richer. This is a unique feature of the Tamil language, not found in other languages. The mountain where the Tamil sage Agastya, the abode of such a flourishing Tamil, resides, is the Podigai mountain. It is the mountain of the Tamil sage. From that Podigai mountain, which is full of sandalwood forests, the southern breeze (thendral kaatru) originates. The southern breeze, mingling with the fragrance of sandalwood trees, grows in the cool, watery slopes, and is a rich breeze. The southern breeze, originating from the Podigai mountain, passes through other cold mountainsides, watery groves, and the regions of the Kaveri river, and then reaches Thiruvarur, and finally Thiruvottiyur. The time when the southern breeze comes is the Vasantha Kalam (spring season). During this spring season, in Thiruvarur, the beautiful Veethi Vidanga Peruman (Lord Thyagaraja) celebrates the auspicious Vasantha festival with great splendor. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal remembers that Veethi Vidanga Peruman will hold court during that Vasantha festival. Veethi Vidanga Peruman, the beautiful Lord of the streets of Thiruvarur, is Thyagesa Peruman. During the Vasantha festival in the spring season, on the sixth day, Thyagesa Peruman will hold court with great splendor. Therefore, when the southern breeze comes to Thiruvottiyur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal remembers the Vasantha festival of Thiruvarur. The state of mind of great people is such that all worldly experiences remind them of the Lord, connecting them to the Lord. In this state, the characteristic of Shivayoga is to practice seeing all enjoyable things in the world as related to Shiva. This practice is very beneficial. Here, we understand that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also sees and enjoys all worldly experiences as related to Shiva. The 271st verse:

"Veṇmatiyiṉ koḻuntu aṇinta vīti viṭaṅka perumāṉ Oṉ mutalār puṭaippaṟanta ōlakkam ataṉ iṭaiyē Paṇṇamarum moḻi paṟavaiyār pāṭal āṭal taṉai Kaṇṇuṟa muṉkaṇṭu kēṭṭārpōla karutiṉār"

Veethi Vidanga Peruman (Thyagesa Peruman), adorned with the crescent moon, holds court. In the assembly hall where Thyagesa Peruman holds court during the Vasantha festival, Paravai Nachiyar's singing and dancing take place. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal imagines as if he is seeing and hearing Paravaiyar's dance and song in the assembly hall, surrounded by beautiful women with lovely foreheads. When the southern breeze, which comes before the Lord of Arur in Thiruvarur, came to mind, the sight of Paravaiyar's dance and song in the assembly where he was seated also came to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's mind. To Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with his focused attention, that scene appeared as if it were actually happening. Now, the 272nd and 273rd verses:

"Pūṅkōyil amarntārai puṟṟiṭam koṇṭu iruntārai Nīṅkāta kātaliṉāl niṉaintārai niṉaivārai Pāṅkāka tām muṉpu paṇiyavarum payaṉ uṇarvār Īṅku nāṉ maṟantēṉ eṉṟu ēcaravāl mika aḻivār Miṉṉoḷir ceñcaṭaiyāṉai vēta mutal āṉāṉai Maṉṉa pukaḻ tiruvārūr makiḻntāṉai mika niṉaintu Paṉṉiya col pattimaiyum aṭimaiyaiyum kaiviṭuvāṉ Eṉṉum icai tiruppatikam eṭuttu iyaṃpi iṟaṅkiṉār"

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal now thinks of Putridam Kondanathar (Lord of the Anthill), who resides in the flower temple of Thiruvarur, who makes the anthill his abode, and who is the Moolasthana Nathar (presiding deity) in Thiruvarur. The Lord mentioned in the previous verses was Thyagesa Peruman. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who is accustomed to worshipping and praising the Lord who resides in the anthill with unceasing great love, and who experiences the great benefit of Shivanantham (bliss of Shiva) that comes from remembering those devotees who remember Him, is now greatly distressed, thinking, "I have forgotten that Lord of Thiruvarur and am staying here!" In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman praises Nambiyarurar, saying, "He remembers those who remember Him with unceasing love." This means that the Lord remembers those devotees who remember Him with unceasing great love. If the Lord remembers all beings in general and bestows grace, then this means that the Lord specifically remembers those who remember Him continuously with great love.

The truth stated in the tenth Sutra of Sivagnana Bodham is, "It is the duty of the leader to protect those who seek refuge, and the devotee who seeks refuge, without deceit, and whose karma is destroyed by the Lord Himself, as examined by the wise." The Thirumudukunram Thevaram states, "He who is always present in the hearts of devotees who praise Him without forgetting the tantra." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal remembers the Shivanantha Bhogam (bliss of Shiva) he received by worshipping and praising such a Lord in the past. He grieves, "I have forgotten such a Lord and am staying here!" Sundaramoorthy Swamigal never forgot the Lord of Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's statement, "I have forgotten Him here," means that he is separated from the Lord of Thiruvarur. He feels "esaravu" (distress) thinking like this. Esaravu means the sorrow that comes from being separated from a precious thing. We remember that there are verses in Thiruvachagam in a section called "Thiru Esaravu." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, greatly distressed by the separation, deeply remembered the Lord with shining red matted hair, who is the first of the Vedas, and who rejoices in the ever-glorious Thiruvarur. He then sang the Thiruppathikam (hymn) that begins with "Patthimaiyum Adimaiyaiyum Kaividuvaan" (I will abandon devotion and servitude), which is rich in words and meaning, set to the tune of Pazhampanchuram, and descended. This Thiruppathikam, which is full of words, was composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who remembered the Lord very deeply. The inner meaning of this Thiruppathikam is to experience and express the same meaning in many ways. In this Thiruppathikam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings with melting heart in each verse, "How many days have I been separated from my Lord of Arur?" and "In what way have I been separated?" and "How have I been separated?" This Thiruppathikam, dedicated to the Lord of Thiruvarur, has twelve verses, two more than the usual ten verses in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppathikams. This Thiruppathikam begins with "Patthimaiyum Adimaiyaiyum Kaividuvaan." "Patthimai" (devotion) is an internal state, and "Adimai" (servitude) is an external state. "Kaividuvaan" means "I will let go." This Thiruppathikam was composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal with a distressed mind, grieving over his own situation, thinking, "I am here, letting go of that devotion and servitude." This Thiruppathikam belongs to the sacred place of Thiruvarur. It was composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal while he was in Thiruvottiyur. It is set to the tune of Pazhampanchuram. It is the 51st Thiruppathikam in the 7th Thirumurai. It is a central jewel in the 7th Thirumurai. The twelve verses of this Thiruppathikam are as follows:

Thiruchitrambalam. "Aḻukku meykkoṭu uṉ tiruvaṭi aṭaintēṉ atuvum nāṉ paṭaṟpālatu aṉṟu āṉāl Piḻukkai vāriyum pāl koḷvar aṭikēḷ piḻaippaṉ ākilum tiruvaṭi piḻaiyēṉ Vaḻukki vīḻiṉum tiruppeyar allāl maṟṟu nāṉ aṟiyēṉ maṟu māṟṟam Oḻukka eṉ kaṇukku oru maruntu uraiyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kaṭṭaṉēṉ piṟantēṉ uṉakku āḷāy kātal caṅkili kāraṇamāka Eṭṭiṉāl tikaḻum tirumūrtti eṉ ceyvāṉ aṭiyēṉ eṭuttu uraippēṉ Peṭṭaṉ ākilum tiruvaṭi piḻaiyēṉ piḻaippaṉākilum tiruvaṭikku aṭimai Oṭṭiṉēṉ eṉṉai nī ceyvatu ellām oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kaṅkai taṅkiya caṭaivuṭai karumpē kaṭṭiyē palarkkum kaḷai kaṇṇē Aṅkai nelliyiṉ paḻattu iṭai amutē attā eṉ iṭar ārkku eṭuttu uraippēṉ Caṅkum ippiyum calañcalam murala vayaṟam muttoṭu poṉmaṇi varaṉṟi Ōṅkumā kaṭal ōtam vantu ulavum oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Īṉṟu koṇṭatu ōr cuṟṟam ōṉṟu aṉṟāl yāvarākil eṉ aṉpu uṭaiyārkaḷ Tōṉṟa niṉṟu aruḷ ceytu aḻittiṭṭāl colluvārai allātaṉa collāy Mūṉṟu kaṇ uṭaiyāy aṭiyēṉ kaṇkoḷvatē kaṇakku vaḻakkākil Ūṉṟukōl eṉakku āvatu oṉṟu aruḷāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Vaḻitta paṭuvāṉ muyalkiṉṟēṉ uṉṉai pōl eṉṉai pāvikka māṭṭēṉ Cuḻittalaippaṭṭa nīr atupōla cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ cuḻalkiṉṟatu eṉ uḷḷam Kaḻittalaippaṭṭa nāyatu pōla oruvaṉ kōlpaṟṟi karakara iḻukkai Oḻittu nī aruḷ āyiṉa ceyyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Māṉai nōkkiyaṟ kaṇvalaippaṭṭu varunti yāṉ uṟṟa valviṉaikku añci Tēṉaiyāṭiya koṉṟaiyiṉāy uṉ cīlamum kuṇamum cintiyātē Nāṉum ittaṉai vēṇṭuvatu aṭiyēṉ uyiroṭum nakar narakattu aḻuntāmai Ūṉam uḷḷaṉa tīrttu aruḷ ceyyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Maṟṟu tēvarai niṉaintu uṉai maṟavēṉ neñciṉāru vāḻavu māṭṭēṉ Peṟṟiruntu peṟātu oḻukiṉṟa pētaiyēṉ piḻaittiṭṭatai aṟiyēṉ Muṟṟum nī eṉṉai muṉintiṭa aṭiyēṉ kaṭavatu eṉ uṉai nāṉ maṟavaṉēl Uṟṟa nōy uṟuppiṉi tavirttu aruḷāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kūṭiṉāy malai maṅkaiyai niṉaiyāy kaṅkai āyiram mukam uṭaiyāḷai Cūṭiṉāy eṉṟu colliya pukkal toḻumpaṉēṉukku collalum āmē Vāṭi nī iruntu eṉ ceyti maṉamē varunti yāṉ uṟṟa valviṉaikku añci Ūṭiṉāl iṉi āvatu oṉṟu uṇṭē oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Makattil pukkatōr caṉi eṉakku āṉāy maintaṉē maṇiyē maṇavāḻā Akatil peṇṭukaḷ nāṉ oṉṟu coṉṉāl aḻaiyal pō kuruṭā eṉa tariyē Mukattil kaṇ iḻantu eṅkaṉam vāḻkēṉ mukkaṉā muṟaiyō maṟaivōti Ukaikkum taṉ kaṭal ōtam vantu ulavum oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Ōtam vantu ulavum karaitaṉ mēl oṟṟiyūr urai celvaṉai nāḷum Ñālattāṉ paravappaṭukiṉṟa nālmaṟai aṅkam ōtiya nāvaṉ Cīlattāṉ peritum mika valla ciṟuvaṉ vaṉ tuṇṭaṉ ūraṉ uraita pāṭal Pattu ivai vallavar tām pōy parakati tiṇṇam naṇṇuvar tāmē"

Thiruchitrambalam. In this Thiruppathikam, in the tenth verse, he mentions Paravaiyar, and in the eleventh verse, Sangiliyar, in a way that shows his sorrow, which is pitiable. Even though he was in Thiruvottiyur, the memory of Thiruvarur never left his heart. This Thiruppathikam was composed with a distressed mind, grieving, "I have forgotten the Lord of Thiruvarur here! How many days have I been separated?" This Thiruppathikam not only reveals Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's inner thoughts but also contains many internal evidences of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's history. In the tenth and eleventh verses, the stories of his marriages to Paravai Nachiyar and Sangili Nachiyar, according to the Lord's command, are obtained. In the tenth verse, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, "You are the seven notes, the fruit of music, the sweet nectar, my friend, and you are with me in all the wrongs I do." "Thurisugal" (wrongs) means faults. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings that the Lord is omnipresent, and therefore, He is present even in wrongs. The Lord blessed him, saying, "Play on earth with the form of a mental sacrifice." The Lord appeared under the Magizha tree as he wished. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, "You are with me in all the wrongs I do," keeping in mind these and other blessings. In the twelfth verse, he sings, "I greatly desire the service of Lord Shiva of Thiruvarur." Even without seeing the Lord of Thiruvarur directly, he sings this, greatly remembering that servile devotion in his mind. Although this Thiruppathikam is about Thiruvarur, it was not composed there, but in Thiruvottiyur, remembering Thiruvarur deeply. This is an internal evidence for this. This Thiruppathikam is very moving, with profound meaning and musical harmony, and is also very memorable. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composed this Thiruppathikam. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 880, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, while in Thiruvottiyur, remembers the Lord of Thiruvarur and composes a Thiruppathikam. The 274th verse:

"Piṉ oru nāḷ tiruvārūr taṉṉai peruka niṉaintu aruḷi Uṉṉa iṉiyār kōyil pukuntu iṟaiñci oṟṟi nakar taṉṉai Akala pukkār tām ceyta capatattāl muṉ aṭikaḷ tōṉṟātu Kaṇmaṟaiya mūrcittār eṉpatu tiruppāṭal"

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who had been thinking of the Lord of Thiruvarur, one day thought deeply of the Lord of Thiruvarur and decided to go to Thiruvarur to worship Him. He entered the Adhipureeswarar temple in Thiruvottiyur, worshipped the Lord, and then set out from Thiruvottiyur to go to Thiruvarur. As he stepped out of Thiruvottiyur towards Thiruvarur, due to the vow he had made, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's eyesight disappeared, and he fainted. He bid farewell to the Lord of Ottiyur by worshipping inside the temple, then left and stepped across the boundary of Thiruvottiyur. At that moment, his eyesight disappeared unexpectedly, due to the vow he had made to Sangiliyamman under the Magizha tree, that he would not leave her. This was a sudden misfortune. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal fainted and became somewhat unconscious. The 275th, 276th, 277th, and 278th verses:

"Ceyvataṉai aṟiyātu tikaittu aruḷi neṭuyirppār Maiviravu kaṇṇārpāl cūḷuṟavu maṟutta ataṉāl Ivviṉai vantu eytiyatām eṉa niṉaintu emperumāṉai Eytiya ittuyar nīṅka pāṭuvēṉ eṉa niṉaintu Aḻukku meykkoṭu eṉṟu eṭutta col patikam Āti nīḻpuṟi aṇṇalai ōti vaḻuttu neñcoṭu Tāḻntu niṉṟu uraippār mātorpākaṉār malarpata muṉṉi Iḻukku nīkkiṭa vēṇṭum eṉṟu iṟantē eytu ventuyar Kaiyaṟaviṉukkum paḻikkum velki nal icai koṭu paravi Paṇintu cālavum pala pala niṉaivār aṅku nātar cey Aruḷatuvāka aṅkai kūppi āṟūr toḻa niṉaintē Poṅkukātal mīḷā nilaimaiyiṉāl pōtuvār vaḻikāṭṭa Muṉpōntu tiṅkaḷvēṇiyār tiru mullai vāyil ceṉṟu iṟaiñci Nīṭiya tiruppatikam caṅkilikkāka eṉ kaṉai maṟaittīr eṉṟu Cāṟṟiya taṉmaiyil pāṭi toṇṭaimāṉukku aṉṟu aruḷ koṭuttu Aruḷum tollai vaṇpukaḻ mullai nāyakaraik koṇṭa Veṇṭuyar kaḷaika eṉa paravi kuṟitta kātaliṉ Neṟikoḷa varuvār vaṇṭulā malarcōlaikaḷ cūḻntu Māṭamāḷikai nīṭu veṇpākkam kaṇṭa toṇṭarkaḷ Etirkoḷḷu vaṇaṅki kāyunākattaṟ kōyilai aṭaintār eṉpavaikal tiruppāṭalkaḷ"

Suddenly, his eyesight disappeared, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was bewildered, not knowing what to do, and sighed deeply. He thought that this misfortune had come upon him because he had broken the oath he made to Sangiliyar. He decided to sing to the Lord, praying for this suffering to be removed. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal thought that his eyesight had disappeared because he had broken the vow. At this point, Sivakavimani Desikanar writes as follows: "If one makes a vow and then acts contrary to it, will their eyesight disappear? Even in these days, people swear, 'I swear it is the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God,' and then they tell lies, give false testimony without any truth mixed in, and break their vows. But no harm comes to them. They live happily without any trouble. In this age, who would believe the story that eyesight disappeared because a vow was broken?" Many people doubt and mock, saying this. Those people are unaware of the nature of time, their own state, and the laws of karma. The manifestation of truth changes from age to age; this is the conclusion of the Gnana Sastras (scriptures of wisdom). We also see this in experience. This is why it is said that Dharma Devata (the deity of righteousness) walks on four legs in the first age, three legs in the second age, two legs in the third age, and one leg in the fourth age. In this Kali Yuga (the fourth age), the manifestation of truth will happen slowly, according to the nature of this age. But no matter what, it will happen; it will not fail. Seeing that the manifestation of truth does not happen immediately, one should not conclude that there is no place for truth here.

The fact that the manifestation of truth changes according to the Yuga Dharma (the dharma of the age) is stated in many scriptures. Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, Rasavatha Padalam, states, "His golden body changed, and he took a suitable form for the people of the fourth age of falsehood." Many other scriptures also mention this. If one asks, "Does the state of truth change according to time?" the answer is that the state in which truth manifests changes, but it never becomes false. The seasons that come in a year, the small periods that come in a day, and so on, are divisions of time, and according to them, the efforts, discipline, etc., of living beings in the world are regulated. We see with our own eyes that these change according to time. Time is a Tattva (principle); it is one of the seven Vidya Tattvas. Therefore, the state in which truth manifests changes according to time, but it never becomes false; this is the rule. Sivakavimani Desikanar also writes about some incidents he experienced. The commentator was also a lawyer in Coimbatore in those days; this is his history. So he gives examples and truths he has seen. A rich man gave false testimony in a criminal court. As soon as he got down from the witness stand, his eyesight disappeared. He went home with the help of others, groping with his hands and feet. His eyesight remained lost until he died. He mentions this incident. He also mentions another incident. Similarly, a rich man gave false testimony in a civil court. From that day on, he fell ill and died within a month. There are many such incidents. Therefore, our ancestors, having seen the truth, advise us not to act too boldly, thinking that the consequences of breaking a vow will not happen immediately. They tell us to live according to the path of truth and be saved. Now, the next part of this verse: Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, realizing that his eyesight had disappeared because he had broken the vow, says that he will sing to the Lord to remove this suffering. The verse says, "I will sing to the Lord for this suffering to be removed." Now, another question arises: "If one does bad things and then suffers the consequences, will singing to the Lord remove it? If so, then these principles give room for those who do evil to do evil, and then pray to the Lord, sing praises, and escape the consequences of their evil deeds." Some people may raise such questions. Engaging living beings in evil deeds is an act of ignorance, which is the darkness of "aanavam" (ego). It is an evil act. Seeking a solution for it, realizing that it is an evil act, is an act of knowledge that living beings acquire when the Lord reveals it. Therefore, it is a rule to seek solutions for all the evil deeds one has done with the help of that knowledge. Just as a person who lives without adhering to the rules prescribed by scriptures, and thus falls ill, seeks a doctor and tries to recover from the illness with the doctor's help, here, singing to the Lord is a medicine to remove the suffering caused by the evil deeds one has committed. This is the truth stated in the Gnana Sastras. Just as a doctor, when truthfully informed about the disease and its history, gives medicine accordingly, so too the Lord, who is the physician of karma, will cure the disease of karma by prescribing the appropriate time and other factors for experiencing and exhausting it. Therefore, remembering the Lord and praising the Lord are the prescribed stages and remedies for the solution of that evil deed. It is true that the disease of karma cannot be exhausted without experiencing it. If people realize their faults, feel remorse, and truly melt and pray to the Lord, the Lord, out of compassion, will remove their suffering. Some people research this. In fact, forgiveness of sins is not a principle of Saivism. It is a principle of external religions like Christianity. It is these principles that encourage people to engage in evil deeds. But the truth discovered by Saivism is that if one remembers and praises the Lord, it acts as a medicine for that disease, and the Lord manifests within it and bestows grace for the ripening of karma in living beings. He will exhaust the consequences of that sin as physical karma, or He will make them experience and exhaust that suffering quickly, or He will make them experience and exhaust that suffering without even knowing that they are experiencing suffering. Therefore, in some way, the Lord bestows grace only after making living beings experience the sufferings appropriate to the karma they have done. This is the principle of Saivism. The Thiruppasuram states, "The way He bestows grace upon His devotees and His prime greatness are immeasurable if one tries to describe them. One need not speak. The principles and actions do not approach. Those who bow down and stand firm are worthy of hearing these." The Thiruvakku of Sivagnana Bodham is, "It is the duty of the leader to protect those who seek refuge." Therefore, the karma of those who worship the Lord will be destroyed in the way mentioned above, and not by the principle of forgiveness of sins. We must understand this. Even in the Thiruppathikams that came from our Paramacharyas, as benefits of the Thiruppathikam, it is said that the karma of those who sing this Thiruppathikam and worship the Lord will be destroyed or will flee. All these mean that the Lord's nature of bestowing grace upon living beings is as explained above. In the upcoming historical accounts, wherever such instances occur, we must understand the histories by keeping this truth in mind. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, praying to the Lord and thinking, "I will remove this suffering; I will sing to the Lord for this suffering to be removed," composes a Thiruppathikam remembering the Lord of Ottiyur. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 881, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the Lord of Thiruvottiyur and sings the Thiruppathikam that begins with "Azhukku Meykodu" (With a soiled body). He sings this Thiruppathikam with a humble heart, praising and worshipping the primal Lord of Thiruvottiyur. He prays and appeals to the Lord's lotus-like feet, asking for the removal of the fault that has befallen him. He is in a state where he has lost his support, and since he has lost his eyesight, he needs the help of others to protect him and guide him. He grieves, thinking, "I lost my eyesight because I broke the vow I made to Sangiliyar, and now people are saying many bad things about me!" He remembers the Lord and sings the Thiruppathikam that begins with "Azhukku Meykodu." This Thiruppathikam belongs to the sacred place of Thiruvottiyur. It is the 54th Thiruppathikam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkēsi. This Thiruppathikam is as follows:

Thiruchitrambalam. "Aḻukku meykkoṭu uṉ tiruvaṭi aṭaintēṉ atuvum nāṉ paṭaṟpālatu aṉṟu āṉāl Piḻukkai vāriyum pāl koḷvar aṭikēḷ piḻaippaṉ ākilum tiruvaṭi piḻaiyēṉ Vaḻukki vīḻiṉum tiruppeyar allāl maṟṟu nāṉ aṟiyēṉ maṟu māṟṟam Oḻukka eṉ kaṇukku oru maruntu uraiyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kaṭṭaṉēṉ piṟantēṉ uṉakku āḷāy kātal caṅkili kāraṇamāka Eṭṭiṉāl tikaḻum tirumūrtti eṉ ceyvāṉ aṭiyēṉ eṭuttu uraippēṉ Peṭṭaṉ ākilum tiruvaṭi piḻaiyēṉ piḻaippaṉākilum tiruvaṭikku aṭimai Oṭṭiṉēṉ eṉṉai nī ceyvatu ellām oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kaṅkai taṅkiya caṭaivuṭai karumpē kaṭṭiyē palarkkum kaḷai kaṇṇē Aṅkai nelliyiṉ paḻattu iṭai amutē attā eṉ iṭar ārkku eṭuttu uraippēṉ Caṅkum ippiyum calañcalam murala vayaṟam muttoṭu poṉmaṇi varaṉṟi Ōṅkumā kaṭal ōtam vantu ulavum oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Īṉṟu koṇṭatu ōr cuṟṟam ōṉṟu aṉṟāl yāvarākil eṉ aṉpu uṭaiyārkaḷ Tōṉṟa niṉṟu aruḷ ceytu aḻittiṭṭāl colluvārai allātaṉa collāy Mūṉṟu kaṇ uṭaiyāy aṭiyēṉ kaṇkoḷvatē kaṇakku vaḻakkākil Ūṉṟukōl eṉakku āvatu oṉṟu aruḷāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Vaḻitta paṭuvāṉ muyalkiṉṟēṉ uṉṉai pōl eṉṉai pāvikka māṭṭēṉ Cuḻittalaippaṭṭa nīr atupōla cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ cuḻalkiṉṟatu eṉ uḷḷam Kaḻittalaippaṭṭa nāyatu pōla oruvaṉ kōlpaṟṟi karakara iḻukkai Oḻittu nī aruḷ āyiṉa ceyyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Māṉai nōkkiyaṟ kaṇvalaippaṭṭu varunti yāṉ uṟṟa valviṉaikku añci Tēṉaiyāṭiya koṉṟaiyiṉāy uṉ cīlamum kuṇamum cintiyātē Nāṉum ittaṉai vēṇṭuvatu aṭiyēṉ uyiroṭum nakar narakattu aḻuntāmai Ūṉam uḷḷaṉa tīrttu aruḷ ceyyāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Maṟṟu tēvarai niṉaintu uṉai maṟavēṉ neñciṉāru vāḻavu māṭṭēṉ Peṟṟiruntu peṟātu oḻukiṉṟa pētaiyēṉ piḻaittiṭṭatai aṟiyēṉ Muṟṟum nī eṉṉai muṉintiṭa aṭiyēṉ kaṭavatu eṉ uṉai nāṉ maṟavaṉēl Uṟṟa nōy uṟuppiṉi tavirttu aruḷāy oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Kūṭiṉāy malai maṅkaiyai niṉaiyāy kaṅkai āyiram mukam uṭaiyāḷai Cūṭiṉāy eṉṟu colliya pukkal toḻumpaṉēṉukku collalum āmē Vāṭi nī iruntu eṉ ceyti maṉamē varunti yāṉ uṟṟa valviṉaikku añci Ūṭiṉāl iṉi āvatu oṉṟu uṇṭē oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Makattil pukkatōr caṉi eṉakku āṉāy maintaṉē maṇiyē maṇavāḻā Akatil peṇṭukaḷ nāṉ oṉṟu coṉṉāl aḻaiyal pō kuruṭā eṉa tariyē Mukattil kaṇ iḻantu eṅkaṉam vāḻkēṉ mukkaṉā muṟaiyō maṟaivōti Ukaikkum taṉ kaṭal ōtam vantu ulavum oṟṟiyūr eṉum ūr uṟaivāṉē"

"Ōtam vantu ulavum karaitaṉ mēl oṟṟiyūr urai celvaṉai nāḷum Ñālattāṉ paravappaṭukiṉṟa nālmaṟai aṅkam ōtiya nāvaṉ Cīlattāṉ peritum mika valla ciṟuvaṉ vaṉ tuṇṭaṉ ūraṉ uraita pāṭal Pattu ivai vallavar tām pōy parakati tiṇṇam naṇṇuvar tāmē"

Thiruchitrambalam. This Thiruppathikam, sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to the Lord of Thiruvottiyur, is very moving. In this Thiruppathikam, the phrases "Even if I am a sinner, I will not abandon your feet, O Lord, who accepts even the dung and milk," and "O three-eyed one, if my eyes are to be counted as a debt, then grant me a staff," and "Like a dog dragged by a stick, remove my suffering and do what is good for me," and "O Saturn who entered my Magam (birth star), how can I live with blind eyes, O three-eyed one, is this justice?" are parts that bring tears to our eyes. This Thiruppathikam was sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal as he left Thiruvottiyur and proceeded towards Thiruvarur, with an unceending love for Thiruvarur. He sings, "With a soiled body, I have reached your feet." "Azhukku" (soiled) refers to the state of impurity, full of dirt like falsehood, not only in the inner faculties but also external impurities. It also refers to the body itself being impure. It signifies the need to think of Lord Shiva in a way that all these impurities should be washed away. The phrase "Piḻukkai vāriyum pāl koḷvar" (They will take the milk even if it has dung in it) is a proverb. Those who raise goats, when they milk the goats, sometimes goat dung falls into the milk. But they remove it from the milk and keep the milk. Similarly, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings to the Lord, "Why don't you purify me by removing my impurities and accept only my loving services? You should accept them in that way." At the same time, he sings to the Lord, "Even if I err, I will not abandon your feet; even if I stumble, I have never strayed from my love for your feet." He further sings in the Thirumullaivayil Thiruppathikam, "I have done many excesses, acting disrespectfully and stubbornly, like a madman." Therefore, these are not Shiva offences. These are merely worldly interactions that disappear. True Shiva offences are those for which there is no atonement. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says here, "I will not abandon your feet." He means, "I have not committed any Shiva offence. Even if I have erred in worldly matters, I have not committed any error in loving your feet." The merits that exist are building ponds, digging wells, providing water shelters, giving medicine, etc. These are "pasu punniyangal" (merits related to the soul). "Pathi punniyangal" (merits related to the Lord) are those that gradually lead to Shivam (liberation) by remembering Shiva. These Pathi punniyangal ultimately lead to moksha (salvation), which is attaining the Lord's feet. Pasu punniyangal, however, lead to enjoyments in heaven and other realms, and without remembering Shiva, they lead to repeated births. Therefore, one must understand Pathi punniyangal and Pasu punniyangal very well, understand the difference between them, and perform Pathi punniyangal to end rebirth. Pathi punniyangal should not be performed on par with Pasu punniyangal. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says, "Even if I stumble, I do not know any other name than your sacred name. Tell me a medicine for my eyes to see." Therefore, it is a good habit to always remember and utter the name of Shiva without ceasing, no matter what joys or sorrows come. Practicing this will bring great benefit. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppandi Kodumudi Thiruppathikam states, "Even if I forget you, O Lord, I will utter 'Namassivaya' (Hail Shiva)." But one should not think that all this will come easily. It does not come easily. It comes as a result of penance and long practice. He continues to sing in the next verse, "Even if I am a liar, I will not abandon your feet." "Pettan" means liar. In the third verse, he says, "You are the nectar in the fruit of the gooseberry in the palm of my hand." This means that just as the parts of a gooseberry, from the outer part of the fruit to the seed inside, are clearly visible when placed in the palm of the hand, so too the Lord reveals His grace to those who see Him. The Thiruvachagam states, "The gooseberry in the palm of my hand." Therefore, no matter who they are, if they surrender themselves to Him with love, He will not speak words that will cause them suffering. "O Lord, who has three eyes, you have made me lose the sight of my two eyes! Is this your grace? You have hidden my eyesight. Now, at least give me a staff." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asked for a staff, unable to even find one for himself. This is a truth we can see here. Isn't it a proverb that "the God who gave eyes will give a staff"? Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, relying on the Lord's grace, prays, "I will not even try to find a small staff for myself; you yourself must grant it." We are about to see that the Lord grants the staff in Thiruvenpakkam. "Suzhithalaippatta Neer" (water caught in a whirlpool) means water in a whirlpool. Just as it spins without stability, I am confused and spinning, and my mind is also spinning in confusion. I am like a dog tied to a stick and dragged. Living with lost eyesight is like living in hell. Even though I had received your grace before, I am a fool who has not received that grace now and has lost my eyesight. I do not know what great mistake I made to deserve this loss of eyesight. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings all this. He sings, grieving that he lost his eyesight because he forgot the vow. But even now, he sings, "I don't know what mistake I made to lose my eyesight to this extent." This is because the suffering that has come upon him now, even though he never forgets the Lord's feet, is a suffering that is disproportionate to his actions, as Sundaramoorthy Swamigal thought in his sacred heart. We also see that he appeals for its removal. He addresses the Lord as "Makathil Pukkatōr Sani Enakku Aanay" (You have become like Saturn entering my Magam star). Astrological texts state that the period when Saturn transits the Magam star is a time of great suffering. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal appeals to the Lord, saying that suffering like that has come upon him. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composes this Thiruppathikam with various beautiful analogies, very movingly. Moreover, from the time he left Thiruvottiyur until he reached Thiruvarur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's sacred history is a heart-wrenching one, and the Thiruppathikams he composed are heart-wrenching. After crossing the boundary of Thiruvottiyur, Nambigal (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), who had lost his eyesight, proceeds to Thiruvarur from there. On the way, he reaches the sacred place of Thirumullaivayil and prays, "Remove my suffering, O Lord." In the same state, he goes to Thiruvenpakkam and appeals to the Lord. The Lord there grants Sundaramoorthy Swamigal a staff and says, "We are here; you may go." After that, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships at Thiruvallangadu and Thiruvooral, and then goes to Thirukachiyekambam and worships. There, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal regains the sight of his left eye. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then leaves Kanchi, worships at Thiruaamathur, Thirunelvayil Arathurai, and Thiruavaduthurai, and then worships at Thiruthuruthi, where he is cured of the skin disease on his body. Then he goes to Thiruvarur and worships, and also regains the sight of his right eye. The Thiruppathikams he composed at these times are very moving. They are Thiruppathikams that are rich in Tamil, containing the essence of sorrow. They are Thiruppathikams that are excellent in word, meaning, and composition. They are Thiruppathikams that serve as excellent internal evidence for Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's sacred history. We mostly see that these Thiruppathikams are set to the tune of Thakkēsi. We see that the Thiruthandagam Thiruppathikams in Thirunavukkarasar Peruman's Thiruppathikams, the Thiruppathikams set to the tune of Megaraga Kurinji in Pillaiyar's Thiruppathikams, and the Thiruppathikams set to the tune of Thakkēsi in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppathikams are greatly excellent in moving the hearts of anyone. We hope that devotees will study these deeply and benefit. Sekkizhar Peruman, taking Nambigal's sacred heart as his own, explains this history in this section in 38 verses, from the 274th verse to the 311th verse. Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman arranges it. Therefore, we will continue to contemplate the upcoming historical sections. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 882, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal departs from Thiruvottiyur, praising and worshipping the Lord, and continues to sing Thiruppathikams. Even though Nambigal praised and appealed to the Lord of Thiruvottiyur, the Lord remained silent. Even the state where the Lord does not bestow grace is indeed grace. Sivagnana Siddhiyar states this: "All that the Lord does is grace in every state." Due to his love for worshipping Thiruvarur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal does not think of returning to Thiruvottiyur, and without minding his lost eyesight, he continues to proceed towards Thiruvarur. On the way, he reaches the sacred place of Thirumullaivayil, near Chennai. His attendants guide Sundaramoorthy Swamigal by holding his hand, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches Thirumullaivayil. There, he worships the Lord and composes a Thiruppathikam, expressing how his eyes were hidden for Sangili. In that Thiruppathikam, composed at the sacred place of Vadathirumullaivayil, the history of that sacred place mentions how the Lord of Thirumullaivayil had bestowed grace upon Thondaiman in the past. He praises that ancient generosity and prays to the Lord of Thirumullaivayil to remove his severe suffering. "Aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyar kaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē" (Remove my suffering, O Pasupatha, Supreme Light) is the refrain that appears in the Thiruppathikam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings this in every verse of the Thiruppathikam.

Thus, the Thiruppathikam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for the sacred place of Vadathirumullaivayil is the 69th Thiruppathikam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkēsi. The verses of this Thiruppathikam are as follows:

Thiruchitrambalam. "Tiruvum meypporuḷum celvamum eṉakku uṉ cīrvuṭaikkaḻalkaḷ eṉṟueṇṇi Oruvarai matiyātu urāmaikaḷ ceytum ūṭiyum uraippaṉāytirivēṉ Murukamarcōlai cūḻ tirumullaivāyilāy vāyiṉāl uṉṉai paraviṭum aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyar kaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Kūṭiya iḷaiyam cati piḻaiyāmai koṭiyiṭai umaiyavaḻkāṇa Āṭiya aḻakā arumaṟai poruḷē aṅkaṉā eṅkuvuṟṟāy eṉṟu Tēṭiya vāṉōr cēr tirumullaivāyilāy tiruppukaḻ viruppāl Pāṭiya aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyar kaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Viṇpaṉiṉ ēttum vētiyā mātar veṟuviṭa vēḻum aṉṟu urittāy Ceṇpakac cōlai cūḻ tirumullaivāyilāy tēvartam aracē taṉ poḻil oṟṟi Mānakar uṭaiyāy caṅkilikkā eṉ kaṇkoṇṭa paṇpaṉiṉ aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyar kaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Poṉṉalam kaḻaṉi putuvirai maruvi poṟivaṟivaṇṭu icaippāṭa Aṉṉalaṅkamala taviciṉmēl uṟaṅkum aḷavaṉ vantu ulaviṭa Aḷḷal ceṉṉel aṅkaḻaṉicūḻ tirumullaivāyilāy tiruppukaḻviruppāl Paṉṉalaṉ tamiḻāl pāṭuvēṟku aruḷāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Cantaṉavēṟum kārakil kuraṭum taṉmayil pīliyum kariyin Tantamum taraḷa kuvaiyum pavaḷakkoṭikaḷum cumantu koṇṭu Unti vantu iḻi pāli vaṭakarai mullaivāyilāy Mācilā maṇiyē pantaṉai keṭuttu eṉ paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Maṟṟu nāṉ peṟṟatu ār peṟavallār vaḷḷalē kaḷḷamē pēci Kuṟṟamē ceyyiṉum kuṇameṉa koḷḷum koḷkaiyāṉ mikaipala ceytēṉ Ceṟṟumītu ōṭum tiripuram eritta tirumullaivāyilāy aṭiyēṉ Paṟṟiyilēṉ uṟṟa paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Maṇikaḻu cevvāy veṇṇakai kariya vārkuḻal māmaiyil cāyal Aṇikaḻu koṅkai aṅkaiyarkaṇṇār aruṇaṭam āṭal aṟāta Tiṇipoḻil taḻuvu tirumullaivāyil celvaṉē elliyum pakalum Paṇiyatu ceyvēṉ paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Nampaṉē aṉṟu veṇṇai nallūril nāyiṉēṉ taṉai āṭkoṇṭa Campuvē umparār toḻutu ēttum taṭaṅkaṭal nañcuvuṇṭa kaṇṭā Cempoṉmāḷikai cūḻ tirumullaivāyil tēṭiyāṉ tiritarvēṉ kaṇṭa Paimpoṉē aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Maṭṭulām malarkoṇṭu aṭiyai vaṇaṅkum māṇi taṉmēl matiyātē Kaṭṭuvāṉ vanta kālaṉai māḻa kāliṉāl āṟuyir cekutta Ciṭṭaṉē celva tirumullaivāyil celvaṉē ceḻumaṟai pakarnta Paṭṭaṉē aṭiyēṉ paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Collarum pukaḻāṉ toṇṭaimāṉ kaḻiṟṟai cūḻkoṭi mullai kaṭṭiṭṭu Ellaiyil iṉpam avaṉ peṟa veḷippaṭṭu aruḷiya iṟaivaṉē eṉṟum Nallavar paravum tirumullaivāyil nātaṉē naraiviṭai ēṟi Palkalai poruḷē paṭutuyarkaḷaiyāy pācupatā parañcuṭarē"

"Viraitaru malarmēl ayaṉoṭu mālum veṟuviṭa nīṇṭa emmāṉai Tiraitaru puṉalcūḻ tirumullaivāyil celvaṉai nāval ārūraṉ Uraitaru mālai ōr añciṉoṭu añcum uḷkuḷirntu ēttavallārkaḷ Narai tirai mūppum naṭalaiyum niṉṟi naṇṇuvar viṇṇavarkku aracē"

Thiruchitrambalam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, "Wealth, true substance, and prosperity are your glorious feet to me," and "I have wandered, speaking disrespectfully and stubbornly, not valuing anyone," expressing the idea that those who rely solely on the Lord need not value anything else in the world. We also recall the sacred words of Thirunavukkarasar Peruman here: "We are not slaves to anyone," and "There is nothing to fear, and nothing to come that will cause fear." Thus, after worshipping at Thirumullaivayil, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal proceeds to Thiruvenpakkam. The devotees in that town, seeing Sundaramoorthy Swamigal arriving at Thiruvenpakkam, come to meet him and lead him. The sacred place of Thiruvenpakkam is currently submerged in the Poondi reservoir near Chennai. The 279th verse:

"Aṇainta toṇṭarkaḷ uṭaṉ vaḷamāka aṅkaṉ nāyakar kōyil muṉ eyti Kuṇaṅkaḷ ēntiyē paravi añcaliyāl kuvitta kai talaimēl koṇṭu niṉṟu Vaṇaṅki nīr makiḻkōyil uḷḷīrē eṉṟa vaṉ toṇṭaṟku ūṉṟukōl aruḷi Iṇaṅkilā moḻiyāl uḷum pōkīr eṉṟu iyaṃpiṉār ētilār pōla"

As mentioned earlier, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, accompanied by the devotees who came to meet him, circumambulated and reached the front of the Lord of Thiruvenpakkam's temple. He praised all the Lord's gracious qualities, worshipped with folded hands raised above his head, and asked, "O Lord, are you residing happily inside this temple?" The Lord then granted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal a staff and, like a stranger, said, "We are here; you may go." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asks the Lord, "Are you residing happily inside this temple?" because he cannot see the Lord directly with his eyes. He asks this because the Lord has not yet bestowed grace upon him. Therefore, understanding that the Lord is not shining brightly inside the temple, he asks, "Are you residing happily inside this temple?" Sundaramoorthy Swamigal knows that the Lord has resided alternately in Thiruvottiyur, under the Magizha tree, and inside the temple. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's question implies, "Are you here inside the temple, or under the Magizha tree?" Earlier, in the Thiruvottiyur Thiruppathikam, he had asked, "Can't you even give me a staff?" Accordingly, the Lord of Thiruvenpakkam gives a staff to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and says, "You asked if we are inside this temple. We are here. You may go." Because the Lord said, "Uḷōm Pōkīr" (We are here, you may go), this sacred place is also known as "Uḷōm Pōkīr Puram" (the place where the Lord said, 'We are here, you may go'), as seen in inscriptions. Thus, the Lord speaks to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal like a stranger, using unfamiliar words. The 280th verse:

"Piḻaivuḷḷaṉa poruttiṭuvar eṉṟu eṭuttu peṇ pākam Viḷaivaṭivil perumāṉai veṇpākkam makiḻntāṉai Aṇinta iṟaiyāṉai pāṭiṉār maḻai tavaḷum neṭumcai Nāvalūr maṉṉavaṉār eṉpatu tiruppāṭal"

The Lord granted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal a staff and said, "Uḷōm Pōkīr." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then sings a Thiruppathikam to the Lord of Thiruvenpakkam, beginning with "Piḻaiyuḷḷaṉa Poruttiṭuvar" (He will forgive faults). Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings about the Lord who delights in Thiruvenpakkam, who is praised by devotees as "Sankaraparanam" (adorned with a snake), and who is adorned with a snake. By singing that the Lord has a feminine half, he implies that the Lord is the abode of compassion. By singing that the Lord approaches snakes, he implies that the Lord accepts even evil as good. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's notes of appeal are embedded in this Thiruppathikam. Thus, the Thiruppathikam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvenpakkam is the 89th Thiruppathikam in the 7th Thirumurai, set to the tune of Seekamarappann. The 1st, 9th, 10th, and 11th verses of this Thiruppathikam are as follows:

Thiruchitrambalam. "Piḻaiyuḷḷaṉa poruttiṭuvar eṉṟu aṭiyēṉ piḻaitta Kāl paḻiyataṉai pārātē paṭalam eṉ kaṇ maṟaippittāy Kuḻaiviravu vaṭikātā kōyiluḷāyō eṉṉa Uḷaiyuṭaiyāṉ uḷḷiruntu uḷōmpōkīr eṉṟāṉē"

"Poṉṉavilum koṉṟaiyiṉāy pōy makiḻkīḻkiru eṉṟu Coṉṉa eṉ kāṇāmē cūḷuṟavu makiḻkīḻē Eṉṉavalla perumāṉē iṅkiruntāyō eṉṉa Oṉṉalarai kaṇṭāl pōl uḷōmpōkīr eṉṟāṉē"

"Māṇṭikaḷum caṅkiliyai tantuvaru payaṉkaḷellām Tōṉṟa aruḷ ceytu aḻittāy eṉṟu uraiikka ulakamellām Īṉṟavaṉē veṇkōyil iṅkiruntāyō eṉṉa Ūṉṟuvatōr kōl aruḷi uḷōmpōkīr eṉṟāṉē"

"Ērārūm poḻil nilavu veṇpākkam iṭam koṇṭa Kārārūm iṭaṟṟāṉai kātalittiṭṭa aṉpiṉṉoṭum Cīrārūm tiruvārūr civaṉ pēr ceṉṉaiyil vaitta Ārūraṉ tamiḻ vallārkku aṭaiyā valviṉai tāṉē"

Thiruchitrambalam. In every verse of this Thiruppathikam, we see Sundaramoorthy Swamigal singing with a melting heart, "Uḷōm Pōkīr eṉṟāṉē" (He said, 'We are here, you may go'). This sacred place of Thiruvenpakkam is the 17th sacred place in Thondai Nadu. It is also known as Thiruvulampudur and Uḷōm Pōkīr Puram. Thiruvenpakkam is submerged in the Poondi reservoir. When the Poondi reservoir, which was created for Chennai's drinking water, was expanded, this temple was submerged. Therefore, the Shiva idols from there were taken and installed in another place, where they are worshipped. The Lord is Venpakkanathar. The Goddess is Minnal Oli Ammai (Goddess of Lightning Light) and Kanivay Mozhi Ammai (Goddess of Sweet-Speaking Mouth). The Sthala Vriksham (sacred tree) is the Ilanthai tree. The idol of Nambigal with the staff is in this temple. The Goddess guided Sundaramoorthy Swamigal like lightning, intermittently. Therefore, the Goddess in this sacred place is named Minnal Oli Ammai. Thiruvallur is to its northwest, on the road to Thiruppachur, on the way to Oottukkottai. This sacred place is submerged in the reservoir and is therefore inaccessible. The 281st verse:

"Muṉṉiṉṟu muṟaippāṭu pōl moḻinta moḻimālai Paṇṇum icai tiruppatikam pāṭiya piṉ paṟṟāya Eṉṉuṭaiya pirāṉ aruḷ iṅku ittaṉai kolām eṉṟu Maṉṉu perum toṇṭaruṭaṉ vaṇaṅkiyē vaḻi koḷvār eṉṟu amaikiṉṟatu"

After singing this musical garland of words, this melodious Thiruppathikam, as if standing before the Lord and expressing his complaint, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships with the great devotees who were with him, thinking, "Is this all the grace of my Lord, who is my support?" Even though Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composed this Thiruppathikam as if appealing to the Lord and expressing his grievances, in reality, it is a verse that expresses joy and overflowing love, praising the Lord's grace. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman describes it as "Muṉṉiṉṟu muṟaippāṭu pōl moḻinta" (He spoke as if standing before the Lord and complaining). Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asked, "Are you here?" And the Lord, granting him a staff, replied, "We are here, you may go." In this Thiruppathikam, we see how he praises and appreciates that reply from the Lord in a friendly manner. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, worshipping the Lord with the great devotees who accompanied him, now continues his journey towards Thiruvarur. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 883, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Verses 282 and 283. "Anganardham pathiyadhanai agandru poy anbarudan pangaya poondhadam panai soozh pazhaiyanoor uzhaiyeidhi thangguvaar ammai thiruththalaiyaale valam kollum thingal mudiyar aadum thiruvalangattin munnindru thozhuthu ethi muththa endru eduththaruli pannum isai thiruppadhigam paadi magizhndhu eththuvaar annindru vananggi poy thiruvooral amarndhu irainji kanni madhil manimaadak kaanchi maanagar anaindhaar enbavai thiruppaadalkal." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having departed from Thiruvenpakkam, proceeds further with the devotees and reaches the boundary of the holy place of Thiruvalangadu.

We see that Thiruvalangadu and Pazhaiyanoor are sung about as a single holy place. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches the boundary of Thiruvalangadu, a place surrounded by lotus-filled ponds and palm trees, where Ammai (Karaikkal Ammaiyar) circumambulated with her head. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having reached the boundary of Thiruvalangadu, stays there without entering the holy place. The greatness of Thiruvalangadu is that it is circumambulated and worshipped. We see that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stayed outside in this manner. In the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, we saw the historical event where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also stayed outside without entering this holy place. This is the place where Ammai walked with her head, isn't it? "Ammai" (mother) here refers to Karaikkal Ammaiyar. If "Ammai" is said plainly, it refers to Karaikkal Ammaiyar in the Saivite tradition. Due to her immeasurable greatness, and the custom of not even uttering her name, she is revered as "Ammai" in the Saivite tradition. We recall here that Sekkizhar Peruman has already shown that Appar also praised Thiruvalangadu. We also see that the Thiruppadhigam (hymn) composed by Ammai is known as "Mootha Thiruppadhigam" (Elder Thiruppadhigam).

We have seen in detail the history of Ammaiyar circumambulating Thiruvalangadu with her head in Ammaiyar's Puranam. Here, we contemplated the state of Ammai, who is seated in Thiruvalangadu, singing at the feet of the Lord and attaining bliss. The Lord is the one who performed the dance of Urdhuva Thandavam, lifting his foot high up to the heavens, and performing the cosmic dance. His dance happens here eternally. This is one of the five great halls of the Lord, known as Rathnasabai (Hall of Gems). Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, standing and worshipping this holy temple, composes a Thiruppadhigam. This Thiruppadhigam is for the holy place of Thiruvalangadu, set in the ancient Panjara Pann (melody), and is the 52nd Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai.

The Thiruppadhigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Muttha muththitharavalla mugil menmulaiyal umai panggaa Siththa siththi thiram kaattum sivane thevar singgame Paththa paththar palar pottum paramaa pazhaiyanoormeya Aththa alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Poyye seythu puramburame thiriven thannai pokamai Meyye vandhu ingu ena aanda meyya meyyar meypporule Paiyaadu aravam araikkasaiththa paramaa pazhaiyanoor meya Aiya alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Thoondaa vilakkin narchothi thozhuvaarththangal thuyar theerppay Poondaay elumbai puram moondrum podiyaachchatra ponniyane Paandu aal vinaigal avai theerkkum paramaa pazhaiyanoormeya Aandaa alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aaven. Mari ner onkan madanallaar valaiyil pattu madhimayanggi Arive azhindhen aiyaa naan maiyaar kandam udaiyaane Pariya vinaigal avai theerkkum paramaa pazhaiyanoor meya Arive alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Velangadu thadangannar valaiyul pattu un neri marandhu Malanggu aadi marandhozhindhen maniye muththe maragathame Palanggu aadi neyyaadi padarpun sadaiyaay pazhaiyanoor Alangadaa unnudaiya adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Ennar thangal eyil eytha enthaay enthai perumaane Kannay ulagam kaakkindra karuthaa thiruththalagaathaay Pannar isaigal avai kondu palarum eththum pazhaiyanoor Anna alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Vandar kuzhali umai nangai pangga Gangai manavaazhaa vindar purangal eriseytha vidaiyaay veda neriyane Pandaal vinaigal pala theerkkum paramaa pazhaiyanoor meya Anda alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Pezhvaay aravin anaiyaanum periya malarmel urai vanum Thaazhaadhu un than saran paniyath thazhalaay nindra thaththuvane Paazhaam vinaigal avai theerkkum paramaa pazhaiyanoor thannai Aazhvaay alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Emman enthai mooththappan ezhil padigaal emaiyaanda Pemman eema purangattil peyodu aadal purivaane Palmaa malargal avai kondu palarum eththum pazhaiyanoor Ammaa alangadaa un adiyaarkku adiyen aavene. Paththar siththar palar eththum paraman pazhaiyanoor meya Aththan alangadan than adimaiththirame Anbaagi siththar siththam vaiththa pugazh siruvan oorana on thamizhgal Paththum paadi aaduvaar paramanadiye panivare." Thiruchitrambalam. Having composed this melodious Thiruppadhigam, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal departs from here, worships the holy place of Thakkolam, known as Thiruvooral, and reaches Kanchi Maanagar (Kanchipuram). Kanchi Maanagar is one of the seven Mukthi Sthalams (places of liberation) and the capital of Thondai Nadu. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as Kanchi Maanagar. Sekkizhar Peruman, without any delay in the journey, such as stopping along the way, quickly narrates this sacred history, showing his intention not to prolong Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's suffering, which began when his sight was obscured after crossing the boundary of Thiruvottiyur.

We see that the historical accounts in this section are moving very quickly, with the intention of not prolonging Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's suffering. From Thiruvottiyur to Kanchi Maanagar, Sekkizhar Peruman only mentioned the completion of the Thiruppadhigams sung in Thiruvenpakkam, where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was blessed with a walking stick. He quickly moved through the other holy places, mentioning the Thiruppadhigams there with verbal participles, and concluded by saying that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reached Kanchi Maanagar to receive one of his eyes. Now, Sekkizhar Peruman, with his sweet poetic skill, is going to narrate the wonderful sacred history of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal receiving the light of one of his eyes in Kanchi Maanagar.

Let us continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 884, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches Thirukachi Ekambam. Verse 284: "Thenilavu pozhil kachchi thirukkama kottamathil oonil valar uyirkkellam ozhiyaadha karunaiyinaal aana thiru arampurakkum ammai thirukkoiyilin mun vaanivalar thiruvaayil vananginaar van thondar." Thirukachi Kamakottam, surrounded by gardens filled with honeybees, is the place in Kanchipuram where Kamakshi Ammaiyar performs penance and fosters dharma (righteousness). This is where the Kamakshi Ammaiyar Temple is currently located. Ammai's compassion flows to all types of mature souls born in creation, according to their nature. Ammaiyar is compassionate to all beings equally.

This is the place where she shows compassion and fosters dharma. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal first seeks and worships Ammaiyar's grace. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the ardent devotee, worships before the towering entrance of Ammaiyar's temple, which reaches up to the sky. We have contemplated in his Puranam the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also worshipping Ammai here. The mother nurtures and matures all the countless beings that come into creation. If it is Ammai's compassionate work to provide worldly enjoyments to the beings that come into creation, then the father's work involves the five functions of protection, destruction, and recreation. Sekkizhar Peruman illustrates this in the subsequent verses.
