Verses 285 and 286: "Thozhudhu vizhundhu ezhundhu arulaal thudiththup poy thol ulagam muzhudhum azhiththu azhiththu aakkum mudhalvar thiru ekambam pazhudhil adiyaar munbu puga pukku panugindraar ezhudha yen thirumunbe yenmozhiyen endru irainji vinnaazhvaar amudhu unna mikka perum vidam unda kannaalaa kachchi ekambane kadaiyanen ennaadha pizhai poruththu ingu yaan kaana ezhil pavala vannaa kan azhiththu arulaay ena veezhndhu vananginaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal prostrates himself, rises, praises with grace, and then enters the Thiruekambam temple of the Prime Lord, who protects, destroys, and recreates all these worlds, performing the five cosmic functions. He enters behind the faultless devotees. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the Lord with grace. This implies that even to worship the Lord, one needs His grace. "Avan arulale avan thazh vananggi" (by His grace alone, one worships His feet) is from Thiruvachagam. In other holy places, it is customary and traditional to first worship the Lord and then, as a continuation of that worship, worship the Goddess. Here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships Ammaiyar separately at Thirukachi Kamakottam. Furthermore, our great Acharyas (spiritual teachers) are those who have the discipline of worshipping no one other than Lord Shiva. Here, in Kanchipuram alone, as an exception to this rule, our great Acharyas have worshipped Ammaiyar's temple.

We see this in their Puranams. Even here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal went to Ammaiyar's temple and worshipped Ammaiyar separately first. This happened by divine grace to enable Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to regain his sight. Sekkizhar Peruman states this as "Oonil valar uyirkkellam ozhiyaadha karunaiyinaal aana thiru arampurakkum ammai." We know that the Thirukamakottam where Kamakshi Ammai resides is a separate temple, and the Thiruekambam where the Lord resides is a separate temple. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships Ammai and then goes to Thiruekambam to worship. How does he worship? He worships by following behind the faultless devotees who go before him. These devotees are blessed to lead Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Therefore, they are faultless devotees. Moreover, they are devotees who remove all the faults of beings. Since Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has no eyesight, it is evident that the devotees lead the way, and he follows behind them. Furthermore, this teaches us the custom of following devotees. This is philosophical. We have also seen that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composed the Thiruthondar Thogai Thiruppadhigam about this. He enters and worships in that manner. Sundaram means falsehood. It also has a meaning of ignorance. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says this because he is a liar and therefore not worthy of speaking anything before the Lord.

"Thannenchari vadhu poyyarka poyththapin than nenje thannai sodum" (Let not one's mind know falsehood; if it does, one's own mind will punish oneself) is from Thirukkural. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal knows that the Lord, who is the life of all lives, knows the falsehood he has committed and what he desires. Therefore, he has nothing else to say to the Lord. He bows with folded hands, indicating that he has committed a mistake and is not worthy of speaking anything. "O Lord, who swallowed the great poison to enable the gods of the celestial world to drink nectar, O Lord with eyes, O Lord of Kachi Ekambam, please forgive the mistakes I, a lowly one, have committed unintentionally, and grant me sight so that I may see your beautiful coral color," thus Sundaramoorthy Swamigal pleads. "Kannalaa" (Lord with eyes) implies one who bestows grace. He implies, "Just as you swallowed poison and gave nectar, please forgive my mistakes and grant me sight." Here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal addresses the Lord as "Kachi Ekambane" (Lord of Kachi Ekambam). Kachi is the place where He openly resides. He addresses Him as "Pavala Vanna" (coral-colored), which refers to the Lord's bodily hue. He addresses Him as "Vidam Undavare" (one who swallowed poison), which refers to the Lord's nature. Therefore, in accordance with the Thiruvachagam "Munnam avanudaiya naamam kettal" (first, she heard His name), Sundaramoorthy Swamigal addresses and worships the Lord in these three ways. He tells the Lord that the mistake was not committed with the intention of doing wrong. "Kadaiyanen ennaadha pizhai" (I, a lowly one, committed an unintentional mistake), he says.

If it were a deliberate mistake, it could not be forgiven; the karmic fruit would have to be experienced to be exhausted. This is an unintentional mistake, so he pleads with the Lord to forgive this mistake, saying that he does not want to experience it any further than he already has. He says that granting him sight is not for any other reason, but to see the Lord's beautiful coral color, and therefore addresses the Lord as "Pavala Vanna." Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal pleads. Verse 287: "Pangkayach chenggai thaliraal panimalar kondu arutchiththu sengkayalkan malaivalli panindha sevadi ninaindhu ponggiya anbodhu paravi pottiya aroorarkku manggai thazhuva kuzhaindhaar maraindha idakkan koduththaar." Kanchipuram is the place where Ammai performs Shiva Puja. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, remembering the sacred feet of Thirukachi Ekambapperuman, which Ammai worshipped by scattering cool flowers with her lotus-like red tender hands, praises and worships with overflowing love. To Nambi Arooran, who thus worshipped, Thiruekambar, whose form softened when embraced by Uma Mangai, grants the sight of his lost left eye. The left side is Ammai's side. Here, it seems that because Sundaramoorthy Swamigal first worshipped Ammaiyar and received her grace, the Lord granted him the sight of his left eye. Thus, Kachi Ekambapperuman grants Sundaramoorthy Swamigal the sight of his left eye.

The place where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal lost his sight was Thiruvottiyur. He regained his left eye in Thirukachi Ekambam. He is yet to regain his right eye in Thiruvarur. These three places—Thiruvottiyur, Kanchipuram (Thirukachi Ekambam), and Thiruvarur—are Prithvi Sthalams (earth element places). As the saying goes, "Oduggi malarththulladhaam," whatever merges somewhere will reappear from there. Moreover, earth (mann) is the first of the 36 Tattvas (principles), and the nature of the first element, Prithvi, is suitable for creation and manifestation. Therefore, such divine miracles have occurred in these places. Upon regaining the sight of his left eye, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the Lord and composes a Thiruppadhigam. Verse 288: "Gnnalanthan idandhavanum nalir visumbu kadandhavanum moolanthan arivariyark kannaliththu mulaichchuvattu kolanthan kaattudhalum kurugi vizhundhu ezhundhu kazhiththu aalanthan ugandhavan endru eduththu aadi paadinaar." Thirumal, who dug the earth, and Brahma, who tried to cross the sky, could not find the beginning and end of our Lord. Our Lord stood unknowable to them. To show Sundaramoorthy Swamigal His form, which bears the mark of Ammai's embrace, He grants him one eye and enables him to see. "Kaattuviththal aaroruvar kaanaadhaare" (who can see unless He shows?) is a saying from Thevaram. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is one who always sees the Lord with his inner eye in a state of Shiva Yoga.

Now, the Lord has granted him sight to see Him with his outer eye as well. Thus, He enabled him to see. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composes the Thiruppadhigam beginning with "Aalanthan ugandhu," aligning with the theme "Kaana kan adiyen petravare" (I, your servant, have received eyes to see). Since he first worshipped Ammaiyar and received her grace, it is implied that the Lord showed him the form bearing the mark of Ammaiyar's embrace. The Thiruppadhigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is the 61st Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Thakkési Pann (melody). The first, tenth, and eleventh verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Aalanthan ugandhu amudhu seythaanai aadhiyai amarar thozhudhiyeththum Seelanthan peridhum udaiyaanai sindhippar avar sindhai ulaanaai ezhavaar Kuzhalaal umai nangai endrum eththi vazhipada petra kaalakaalanai Kamban emmaanai kaanakkan adiyen petravare. Elgalindri imayavarkonai eesanai vazhipaadu seyvaal pol Ullaththu ulgi ugandhu umai nangai vazhipadach chendru nindravaa kandu Vellam kaatti veruttida anji verivioadi thazhuva velipatta Kallakkambanai engal piraanai kaanakkan adiyen petravare. Petram eru ugandhu era vallaanai periya emperumaan endru eppodhum Katravan paravappaduvaanai kaanakkan adiyen petradhu endru Kottravan kamban kooththan emmaanai kulirpozhil thiru naaval arooran Nattramizh ivai eer aindhum vallar nanneri ulagu eyththuvarthame." Thiruchitrambalam. Verse 289: "Paadi miga paravasamaay panivaarkku paavaivudan neediya kolam kaatta niraindha viruppudan irainji soodiya anjaliyinaray thozhudhu purambondhu anbu koodiya mey thondarvudan kumbittu angu inidhu amarvaar enbadhu thiruppaadal." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, thus singing, becomes greatly ecstatic and bows. The Lord shows him His long form, accompanied by the Goddess. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with overflowing desire, worships Him, bows with folded hands on his head, and then comes out of the temple. He then joins the true devotees, bows with them, and happily resides there. Let us continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 885, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after regaining his left eye in Kanchipuram, stays there for a few days, worships the Lord, and then begins his pilgrimage towards Thiruvarur. Verses 290 and 291: "Maamalaiyaal mulaichchuvadum valaiththazhumbum anindha madhippoo malivaar sadaiyarai pottri aruladhu aagaththé malarvaar pozhil kaanchi thirunagaram kadandhu agazhvaar paamalar maalai padhigam thiruvaroor mel paravi andhiyum nanpagalum ena eduththu aarvaththudan nasaiyaal enthai piraan thiruvaroor endru kol eythuvadhu endru sandha isai paadi poy thaanggariya aadharavu vandhu anaiya anbarudan magizhndhu vazhi kolgindraar enbavai thiruppaadalkal." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises the Lord with long matted hair, who bears the mark of Ammaiyar's embrace and the scar from her bangles, and whose grace is abundant. The Lord's grace to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal in Kanchipuram is limited to granting only his left eye. Having received the Lord's grace, he crosses the boundary of Kanchi city and proceeds towards Thiruvarur. At that time, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composes a Thiruppadhigam remembering Thiruvarur. It is the Thiruppadhigam that begins with "Andhiyum Nanpagalum" (Dusk and Noon). In it, he sings with melodious rhythm, indicating his desire to know when he will reach the Lord's Thiruvarur. "Enthai piraan thiruvaroor endru kol eythuvadhu" (When will I reach my Lord's Thiruvarur?) is the theme and inner meaning of this Thiruppadhigam.

In each verse of this Thiruppadhigam, which begins with "Andhiyum Nanpagalum," Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asks, "Endru kol eythuvadhe?" (When will I reach?). These lines form the crown of the Thiruppadhigam. He praises the Lord of Aroor in various ways in all the verses, saying, "Enthai piranarai en uyirkku in amudhai idubali kolliyai ezhulagaazhiyai en maniyai em iraiyai" (My Lord, the sweet nectar of my life, who receives offerings, the ruler of the seven worlds, my gem, my Lord), and sets it to the question, "When will I reach the Lord in Thiruvarur?" Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this Thiruppadhigam as "Sandha Isai Paadi" (singing with melodious rhythm). "Isai" here refers to "Pann" (melody). It means a Thiruppadhigam set to music. The "Pann Puraneermai" (melody of the outer nature) of this Thiruppadhigam is suitable for dawn. Therefore, we understand that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal departs from Kanchipuram towards Thiruvarur at dawn, during the Vaikarai Yamam (early morning). This also implies that the time for his remaining suffering, which is like darkness, to disappear is approaching. The Thiruppadhigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is the 83rd Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Puraneermai Pann. The first, second, third, and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Andhiyum nanpagalum anju padham solli mundhi ezhum pazhaiya valvinai moodaamun Sindhai paramariya then thiru aaru pukku enthai piranarai endru kol eythuvadhe. Nindra vinai kodumai neengga irupozhudhum thundrumalar ittuchchoozhum valam seythu Thenran manam kamazhum then thiru aroor oor pukku endhan manam kulira endru kol eythuvadhe. Munnai mudarpiravi moodhariyamaiyinaal pinnai ninaindhanavum pedhuravum ozhiya Sennal vayalkazhani then thiru aroor pukku en uyirkku in amudhai endru kol eythuvadhe. Minnedum sedaiyanmeviya aroorai nannedum kaadhalmaiyaal naavalarkon oorana Pannedum sol malarkondu ittana paththum vallar pon udai vinnulagam nannuvar punniyare." Thiruchitrambalam. Verse 292: "Mannu thiruppadhigal thorum vanniyodu koovizhamum sennimisai vaiththu uvandhaar koyilin mun sendru irainji pannu thamizh thodai saaththi paraviye pondhu anaindhaar annamali vayal thadanggal soozhndha thiru aamaaththoor." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, on his way to Thiruvarur, joyfully places the Vanni (Prosopis cineraria) and Vilvam (Aegle marmelos) leaves on his head at each holy place, goes before the Lord's temples, worships, offers garlands of Tamil verses, praises, and then proceeds. These are the places on the way from Kanchipuram to Thiruvarur. These include Thiruvil, Thirukkurangganil Muttram, Purisai Nadu Purisai, Thiruvenkuntram, Thindisaram, Thiruppuravaar, Panangattur, and other places. These are all places located on the road directly south from Kanchipuram. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships all these places as he goes. However, due to our lack of merit, we do not have Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppadhigams for these places. Most of these places are Vaipu Sthalams (places mentioned in hymns but not necessarily having a dedicated hymn) and some are Thevaram-sung places. Some of these places are also Vaipu Sthalams in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppadhigams. Having passed through all these places, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches Thiru Aamathur, a place surrounded by fields and ponds where swans abound.

Verse 293: "Angganarai aamaaththoor azhagar thamai adivananggi thangum isai thiruppadhigam paadi poy thaaranikku manggalamaam perum thondai valanaadu kadandhu anaindhaar senggan valavan pirandha seer naadu neer naadu." Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Lord residing in Thiru Aamathur as "Angganar Aamathur Angganar" (the compassionate Lord of Aamathur), because he was like a mother to the cows there. He also refers to Him as "Aamathur Azhagar" (the beautiful one of Aamathur). "Azhagar" is the Lord's name in Thiru Aamathur. The Lord's name here is also Abirameswarar and Azhagiyanathar. The Goddess's name is Mukthambigai. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bows to the Lord in such a Thiru Aamathur and composes a Thiruppadhigam. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this Thiruppadhigam as "Thangum Isai Thiruppadhigam" (a melodious hymn that lingers). "Thanguthal" means to remain stable. This is a melodious Thiruppadhigam with a lingering sound. "Thanggalvosai" means that in each line of the song, the first words are repeated twice in a poetic device called "sol porul pinvaru nilai." In this way, the structure of this Thiruppadhigam is such that the sound lingers, making it impossible to sing the verses continuously and quickly. We see this in all the verses, such as "Kandanen Kandanen" (I saw, I saw), "Paaduvan Paaduvan" (I will sing, I will sing), and "Theduvan Theduvan" (I will search, I will search).

Similarly, we see that the sound lingers in the last word of each line. The "Pann" (melody) for this Thiruppadhigam is Kollikkavvanam. "Thangum Isai" also means a Thiruppadhigam that remains eternally in the Lord's feet in a state of Shiva Yoga. The Thiruppadhigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiru Aamathur is the 45th Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Kollikkavvanam Pann. The following are the first, second, third, and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam: Thiruchitrambalam. "Kandanen kandanen kaarigaiyaal than karuththanaay Aandanen aandanen aamaaththoor em adigalukku Poondanen poondanen poy endru solluvan kelmingal Meendanen meendanen vedhavithth allaadha varkatke. Orndhanen vorndhanen ullaththulle nindra on porul Serndhanen serndhanen sendru thiruottriyur pukku Saarndhanen saarndhanen sanggili menthol thadamulai Aarndhanen aarndhanen aamaaththoor ayyan arul adhe. Theduvan theduvan semmalar paadhanggal naaldhorum Naaduvan naaduvan naabikku mele or naal viral Maaduvan maaduvan van kai pidiththu magizhndhu ule Aaduvan aaduvan aamaaththoor em adigale. Aiyyanai aththanai aaludai aamaaththoor annanai Meyyanai meyyarkku meypporulana vimalanai Maiyanai maiyani kandathanai vanthondan oorana sol Poyvondrum indri pulambuvar porkalil servare." Thiruchitrambalam. Having composed the Thiruppadhigam in Thiru Aamathur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal crosses Thondai Nadu. This Thondai Nadu is sung by Sekkizhar Peruman as "Thaaranikku Manggalamaam Perunthondai Valanaadu" (the prosperous Thondai Nadu, auspicious to the earth). What does "Mangalam" mean for a country? It means the qualities that bring essential prosperity and glory to that country. The special feature of Thondai Nadu is that the entire country shines with Shiva-consciousness. Sekkizhar Peruman has extensively sung about the holy places of Thondai Nadu in the Puranam of Thirukurippu Thonda Nayanar. Not only that, but Thondai Nadu is also the country where Kanchipuram, where Ammaiyar performed penance and received boons, is located. Therefore, because Ammaiyar performed penance and received boons, Thondai Nadu possesses Kamakottam, which fosters all the dharmas that save the world.

Therefore, this Thondai Nadu becomes a prosperous country auspicious to the earth. "Thondai Nadu Saandrör Udaiththu" (Thondai Nadu is rich in scholars) means it is a country that holds many scholars within itself. That is a unique specialty of Thondai Nadu. In accordance with "Evvazhi nallavar aadavar avvazhi nalla vaazhiya nilane" (wherever good men are, there the land flourishes) and "Ulaginil ellam mangalam tharum malarvilam podhagam" (the flower-like elephant that brings auspiciousness to the whole world), Thondai Nadu possesses such greatness. Having crossed such a glorious Thondai Nadu, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal proceeds to Chola Nadu, which is the birthplace of Kochchenggatchozha Nayanar. Although many great people were born in Chola Nadu, Kochchenggatchozha Nayanar was born with divine grace, knowing his previous state. That is the specialty of his birth. Sekkizhar Peruman describes Chola Nadu as the country blessed with the greatness of Kochchenggatchozha Nayanar, who ruled by building 78 Maadak Kovils (temples with elevated platforms) for Lord Shiva. He refers to it as "Neer Nadu" (water country), which means the Kaveri country. Verse 294: "Annaattin marunggu thiru araththuraiyaich chendru eythi minnaarum padai mazhuvaar virai malarththaal panindhu ezhundhu solmaalai malar kalvaay agil enum thodai saaththi man aarvaththu thiruththondarvudan magizhndhu vaiginaar." Within the boundary of that country, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, a place on one side. That is, Thirunelvaayil Araththurai is a place in Nadu Nadu (central region) before entering the boundary of Chola Nadu. There, he prostrates himself at the Lord's flower-like feet, rises, and offers the garland of Tamil verses beginning with "Kalvaay Agil." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal joyfully resides there with the devotees, full of love. If this place is part of Nadu Nadu, and Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visited this place after stating that he went to Chola Nadu, it implies that Nadu Nadu was under the rule of the Pallavas, who were of the Chola royal lineage, during those days. Therefore, it was considered part of Chola Nadu. Nadu Nadu was ruled by the Munaiyatharaiyar lineage, who were subordinate kings to the Cholas at that time. From Thiru Aamathur, there was a path that went directly southwest through Viluppuram and Ulundurpettai to Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, crossing the Niva River. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman's journey from Thillai to Thirunarayur in the west and then to Seerkazhi, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman's journey from Thirunelvaayil Araththurai back to the Chola Nadu places, worshipping them, and then to Seerkazhi via Thirunarayur and Thirukaruvariyalur, followed these paths. Here, the point is that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, on his way from Thiru Aamathur to Thiruvarur, worshipped places like Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, Thiruvaavaduthurai, and Thiruthurutthi. We will see this history. We also see internal evidence of this in Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppadhigams, as his own words. The Thiruppadhigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal in Thirunelvaayil Araththurai is the 3rd Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Indhalappann (melody). The first, third, and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Kalvaay agilum kadhir maa maniyum kalandhu undhi varum nilavin karaimel Nelvaayil araththurai needu uraiyum nila velmadhi soodiya nirmalanai Nalvaayil seythaar nadandhaara uduththaar naraiththaar irandhaara endru Naanilaththil sellaay kazhugindradhu arindhu adiyen thodarndhen uyyappovadhu or soozhal sollee. Putraadum aravam arai aarththu ugandhaay punidhaa poruvelvidai oordhiyinaay Etre oru kan ilan ninnaiyallaal nelvaayil araththurai nirmalanai Matrel oru pattru ilan emperumaan vandaar kuzhalaal manggai panggine Attraar piravikkadal neendhi eri adiyen uyyappovadhu or soozhal sollee. Neervoorum neduvayal soozh puravin nelvaayil araththurai nirmalanai Theroor neduveedhi nanmaadamali then naavalarkon adiththondan Ani arooran uraiththana narchamizhin migumaalai orpaththu ivai kattruvallar Kaarvoor kazhivandu arai yaanai mannar avar aagi or vinmuzhudhu aalbavare." Thiruchitrambalam. Having composed the Thiruppadhigam in Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal stays there happily with the devotees for a few days. Let us continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 886, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Verse 295: "Paramar thiruvaraththuraiyai panindhu poy pala padhigal viravi mazhvidai uyarththaar virai malarththaal thozhudhu ethi uravu neerththadam ponni adaindha anbarudan aadi aravanindhaar amarndha thiru aavadhu thanthuraiyai anaindhaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having worshipped the Lord's holy place of Thiruaraththurai, praises many holy places where the Lord resides and reaches the holy place of Thiruvaavaduthurai, where He is enshrined. From Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal crossed the Niva River near Thiru Yerukkaththampaliyur and then proceeded directly south through Jayankondacholapuram, crossed the Kollidam River near Thiruvaaypadi, and reached the Kaveri River. This is the route Sundaramoorthy Swamigal took from Thirunelvaayil Araththurai to Thiruvaavaduthurai. Not only this route, but there is also another route that seems plausible: from Thirunelvaayil Araththurai, along the northern bank of the Niva River, crossing the Niva River near Koodalaiyattru, and then proceeding directly south, crossing the Kollidam River and the Kaveri River, and reaching near Kanjanur and Kodikka. The places along the first route include Govandapuththur, Vijayamanngai, Kottaiyur, Kudamookku, and others. The places along the second route include Thirupanandhaazh, Thirumanggalakkudi, Kanjanur, and others. This verse mentions that he reached Thiruvaavaduthurai after crossing the Kaveri. Therefore, it is likely that he came via the second route.

He then reaches Thiruvaavaduthurai, a cool place that has the power to cure the heat of birth, along with the devotees who accompanied him and bathed in the Kaveri. Verse 296: "Anggu anaivaar thamai adiyaar edhir kolla pukku aruli ponggu thirukkoiyilinai pudai valam kondu ul anaindhu ganggai vaazh sadaiyaay or kannilen ena kavalvaar ingu enakku aar uravu ennum thiruppadhigam eduththu isaiththaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal reaches Thiruvaavaduthurai. The devotees welcome Nambi. He enters the holy place, circumambulates the overflowing temple, and then enters inside. He then composes a Thiruppadhigam, beginning with "Gangai Vaazh Sadaiyaay" (O Lord with matted hair where Ganga resides), lamenting, "I have no eye here, who is my kin?" He composes the Thiruppadhigam such that the theme "Ingu enakku aar uravu" (Who is my kin here?) is embedded within it. "Aar enakku uravu amarargal ere" (Who is my kin, O Lord of the celestials?) is the crown of this Thiruppadhigam. Both Thiruppadhigams composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for Thiruvaavaduthurai are set in the Thakkési Pann. The Thiruppadhigam beginning with "Maraiyavan" (the Brahmin) was composed during a previous visit. This Thiruppadhigam, beginning with "Gangai Vaazh Sadaiyaay," is very moving. This Thiruppadhigam is the 70th Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai. The first, second, and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Gangai vaazh sadaiyaay gannanaadhaa kaalakaalane kaamanu gannale Ponggumaa kadal vidamizhaththaane boothanaadhanai punniyaa punidhaa Sengganmaalvidaiyaay theliththene theerththane thiruvaavaduththuraiyul Angganaa ena anjal endru arulaay aariyanakku uravu amarargal ere. Mannin mel mayanggik kidappene valiya vandhu ena aandu kondaane Kannilen udambil adu noyaal karuththazhindhu unakke poraiyanen Thennilayérikkum sadaiyane devane thiru aavaduththuraiyul Annanale ena anjal endru arulaay aariyanakku uravu amarargal ere. Vendhalai pirai kondraiyum aravum verimaththamum viravi munmudiththa Endaimaa malar senjsadaiyanai eesanai thiru aavaduththuraiyul Andavanaai singgadiyappenn anukka vanthondan aarvaththaal uraiththa Than thamizh malar paththum vallargal saadhalum pirappum aruppaare." Thiruchitrambalam. Now, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal departs from Thiruvaavaduthurai and proceeds to Thiruthurutthi. Verses 297 and 298: "Thiruppadhigam kodu paravi panindhu thiruvarulaal poy virippinodum thiruththuruththithanai mevi malargalul aruththiyinaal pukku irainji adiyenmel uttra pini varuththam ena ozhiththu arulavendum ena vanangguvaar paraviye panindha avarkku paramar thiruvarul purivaar viraviya ippini adaiya thavippadharkku veru aaga varamalar vandarai theerththa vadagulaththukkuzhi ena karavil thiruththondardhaam kaiththozhudhu purappattaar." Having sung the Thiruppadhigam in Thiruvaavaduthurai, praised the Lord, and worshipped Him, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal receives His divine permission and proceeds further. He reaches the holy place of Thiruthurutthi with great desire, enters the temple, and worships the Lord's feet with devotion. What does Sundaramoorthy Swamigal say to the Lord in his worship? He asks the Lord to remove the suffering of the disease that has afflicted his body. Therefore, we see here that when he arrived at this place, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had a new disease, and he appeals to the Lord of Thiruthurutthi to remove it. The local tradition also states that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal suffered from a skin disease. To Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who thus pleaded, the Lord grants His grace. The Lord instructs him to bathe in the northern pond on the northern side of this temple, saying that it is different from other holy waters and will completely cure this disease that has afflicted him. This holy place has a northern pond on its northern side, distinct from other holy waters. The Lord instructs him to bathe there. The Lord specifically instructs him to bathe in the holy water for this purpose. That is, while bathing for daily rituals and for worshipping the temple is customary, the Lord's command here is to bathe separately in the northern pond to cure this disease. The northern pond mentioned by the Lord is located in the northern courtyard of the Lord's temple within the temple premises. On its bank, there is a separate temple for Nambi. There, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's idol is enshrined in a standing posture with one eye. That is a wonderful idol that melts the heart. It is a great idol worthy of being seen and worshipped. Many devotees worship here and regularly bathe in this pond to cure diseases and be freed from other sufferings. "Theertham" means purity. It came to mean water that purifies. Thus, with the Lord's grace, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, along with the guileless devotees, departs from before the Lord and goes to the northern pond. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's Thiruppadhigam, in which he pleaded with the Lord to remove his suffering from the disease, is not available to us due to our lack of merit. Verse 299: "Mikka punal theerththaththin mun anaindhu vedhamellam thokka vadivaay irundha thuruththiyaar thamai thozhudhu pukku adhanil moozhgudhalum puthiya pini adhu neenggi akkaname mani oli seer thirumeni aayinaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes before that holy water, the northern pond, worships the Lord of Thiruthurutthi, who is the embodiment of all the Vedas, and enters the holy water. The water, as one of the Lord's eight forms, has the great grace of purifying both inside and out. In this holy place, the Lord, who embodies all the divine qualities mentioned in the Vedas, is seated, manifesting Himself. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worships Him and bathes in this pond. It is customary to worship and praise the Lord while bathing. We see the themes of Thiruvembavai and Thiruvachagam, such as "Udaiyaan porpaadham eththi irunjunai neer aadelor empavaay" (Praising the Lord's golden feet, let us bathe in the great pond, O maiden) and "Paadha thirampaadi aadelor empavaay" (Singing the glory of His feet, let us bathe, O maiden). Furthermore, here, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bathes according to the Lord's command. Therefore, remembering and worshipping the Lord becomes a special rule here. We should remember the Thirumurai sayings here, such as "Gangai aadilen kaveri aadilen engum eesan enaadhuvarkku illaiye" (What use is bathing in Ganga or Kaveri if one does not say 'Isan' everywhere?) and that there is no benefit if one bathes in crores of holy waters but has no love for Lord Shiva. The moment he emerged from the bath, the disease that had afflicted Nambi's body disappeared. This disease was not present before but appeared recently. It is a traditional belief that the disease that afflicted Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's body was due to heat. Nambi's body was naturally radiant. Just as the light of a gem is inseparable from it, the radiance of Nambi's body was of that nature. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was known as "Azhagar" (the beautiful one) because his body possessed the beauty of the Lord's form. We see that when he was playing, King Narasimha Munaiyaraiyar saw Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and was filled with love for him. In Thirukkai, Upamanyu Mamunivar worshipped Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, seeing his radiant form.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who possessed such a radiant body, saw that upon emerging from the holy pond, the disease that had afflicted him had disappeared, and his natural radiant body shone forth. Verse 300: "Kandavargal adhisayippa karaiyeri udaipunaindhu mandu perum kaadhalinaal koyilinai vandhadaindhu thondar edhir minnumaa megam ennum solpadhigam endhisaiyum arindhu uyya ezhu eduththu isaiththaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, to the astonishment of those who saw him, climbed out of the northern pond, changed his wet clothes, and with great love, came to the temple. Those who saw him were astonished. The people who saw Sundaramoorthy Swamigal before he bathed in the holy pond, with the disease afflicting his body, and then saw him after he emerged, radiant and free from the disease, were astonished, wondering what miracle they had witnessed. The devotees also rejoiced. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after worshipping the Lord inside the temple, came out and composed a Thiruppadhigam before the assembled devotees, beginning with "Minnumaa Megam" (Shining Cloud). Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composed this Thiruppadhigam, saying, "En udambu adum pini idar keduththaanai naan marakkumaaru ennain" (How can I forget Him who removed the suffering of the disease that afflicted my body?). This Thiruppadhigam was composed in the third person, referring to the Lord. Therefore, it is understood that this Thiruppadhigam was sung before the devotees. The great ones do not speak to worldly people, only to devotees.

The state of commanding worldly people is different from the state of singing before devotees. The theme of this Thiruppadhigam is that the world should know and be saved by this divine greatness, in accordance with the Thirumandhiram saying, "Naan petra inbam peruga ivvaiyagam" (May the joy I received spread throughout the world). This Thiruppadhigam was composed to praise the immense grace the Lord bestowed upon him. This Thiruppadhigam, sung for Thiruthurutthi and Thiruvelvikudi together, is the 74th Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Gandhara Pann (melody). The first and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Minnumaa megamgal pozhindhu izhindhu aruvi vedipadak karaiyodum thirai konarndhu etttrum Annamam kaveri agan karai urai vaar adi inai thozhudhu ezhum anbaram adiyaar Sonnavaaru arivaaru thuruththiyaar velvikudivullar adigalai sediyanen naayen Ennai naan marakkumaaru emperumaanai en udambu adum pini idar keduththaanai. Manggaivor kooru ugandhu eru ugandhu eri maaralaar thiripuram neeru ezhachchettrra Anggaiyaan kazhal adiyandri mattrra ariyaan adiyavarkku adiyavan thozhuvan arooran Ganggaiyaar kaveri thuruththiyaar velvikudivullar adigalai serththiya paadal Thanggaiyaal thozhudhu tham naavin mel kolvaar thavaneri sendru amarulagam aalbavare." Thiruchitrambalam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal explicitly states in verses 1, 3, 5, and 6 that his disease was cured. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having sung the melodious Tamil verses and not forgetting the Lord's grace, resides there with countless devotees. Let us continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 887, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkaama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal resides in Thiruthurutthi. Verse 301: "Panniraindha thamizh paadi paramar thiru arulmaravaa thenniraindha thondarudan panindhu angun uraindhu egi unniraindha padhipiravum udaiyavar thazh vananggi poy kanniraindha thiruvaroor mun thondra kaangindraar enbadhu thiruppaadal." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having sung the melodious Tamil Thiruppadhigam, and not forgetting the immense grace the Lord bestowed upon him, worships the Lord with countless devotees. He resides in Thiruthurutthi, praising the Lord, not forgetting His grace, as he sang "Ennai naan marakkumaaru" (How can I forget myself?). He worships the Lord with countless devotees. "Enniraindha" means countless devotees, and also devotees whose minds are filled with Shiva. "Niraithal" means to fill completely, leaving no room for anything else. They are those who always remember only Lord Shiva and nothing else. We saw that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, after bathing in the northern pond in Thiruthurutthi and being cured of his new disease, did not go directly before the Lord but sang this Thiruppadhigam before the assembled devotees. Therefore, from there, he joins those devotees and then goes before the Lord to worship. This means that he shared his experience with the devotees, praising the Lord's unique grace, and thus experienced the joy with them. This not only informed the devotees of the divine grace but also increased his joy by sharing it with them. The devotees mentioned here are those who accompanied Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and waited there until he bathed in the northern pond and received divine grace. After he returned from bathing, they saw Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's radiant body and worshipped him. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings to these devotees, saying, "You see how He removed my suffering, how can I forget myself?" He composed that Thiruppadhigam in a way that praises divine grace. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who was always filled with the Lord in his heart, was commanded by the Lord on the very day he was taken into His service. From that day, he made it his rule to remember and visit all the Lord's holy places and worship them. Such a Sundaramoorthy Swamigal now sees Thiruvarur, which is filled with the Lord, appearing before him, filling his eyes. He sees Thiruvarur appearing before him, filling his eyes. Thiruvarur is a holy place whose beauty is inexhaustible, a sight that once seen, one cannot turn away from. We see Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praising it in various ways as "Ani Aroor" (beautiful Aroor), "Kulir Aroor" (cool Aroor), "Vizh Aroor" (great Aroor), "Valar Aroor" (growing Aroor), and "Than Aroor" (his own Aroor). Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was always immersed in seeing "Solai Arooranai" (Lord of the groves of Aroor), "Pazhana Thiru Ani Arooranai" (Lord of the beautiful Aroor with fertile fields), and "Thamarai Poygai Arooranai" (Lord of Aroor with lotus ponds) in his mind. Now, he sees such a Thiruvarur before his eyes, filling them completely. Verse 302: "Andru thirunokku ondraal aara kandu inburaar nindru nilamisai veezhndhu nedhuyirththu ner irainji van thondar thiruvaroor mayanggum maalaiyil pugundhu thundrusadai thoovaayaar thamai munnam thozha anaindhaar." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sees Thiruvarur appearing before him. However, he sees that Thiruvarur with only one eye. Even with one eye, he is not completely happy. Standing at the very place where he saw the town, he falls to the ground, sighs deeply, and worships directly. Falling to the ground and worshipping upon seeing a Shiva temple is the custom of Shiva temple darshan. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having worshipped in this manner, sighs deeply. This sigh is due to his unbearable sorrow. The sigh is because he, who used to see Thiruvarur with both eyes, is now seeing it with only one eye, and his mind is filled with unbearable sorrow. He stands directly and worships the holy place. It is dusk, when the light fades and darkness enters, a time when the eyes are confused. It is a time that causes confusion in the eyes. Therefore, it is called the time when the eyes are confused, and it is also called the time that confuses the time itself. It is the twilight hour when night and day merge. In that twilight hour, he enters the town of Thiruvarur. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then goes to the Thirupparavaiyul Mandali temple in Thiruvarur. The Lord enshrined in the Aroor Paravaiyul Mandali temple is known by the name "Thoovaayaar." "Thoo" means to eat, and "Vaayaar" means one who has a mouth. So, "Thoovaayaar" means one who has a mouth that eats. This means that when the great flood of the deluge came upon Thiruvarur, the Lord here swallowed that flood, preventing it from spreading over Thiruvarur and submerging it. Therefore, the Lord enshrined here is known by the name "Thoovaayaar," meaning one who has a mouth that eats the flood. "Paravaiyul Mandali" is the name of the temple.

"Paravai" means sea, and "ul" means to eat without overflowing. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal begins this Thiruppadhigam with the Lord's name, "Thoovaayaar." Before worshipping the Lord enshrined in the anthill in Thiruvarur, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal goes to the Paravaiyul Mandali temple in Thiruvarur and worships the Lord there. "Thoovaayaar" can also be interpreted differently from the mythological reason mentioned earlier. If "Thoovaayaar" is split as "Thoo Aayaar," it means one who has become a support. "Mananthooymai seyvinai thooymai irandu inam thooymai thoovaavarum" (Purity of mind, purity of action, purity of both lineages will come through purity) is from Thirukkural. Furthermore, "Thoovaayaar" can also mean one who has a mouth that uttered pure Vedic and Sivagama statements. Verse 303: "Ponggu thiruththondarvudan ul anaindhu pokku irainji thunggu isai thiruppadhigam thoovaayaa endru eduththé ingu emadhu thuyarkalaindhu kankana kaattaay endru angganardham munnindru paadi arunthamizh punaindhaar enbadhu thiruppaadal." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, along with the overflowing devotees, enters the temple, bows before the Lord, and composes a melodious Thiruppadhigam, beginning with "Thoovaayaa." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings before the Lord, with the intention of pleading with the Lord to remove his suffering here and to show him his eyes, and thus offers this garland of rare Tamil verses. "Ingu emadhu thuyarkalaindhu kan kana kaattaay" (Remove our suffering here and show us our eyes) is the theme of this Thiruppadhigam. "Angganar" means one who is compassionate. "Angganmai" means compassion. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is asking for his eyesight, so he sings, referring to the Lord as "Angganare" (O compassionate one), "Kan Udaiyavare" (O one with eyes), and "Kan Thara Vallavare" (O one capable of giving eyes). The Thiruppadhigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is for the Thirupparavaiyul Mandali temple in Thiruvarur. It is the 96th Thiruppadhigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Panjamam Pann (melody). The first and tenth verses of this Thiruppadhigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "Thoovaayaa thondu seyvaar padu thukkanggal kaavaaye kandu kondaar aivar kaakkilum Naavaayaal unnaiye nallana solluverku aavaa en paravaiyul mandali ammane. Karandhaiyum vanniyum maththamum koovizham parandha seer paravaiyul mandali ammanai Nirambiya oorana uraiththana paththu ivai virumbuvaar melaiyaar melaiyaar melare." Thiruchitrambalam. Thiruvārūr Paravaiyul Mandali is the 89th temple on the southern bank of the Kaveri in Chola Nadu. It is known as Thulānāyanār Kovil. This temple is located to the southwest of the Thiruvarur temple's Maha Rath (great chariot) level, on the eastern street, to the east of the Thiruvarur temple. At one time, when the sea rose due to Varuna's command over Thiruvarur, the Lord here swallowed that sea and became enshrined, which is why this place is called Paravaiyul Mandali. The name Thoovaayā Nayanār has colloquially become Thulānāyanār. "Mandali" can be split as "Man Thali," meaning a temple that remained steadfast on this earth, not submerged by the sea. This is the place where Durvasa Muni worshipped the Lord and received boons. The idol of Durvasa Muni is enshrined and worshipped in the Vinayagar temple. The Lord's name is Mandaleswarar. The Lord's form shines like crystal. The Goddess's name is Panjinum Melladiyāl (one with feet softer than cotton). The holy waters associated with this place are Kamalalayam Teertham, Sanga Teertham, Gaya Teertham, Vani Teertham, and Sengazhuneer Odai. Behind this temple are the Thiruneelakanda Nayanar temple and, in the southern sanctum, the Paravai Nachiyar temple. These are the details of the Thiruvārūr Paravaiyul Mandali temple. Let us continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 888, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having arrived at Thiruvarur Paravaiyul Mandali, is composing a Thiruppathigam (a devotional hymn). The 304th verse states: "Having worshipped the Lord with the matted locks adorned with the Ganga, he came out and stayed elsewhere, joining with the Thiruthondar (devotees) who were with him. He then approached the Thirumoolattanam (the main shrine) of the Lord who bears the bull banner, knowing it was the time for the matchless Arthajama (midnight) worship." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having worshipped the Lord whose matted locks are adorned with the Ganga at Thiruvarur Paravaiyul Mandali, came out and stayed for a while in a secluded spot. It is the custom not to enter the temple outside of worship times. Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal delayed for a short period and entered during the Arthajama worship. The Arthajama puja is a peerless time of worship where boons are granted as desired. Accordingly, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal arrived at that time before the Thirumoolattanam of the Lord Puttidam Kondanathar (Lord who resides in the anthill) inside the Thiruvarur Poongkoil (flower temple).

The 305th and 306th verses are: "As the prime devotees approached him, he looked at their faces, and with flawless music, he composed the Thiruppathigam, 'Kurugupaya,' inquiring as if he were a stranger, and with affection, he sang it in the Kaikkilai (a poetic theme of unrequited love) genre, and then joined them. He went before the magnificent Thirudevasiriyan (a hall in the temple), worshipped, and with folded hands, bowed to the cloud-laden gopuram (temple tower) and entered. He then worshipped the garland-filled Poongkoil and approached it, falling to the ground with immense love." Seeing and hearing of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's arrival at the Thiruvarur temple, devotees gathered there. All the devotees came forward to greet him. Looking at their faces, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal composed a Thiruppathigam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang the Thiruppathigam beginning with "Kurugupaya" with flawless music. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, standing like a stranger, looked at the faces of those devotees and sang the Thiruppathigam, addressing the devotees as if to ask, "Can you make them understand?" In this Thiruppathigam, he expresses his sorrow, as if asking birds to convey it. "Ethilar" means "stranger." When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal first came to Thiruvarur, he asked the devotees there, "Which of the six towns is he from, and can you tell me about him?" There is a unity in the diversity within that Thiruppathigam. The Thiruppathigam starting with "Kurugupaya," composed here, was also sung addressing the devotees. Here, we see the beauty of Tamil, where unity and diversity are revealed.

The state of mind filled with anxiety due to not receiving the desired object for many days is called "Esaravu." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings this Thiruppathigam in the "Kaikkilai" genre, which expresses love through the sorrow of "Esaravu." "Kaikkilai" refers to the state of mind of one-sided love. With such a sentiment, he sings this Thiruppathigam and joins the devotees. This Thiruppathigam is set in the Kollipann (a musical mode). The 1st, 2nd, and 11th verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "O you who can make them understand these things: how to drink, worship, and melt with remembrance for the Lord of Arur, where the juice of dense sugarcane flows by the fields, and where the Kurugu (a type of bird) flies!" "O my flying parrots, O my singing mynahs! Can you make them understand that I cannot forget my Lord, who is like a cruel one, that my bangles do not stay, and that I have no sleep?" "O devotees, sing the praises that Uuran (Sundarar), the true devotee of Singadiyappan, whose heart is set on the Lord, the Father who is worshipped and remembered eternally, whose golden feet are praised!" Thiruchitrambalam. Having thus composed the Thiruppathigam, he joined the devotees and entered the temple.

There, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal first worshipped the magnificent Thirudevasiriyan mandapam (hall). Upon entering the Thiruvarur temple courtyard, the first thing one sees is the Devasiriyan mandapam. It is a place filled with gatherings of devotees. Therefore, in accordance with the custom of first worshipping the devotees, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal first worshipped the Thirudevasiriyan mandapam. Having worshipped thus, he then bowed with folded hands to the cloud-laden gopuram and entered. This is the first gopuram of the main temple, after worshipping the Devasiriyan. This is the place where the Lord appeared before Nambigal (Sundarar) and gave him the opening line for the Thiruthondar Thogai (a hymn listing the devotees): "I am a servant to the devotees of Thillai Vaazh Andhanar (Brahmins of Chidambaram)." Having worshipped that gopuram, he entered and reached the Thiruppoongkoil. He worshipped and approached the Thirumaligai (palace) called Poongkoil, which is adorned with many garlands. The Poongkoil is the palace inside the Thiruvarur temple where Puttidam Kondanathar and Thyagesa Peruman reside. There, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal fell to the ground with immense love.

He fell to the ground, overcome by love. It was not a conscious act of falling, but his body falling to the ground due to his overwhelming emotion. The 307th verse states: "Having fallen and risen, he worshipped with folded hands, stood before the Lord, and wept. With one eye, which had lived, he was not satisfied, and his mind was distraught. He pleaded, 'Lift me from the deep ocean of sorrow, and grant me the other eye, for my lowly desire to be fulfilled!'" As mentioned before, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who fell to the ground, worshipped and stood before the Lord, weeping. He was not satisfied with seeing with only one eye, which had lived, and his mind was distraught. He pleaded, "Lift me from this very deep ocean of sorrow and grant me my eye, so that my lowly desire may be fulfilled!" Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to the left eye as "lived flower-like eye," as Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had received sight in that eye at Thiruvottriyur to see Thiruekambara, as in "How I, a servant, received the eye to see the form of the Lord." Therefore, he yearned for the full vision of the Lord's form. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with a melting heart, lamented that seeing the Lord with only one eye was not a complete vision. He pleaded with the Lord to lift him from this deep ocean of sorrow, which he could not comprehend, and to forgive his great sin of breaking his vow, and to grant him his eye.

The 308th verse states: "The king of Thirunavalur, Sundarar, worshipped the Lord residing in Thiruvarur, the nectar of Thirumoolattanam, desiring to drink Him with his eyes, and pleaded for the other eye with passionate longing, and then composed a Thiruppathigam beginning with 'Meela Adimai' (unending servitude)." To drink the Lord, who is un-drunk sweet nectar, with his eyes, he pleaded for the sight of his right eye, in addition to the left eye he had received in Kanchipuram, and then composed a Thiruppathigam beginning with "Meela Adimai." The 309th verse states: "Beginning with 'Meela Adimai,' he sang a fearless Thiruppathigam, in the spirit of servitude and friendship, saying, 'O Lord, who consumed poison to save all the hosts of devas from perishing, and remained steadfast, you will not bear the suffering that comes to your true devotees who lovingly cherish your feet.'" Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worshipped the Lord, who, beginning with "Meela Adimai," had consumed poison to save all the hosts of devas from perishing and remained steadfast. He sang a beautiful Thiruppathigam with the spirit of servitude and friendship, implying, "You will not bear the suffering that comes to your true devotees who lovingly cherish your feet." Although it is the Lord who, according to destiny, causes suffering to His devotees for the purification of their karma, and even though that suffering is caused by Him, He shows compassion, unable to bear the suffering of His devotees when they experience it. Thus, he composed the Thiruppathigam beginning with "Meela Adimai," combining the two qualities of servitude and friendship. The nature of the verses, such as "Vaazhndhu Potheere" (may you live long) and "Neere Pazhippatteer" (you are blamed), are parts where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal expressed both his servitude and his friendship with the Lord.

Thus, the Thiruppathigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is a Thiruppathigam for the Thiruvarur shrine. It is the 95th Thiruppathigam in the 7th Thirumurai, set in the Senturutthi pann (a musical mode). This Thiruppathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. "O Lord of Thiruvarur, if we, your servants, who are your unending slaves and desire no one else, whose hearts burn like an unquenchable fire within, and whose faces are greatly withered, tell you our suffering, will you live on untouched?" "You sell, I am not a pawn, I willingly became your servant. I have done no wrong. You have made me a wretch. Why did you take my eyes, O Lord? You are blamed! If you do not give me the other eye, may you live on untouched!" "O Lord of Arur, where the Anril (a bird) does not cease to reach the groves! Like cows that yield milk when their calves butt them, if your servants, who sing praises eternally, cannot see, and fall into a pit after hitting a hill, may you live on untouched!" "O dweller of Thurutthi, O Lord of Pazhanam, O dweller of Sootrutthurai! You have Thiruvarur as your abode, and your mind is there. If your loving servants tell you their suffering, and you cause them distress and then command them to serve in the next life, may you live on untouched!" "Is this Thiruvarur, with groves where red corals shine? Is this how it is for us, your servants, O my Lord? If your servants, who sing many praises, cannot see, and cry out, 'Is this justice, O my Lord?' may you live on untouched!" "O Lord with the matted locks adorned with the Konrai (golden shower tree) garland, like gold, in Thiruvarur, where the red-legged crane reaches the rice stalks! If your servants, without wealth, become weak and cannot see, and their minds are distressed, may you live on untouched!" "O Lord of Arur, where the female elephant reaches the groves! Is this how it is for us, your servants, O Lord? If you show illusion, show birth, show an unforgetting mind, show the body, and then take away our eyes, may you live on untouched!" "We were born in a family that is like a toddy, like an ocean, like a vessel, like the earth, and like mingled words, and we praise you without despising you. O Lord, you do not know blame! If we, your singing devotees, wander without finding our way, may you live on untouched!" "They say that even separation from a ghost is unpleasant for others. If you desire the fruit, is it not the raw fruit that is considered? Even though we wander like dogs in the middle, and are your servants, if you do not open your mouth, O Lord of Thiruvarur, may you live on untouched!" "Is this Thiruvarur, with groves where red Serundhi (a type of flower) blossoms? You have taken Thirumoolattanam as your abode. We praise you without despising you, whether sitting, standing, or lying down. If we, who have come with suffering, tell you something, may you live on untouched!" "O Lord with the dark throat, eight shoulders, three eyes, and many arts, whose feet are in Thirumoolattanam of Arur! You took my eyes, O Lord! You are blamed! You who have the part of the breasted woman, may you live on untouched!" Thiruchitrambalam. This Thiruppathigam is special because it comes from true experience. Sivakavimani Desikan has said that he knows people who have regained their sight by reciting this. Sekkizhar Peruman then continues to describe the divine miracle that occurred after this Thiruppathigam was composed.

The 310th verse states: "The holy Lord, Puttidam Kondanathar, the Lord of the elements, took pity on the suffering of Vanthondar (Sundarar), which arose from love, and cast his merciful divine gaze. When he granted the cool, flower-like eye, Sundarar opened his eyes clearly, his face blossomed, and he fell at the Lord's lotus feet, his heart overwhelmed with bliss." The Lord Puttidam Kondanathar, the Lord of the elements, took pity on the suffering of Vanthondar (Sundarar), which arose from his incessant loving plea, and cast his merciful divine gaze. When he granted the cool, flower-like eye, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal opened his eyes clearly, his face blossomed, and he fell at the Lord's lotus feet, his heart overwhelmed with bliss. The Lord, who is gracious, had previously caused Nambigal to lose his eye, which was also an act of divine grace, but it was a harsh grace. Now, the Lord's action was a compassionate grace.

The 311th and 312th verses are: "Falling and rising many times, he worshipped and praised greatly. Overwhelmed with joy, he danced and sang, immersed in a flood of bliss. With both eyes, he drank the grace of the rich, clear coral-like form that arose from the golden anthill. Having worshipped and praised for a sufficient time, he circumambulated the golden jeweled temple, out of his good desire, for the welfare of the world, and then, with the virtuous devotees, approached the Thirudevasiriyan, passing through the gate where Brahma and Vishnu await their turn." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, falling to the ground and rising many times, performed various prostrations (Ashtanga, Panchanga, Thrayanga), sang praises, and was immersed in a flood of bliss. Earlier, he had seen with one eye and was not satisfied. Now, having received the other eye, he drank the Lord with both eyes. He drank the un-drunk sweet nectar with his eyes, thereby immersing himself in the experience of bliss and reveling in it. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had arrived for the Arthajama worship. Therefore, he continued to praise the Lord until the Arthajama worship ended. After the Arthajama worship, the temple doors would be closed. So, before that, he circumambulated the temple and came out. He came out through the first gate. This is the place where the Lord appeared to Nambigal and gave him the opening line for the Thiruthondar Thogai. This place is called Kodinidam or Ottravayil.

It is the place where the devas (celestial beings) wait, observing the time, to present their grievances. Passing through that gate, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with the virtuous devotees, reached the side of the Thirudevasiriyan mandapam. He is Nambi, who came for the welfare of the world, so that the southern land, which had performed great penance, might flourish, and the flawless Thiruthondar Thogai might be given. This Nambi, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who came for the welfare of the world, is now residing beside the Thirudevasiriyan mandapam. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 889, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman has sung the history of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal receiving his right eye and residing in the Thiruvarur temple. Now, Sekkizhar Peruman sings the continuation of Paravai Ammaiyar's history. Earlier, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had departed from Thiruvarur to undertake pilgrimages to various temples. Therefore, Paravai Nachiyar experienced sorrow due to separation from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. In addition to this, Paravai Ammaiyar received another piece of distressing news: Sundaramoorthy Swamigal had married Sangili Ammaiyar in Thiruvottriyur. Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman will now sing the history, starting from how Paravai Ammaiyar was in distress due to her sulk (oodal) caused by these two sorrows.

Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about the history of the Lord going as a messenger twice to appease Paravai Ammaiyar's sulk towards Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and the history of Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar, which follows this narrative. The 313th verse: "After Nambi (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal) departed, leaving Nankai Paravaiyar (Paravai Ammaiyar), she was weakened by loneliness in her jeweled palace. Days passed, with nights becoming days and days becoming nights, as her overflowing love caused her to wither. After some days had passed..." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having departed, Paravai Ammaiyar is weakened by loneliness in her beautiful palace. Due to her loneliness, Paravai Ammaiyar is in distress. All those times, the daytime passes like nighttime, and the nighttime passes like daytime. Due to her separation from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, she cannot sleep, and thus night becomes day. Tamil literature, in the context of Akapporul (love poetry), speaks of the sorrow that comes at night, such as being associated with the sea and suffering when the moon appears. How does day become night? Without the presence of her beloved, the daytime loses its splendor and light, becoming dark. She does not have the usual human excitement during the day. The thoughts of union and weariness that belong to the night occur during the day for Paravai Ammaiyar, and the wakefulness and going out that belong to the day occur during the night. Therefore, night becomes day, and day becomes night. Thus, the days pass without her realizing the difference between day and night, as she suffers from loneliness and distress. Her overflowing love causes her to wither in distress. The 314th verse: "The truthful news that Thirunavalurar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), who is steadfast in righteousness, went to Thiruvottriyur and married Sangiliyar, the woman with full breasts, was conveyed to her by those who came to her." The sorrow caused by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's departure has been explained so far. Now, Sekkizhar Peruman explains another sorrow that comes to Paravai Ammaiyar. It is the news that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal is properly married to Sangili Ammaiyar in Thiruvottriyur and living there. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who followed the path of Shiva, a path of righteousness, having received the grace of penance from the Lord, was told by some people that he had properly married Sangili Ammaiyar in Thiruvottriyur. When some people first conveyed this news, Paravai Ammaiyar asked them to investigate the truth of this news. They went to Thiruvottriyur, saw Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Sangili Nachiyar living as husband and wife, and confirmed to Paravai Ammaiyar that the news she had already received was true. We also see this in the story of Karaikkal Ammaiyar. Worldly wisdom states that one should not simply believe what others say, but should send some trusted people to investigate and confirm the truth, and then proceed with what needs to be done. When Paravai Ammaiyar confirmed the truth of this news, anger came to her, without her even realizing it. It was an anger that arose from her feminine nature. It was not an anger that Paravai Ammaiyar intentionally created. Moral texts state that chaste women should not be angry with their husbands. Therefore, it is not appropriate to be angry with her husband. However, here, anger comes to Paravai Ammaiyar without her even realizing it. It was an anger that could not be distinguished from her sulk. This is because it was an anger that arose from her inability to tolerate that the joy of her beloved, who belonged only to her, was now shared with another. Therefore, unable to bear that anger, Paravai Ammaiyar's body weakens.

In the 315th verse, Sekkizhar Peruman explains how Paravaiyar's actions were when her body was weakened. "She would not sleep on the soft flower bed, nor would she sit comfortably after waking up. She would not sit on the golden flower throne, nor would she stand, nor would she walk around, nor would she go outside. She would not forget the flower-like rain, nor would she remember it. What would she do? She was caught between a sulk that melted her bones and separation." Due to that anger, Paravai Ammaiyar could not sleep on the flower bed. Even though it was a flower bed, Paravai Ammaiyar could not sleep. Those who are weakened usually lie down and sleep. By sleeping, the body rests, and then the weakness disappears, and they regain strength. This is generally what medical texts say. But here, the weakened Paravaiyar cannot sleep. Well, if she cannot sleep, even if she rests on the bed for a while, her body's weakness will disappear. But Paravai Ammaiyar's mind is withered and her heart is burning, so she cannot even sit on the flower bed. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, "Inithu Amarar" (She does not sit comfortably). Well, if she cannot lie down comfortably on the bed, she can sit on the flower throne for a while. But she cannot even sit on the flower throne. Well, if she cannot sit on the flower throne, can she stand up? She cannot even stand up. Well, if she can walk around inside the palace, she cannot even walk around. Can she go outside the palace and change her mind? She cannot even do that. Can she forget Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who is the cause of all these states? She cannot forget him. Due to anger, his memory cannot be removed. Can she remember Sundaramoorthy Swamigal? Due to anger, she cannot even remember him. Therefore, Paravai Ammaiyar's mind is neither remembering nor forgetting. Therefore, when she cannot do any work, either outwardly or inwardly, what else can Paravai Ammaiyar do? Paravai Ammaiyar was caught between the two states of sulk and separation. This state of being caught between these two states is a unique state where she is neither sulking nor separated, but suffering. It is a state where she cannot be separated due to anger, and she cannot even remember in her mind. It is a unique state between these two. Her state is one that melts the bones. Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings this verse. This verse beautifully explains the state of mind of one who is separated, and the state of mind of a heroine who hears that her beloved has married another woman. It is a very high-quality Akapporul (love poetry) verse with a beautiful narrative. We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 890, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. We have contemplated Sekkizhar Peruman's portrayal of Paravai Ammaiyar's situation. The 316th verse: "As she was distraught with sorrow and helplessness, in those days, Aaroorar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), whose head was adorned with the crescent moon, approached the temple. The attendants, who used to go to the palace of the doe-eyed lady, were not allowed to enter and remained outside." As Paravai Ammaiyar was thus distraught with sorrow and helplessness, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, having now received his right eye, was residing before the Poongkoil (flower temple) of the Thiruvarur temple. At the same time, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's attendants went to Paravai Ammaiyar's palace. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's attendants went to Paravai Ammaiyar's palace as usual. However, they were not allowed to enter Paravai Ammaiyar's palace. So, they remained outside. We saw that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal arrived at the Thiruvarur temple during the Artha Jama Puja (midnight worship). Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal entered Thiruvarur in the evening and arrived at the Thiruvarur temple for Artha Jama. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's attendants also stayed with him for his service until the Artha Jama time. After the Artha Jama Puja was completed and everyone in the town was asleep, the attendants went to Paravai Ammaiyar's palace after delaying for so long.

Paravai Ammaiyar had learned about the events that had taken place in Thiruvottriyur. Therefore, the attendants, having somewhat guessed Paravai Ammaiyar's changed mood, delayed until everyone in the town was asleep and then went to Paravai Ammaiyar's palace. The Thiruthondars (devotees) are always with Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, but the attendants do not always need to be with him. Their job is to perform the necessary services for Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. So, now they go to Paravai Ammaiyar's palace, and since they are not allowed to enter, they stand outside the palace. These attendants, who have the great privilege of serving Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, are not like other attendants in the world. Such glorious attendants are standing outside Paravai Ammaiyar's palace. The 317th verse: "Some of them, seeing their situation, went before the Lord of Thiruvarur and reported, 'Paravai Ammaiyar has learned all the events that took place in Thiruvottriyur. Therefore, we were not allowed to enter her palace and are standing outside.'" The attendants stood before Paravai Ammaiyar's palace, and some of them left and went to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to inform him of the situation. They told Sundaramoorthy Swamigal that Paravai Ammaiyar had learned all the events that took place in Thiruvottriyur, and that they were not allowed to enter her palace and were standing outside.

The 318th verse: "Hearing that news, Vanthondar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), with a distraught mind, wondered, 'What can be done now?' He then sent some learned people, who understood the ways of the world, to Paravaiyar, his beloved, to appease her anger with appropriate words." Hearing this news, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's mind was distraught. He wondered what he should do now. He called some wise people who had learned the ways of the world and understood worldly justice. He asked them to go to Paravaiyar, his beloved, and, knowing her anger, to appease it with good words. These people were knowledgeable about worldly affairs, experienced, and capable of performing tasks. They knew how to approach different people in different situations and how to achieve their goals. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sent such people to Paravai Ammaiyar. The 319th verse: "Those who went by Nambi's (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's) grace reached Nankai Paravaiyar's beautiful golden palace. With a manner that would appease her anger, they approached the lightning-waisted lady, who was immersed in the ocean of intense sulk, and said, 'Is this befitting our Queen?' and spoke many words." Those people who went by Nambi's grace reached Nankai Paravaiyar's beautiful palace. They went there with the intention of appeasing her anger. Paravai Ammaiyar was immersed in the ocean of separation, which caused her mind to burn. Those people went before Paravai Ammaiyar and said, "Is this befitting our Queen?" and spoke many words. They addressed Paravai Ammaiyar as "Our Queen," praising her greatness and right, and tried to appease her anger.

This is one of the methods used by learned people. This is called the Sama Upaya (method of conciliation). Among the four Upayas (methods) of Sama, Bheda, Dana, and Danda, this is called Sama Upaya. They spoke such words. The 320th verse: "When they spoke many more words with the method of differentiation, the lady refused and did not change her mind from the anger she held. She said, 'If you speak further about his faults, my life will surely depart.' They too became afraid and left." First, those wise people spoke about the Sama Upaya. After that, they adopted the Bheda (differentiation) method. This is the second type of Upaya. They adopted the Bheda Upaya and spoke in many ways to appease Paravai Ammaiyar's anger. When the Sama Upaya did not work, they resorted to the Bheda Upaya. We see these methods in the Ambuil Paruva (moon section) of Pillaitamil (a genre of Tamil literature). Even though they spoke all these words, Paravai Ammaiyar refused their statements and did not change her mind from the anger she held. Paravai Ammaiyar said to those who came, "If you speak further about his (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's) faults, my life will surely depart." When she said this, those who came became afraid. We saw that they only used the first two Upayas among the four types of Sama, Bheda, Dana, and Danda. The Upayas used to unite separated lovers are only the first two. Therefore, when they used both and it did not work, Paravai's anger increased, and she said, "If you speak about Sundaramoorthy Swamigal anymore, my life will depart." So, they became afraid and went to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and told him everything that had happened.

The 321st verse: "When they spoke, he was filled with fear and weariness. He could not find a companion to help him. In his anxious heart, he was immersed in sorrow and could not rise. In the midst of that night, in that ocean of sorrow, the elders who had departed from there reported everything that had happened to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the leader of Thirumunaippadi Nadu." When they spoke, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was filled with fear and weariness. He could not find a companion to help him in that ocean of worry. He was immersed in great sorrow. That anxiety burned Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's heart. "Sindha Kulam" means "Sindhai Aakulam," and "Aakulam" means sorrow. Therefore, "Sindha Kulam" means mental anguish. So, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was in that ocean of sorrow with mental anguish, unable to find a companion to help him out of that ocean. He was immersed in great sorrow in the middle of that night, that is, midnight. The 322nd and 323rd verses: "Those around him slept. The Artha Jama worship was completed. In the deep darkness, where the world was silent and even ghosts slept, the Lord, whose head was adorned with fragrant Konrai flowers and who wore the crescent moon and a snake, his friend, sat alone, grieving and contemplating. He thought of the Lord's feet, saying, 'Oh, my Lord, I am caught in this trouble, which is a result of my past karma, and Paravai is the cause of it. You must come and save me in this hour. If you come and remove the sulk of that swan-like woman, I will be saved. Otherwise, there is nothing else I can do.'" In that night, everyone around Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was sleeping. It was the time when the Artha Jama Puja was completed. So, it was a time when all the people of the world had stopped their activities and were sleeping. It was a deep dark night when even ghosts slept. The Artha Jama worship in the temple and the daily worship rituals associated with it were all completed, and the temple was closed. So, those who were with Sundaramoorthy Swamigal were also sleeping. It was past midnight. It was a time when even the night, which usually moves, was still. At that time, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was sitting alone, grieving and contemplating. At that moment, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, the friend of the Lord, who wore the fragrant Konrai flowers on his head and had a snake and the crescent moon, was thinking of the Lord's feet. He thought, "Oh, my Lord, who owns me! You must grant me grace so that I can reach Paravai, who is the cause of this trouble, which is a result of my past karma. If you come in this midnight and remove the sulk of that swan-like woman, I will be saved. Otherwise, there is nothing else I can do." We will continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman's Periya Puranam, Part 891, Vampara Vari Vandu Sarukkam, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the middle of this night, prays to Lord Shiva. He thinks of the Lord's feet, saying, "If you come and remove Paravaiyar's anger, I will be saved. Otherwise, there is nothing else I can do. There is no way for me to be saved." As soon as Sundaramoorthy Swamigal thought of the Lord's feet, the Lord, who cannot bear the suffering of his devotees, appeared to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The 324th verse: "The Lord, who cannot bear the suffering of his devotees, and who would not leave his chosen friend's (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's) wish unfulfilled, appeared before his devotee, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with the marks of bangles and breast prints on his golden, tender, sprout-like hand, and with feet that even Vishnu could not see, touching the ground." The Lord, who cannot bear the suffering of his devotees, would he not fulfill the wish of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, his chosen friend? Certainly not. Therefore, the Lord, who has the marks of bangles and breast prints on his beautiful, tender, sprout-like hand, which is the hand of Kamakshi Ammaiyar, and whose feet even Vishnu could not see, appeared before his devotee, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with those feet touching the ground. The reason for granting such a vision to his devotee, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, is explained in the first part of this verse, which Sekkizhar Peruman has composed as his own statement: "The Lord, who cannot bear the suffering of his devotees, and who would not leave his chosen friend's wish unfulfilled." This part is Sekkizhar Peruman's own poetic statement. The truth that "Sivan knows those who love him" is explained here, as stated in the Gnana Sastras (scriptures of wisdom). Such a Lord, with great compassion, appeared before Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The 325th verse: "Seeing the Lord appear, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, with unbearable joy, trembled in all his limbs, his hair stood on end with ecstasy. Nambi Aaroorar (Sundaramoorthy Swamigal), with his lotus-like hands folded over his head, fell at the red lotus feet of the Lord, the husband of Ambika." Seeing the Lord appear, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was filled with unbearable joy. Due to this unbearable joy, all of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal's limbs trembled, and his hair stood on end with ecstasy. Nambi Aaroorar, with his lotus-like hands folded over his head, fell on the ground at the red lotus feet of the Lord, who has Ambika as a part of him. Now, the Lord speaks to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The 326th verse: "The Lord, seeing his friend who had fallen and praised him with great devotion, asked, 'What is your sorrow?' Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, bowing, explained his plight, saying, 'I am caught in a fault that I myself initiated, and I am suffering. You must still lift me up and save me.'" The Lord, seeing his friend who had fallen and praised him with great devotion, asked, "What is your sorrow?" Would the Lord, who knows all the inner feelings of Nambigal, not know Nambigal's sorrow? However, the Lord asked this for the sake of worldly understanding. When the Lord asked this, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, bowing to the Lord, explained his plight. He said, "Oh, Lord, I am suffering, caught in a fault that I myself initiated. You must still lift me up from that fault and save me. That is your duty." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal asks the Lord to save him from his suffering, which arose from his love for Sangiliyar, the vow he made, and his breaking of that vow, just as the Lord had saved him before.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal further says in the 327th verse: "Oh, Lord, you yourself granted me grace in Thiruvottriyur, and I married Sangili, the woman with beautiful eyes. Paravai, the slender-waisted lady, has learned all this and has decided that if I approach her, she will die. What can I do?" Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says to Lord Shiva, "Oh, Lord, you yourself granted me grace in Thiruvottriyur, and I married Sangili. Paravai has now learned all these things and has decided that if I approach her, she will die. Therefore, I do not know what to do." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal pleads with the Lord, implying that since all this suffering came about due to his grace, it is his duty to resolve it. He further pleads. The 328th verse: "Sundaramoorthy Swamigal said to the Lord, 'Oh, Lord, if I am your servant here, and if you are my Lord, a better friend than a mother, then seeing my distraught and weary state, you must go to Paravai's palace this very night and appease her sulk.'" Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says to the Lord, "Oh, Lord," addressing him as "My Master." He says, "If I am your servant here, and if you are my Lord, a better friend than a mother, then seeing my distraught and weary state, you must go to Paravai's palace this very night and appease her anger." Sundaramoorthy Swamigal says, "If it is true that I am your servant, and if it is true that you are my Lord, a better friend than a mother, and if it is true that you are my Master, and also my friend, then you must appease Paravai's sulk this very night." If I say, "If I am your servant," it is enough, because it will be clear that the Lord is his Master. But why does Sundaramoorthy Swamigal say again, "If it is true that you are my Master"? This is because Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was forcibly stopped and accepted as a servant by the Lord himself. Thus, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal speaks in both ways. Can one plead with the Lord in this way, asking him to appease his wife's anger? The answer is that the Lord is both his Master and his friend.
